text:
Preface
The companion to the course book: the fourteen in-class labs and the eleven assignments, in one place you can search.

title: Business Forecasting — Workbook
text:
How to use it
The labs here are for reading, not running. Code is shown but not executed, so the workbook opens instantly. Each lab links to its executable version, which is the one to open beside your editor when you actually do the work.
Each step carries a collapsible Walkthrough — what was said about that step in class, including the numbers it produces. Open it when you are stuck or want to check your reading of a result; ignore it while you are still working the step out.
Every lab also ends with what your run should produce. Where a model is stochastic your numbers will differ, and several labs are entirely about how much they differ and what that means.
On the suggested time. Each lab opens with one — thirty-five to forty-five minutes. That is the pace of a classroom slot with an instructor on hand, not a target you are being measured against. Alone, expect longer: reading the walkthrough, re-running a cell, and looking something up all cost time that the number does not include. Nothing about this course is graded on speed.

title: Business Forecasting — Workbook

A word on the numbers
Everything in this workbook is generated from the labs, the assignments and the class narration themselves, so a value quoted here cannot disagree with the lab that produced it. Where a number looks surprising, that is usually the point: a good deal of this course is about results that contradict what the method’s reputation would suggest.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Lecture 1 made a claim that sounded like housekeeping: always beat a benchmark first. In the next 35 minutes you are going to test that claim on a real Walmart series, and then watch it fail on a different one.
The business question: you are forecasting weekly HOUSEHOLD-goods demand at store TX_1 to set inventory a year out. Which method should you actually ship?
Suggested time: ~35 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv (run python scripts/prep_m5.py if it is missing).
crumbs: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.2 Setup
Nothing to fill in here — run it and move on.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing, SimpleExpSmoothing, Holt
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    """Find the processed data file whether you render from the repo root or from
    this file's own folder."""
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

weekly = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])

def get_series(store, cat):
    return (weekly[(weekly.store_id == store) & (weekly.cat_id == cat)]
            .set_index("week_start")["units"].sort_index().astype(float))

y = get_series("TX_1", "HOUSEHOLD")

N_TEST = 52
train, test = y.iloc[:-N_TEST], y.iloc[-N_TEST:]
print(f"{len(y)} weeks total — train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}")

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.3 Step 1 — Look at it first
Never fit anything before you have seen the series.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
ax.plot(train.index, train.values, label="train", lw=1.4)
ax.plot(test.index, test.values, label="test (held out)", lw=1.4)
ax.set_ylabel("units / week"); ax.set_title("TX_1 HOUSEHOLD")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout()

Notice: the series roughly doubles over five years, and the level is still moving at the end. Hold that thought — it is the whole lab.







Walkthrough





Never fit anything before you’ve looked at the series. This takes ten seconds and it will save you an hour.
Two things. First, the level roughly doubles across five years — this store’s household aisle is growing, and growing substantially. Second, and this is the one to hold onto: the level is still moving at the end of the training window. It hasn’t flattened out. Whatever we fit has to say something about where the level goes next.
That single observation is the whole lab. Everything that happens in the next twenty minutes is a consequence of the level moving.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.4 Step 2 — Establish the benchmark
Before any model, the thing to beat. Seasonal naive says: this week next year looks like this week last year.

def rmse(actual, pred):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(actual) - np.asarray(pred)) ** 2)))

def mae(actual, pred):
    return float(np.mean(np.abs(np.asarray(actual) - np.asarray(pred))))

seasonal_naive = y.shift(52).iloc[-N_TEST:].values

results = {"Seasonal naive": (rmse(test, seasonal_naive), mae(test, seasonal_naive))}
print(f"Seasonal naive  RMSE {results['Seasonal naive'][0]:,.0f}")

Your turn: before running anything else, write down a number — what RMSE do you think a proper exponential smoothing model will get? You will check it in Step 4.







Walkthrough





Before any model, the thing to beat.
Seasonal naive says: this week next year looks like this week last year. That’s it. One line — y.shift(52). No parameters, no fitting, no estimation.
Seasonal naive  RMSE 973
Nine hundred and seventy-three. Remember that number, because everything from here is measured against it. If a model can’t beat 973, it does not deserve to be in production no matter how sophisticated it is.






Try it






Pause here. Before you run anything else, write down a number — an actual number, on paper or in a comment. What RMSE do you think a proper exponential smoothing model will get on this series?
I’m asking you to commit because in Step 4 you’re going to check it, and the gap between what you expected and what happened is worth more to you than the result itself. Guessing privately and then quietly adjusting is not the same exercise. Write it down. Then come back.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.5 Step 3 — Fit the three models
All three calls come straight from Lecture 1. Run this, then predict the ordering before you look at Step 4 — write your guess down.

# SES — level only.
ses_fit = SimpleExpSmoothing(train).fit()
results["SES"] = (rmse(test, ses_fit.forecast(N_TEST)),
                  mae(test, ses_fit.forecast(N_TEST)))

# Holt — level + trend. Undamped for now; we come back to damping in Step 5.
holt_fit = Holt(train).fit()
results["Holt"] = (rmse(test, holt_fit.forecast(N_TEST)),
                   mae(test, holt_fit.forecast(N_TEST)))

# Holt-Winters — level + trend + seasonality, additive, period 52.
hw_fit = ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add",
                              seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=52).fit()
results["Holt-Winters"] = (rmse(test, hw_fit.forecast(N_TEST)),
                           mae(test, hw_fit.forecast(N_TEST)))







One constraint to respect



Holt-Winters must estimate a seasonal index for each of the 52 weeks, and it needs two full cycles — 104 observations — to initialize. You have 225 training weeks, so you are fine here. You will not always be.









Walkthrough





(Screen: run the three-model cell. It takes a few seconds — Holt-Winters is estimating 52 seasonal indices.)
Three models, three lines, all straight from Lecture 1. SES — level only. No trend, no seasonality. The simplest thing that could work.
Holt — level plus trend. Undamped for now; we come back to that in Step 5, and the fact that I’m flagging it should tell you something. Holt-Winters — level, trend, and seasonality, additive, period 52.
One constraint worth respecting. Holt-Winters estimates a seasonal index for every one of the 52 weeks, and it needs two full cycles — 104 observations — just to initialize. You have 225 training weeks, so you’re fine. You will not always be fine. When you get to a series with three years of weekly data and you’re wondering why Holt-Winters won’t fit, this is why.






Try it






Before you scroll to Step 4: predict the ordering. Which of these three wins, which comes last? Write it down next to your number from Step 2.
Most people rank them by sophistication — Holt-Winters first, because it models the most. See whether you did.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
text:
1.6 Step 4 — Compare honestly

tbl = (pd.DataFrame(results, index=["RMSE", "MAE"]).T
         .sort_values("RMSE").round(0).astype(int))
print(tbl.to_string())

Stop before reading on: did any model beat the benchmark? By how much? And was it the model you expected in Step 2?
In the room: say your answer to the person next to you, and make them say theirs.
On your own: score yourself against what you already wrote down. Scroll back to the RMSE number from Step 2 and the ordering from Step 3, and write two lines in a comment:
# guess ____, actual ____, off by ____
# ordering: right / wrong — first model I misplaced was ____
Grading your own prediction in writing is the part that matters. It is what makes the next result inform you rather than just agree with you.







Walkthrough





                RMSE   MAE
SES              427   352
Holt-Winters     885   814
Seasonal naive   973   848
Holt            1166  1029
Read that from the bottom.
Holt is last. Eleven sixty-six. Worse than the benchmark — worse than shifting the series back a year and calling it a day. Holt is the model that adds a trend to SES, and this series has an obvious trend. It should have helped. It made things twenty percent worse than doing nothing.
Holt-Winters is third. Eight eighty-five. It beats the benchmark, but only just, and it loses badly to a model with no trend and no seasonality in it at all. This is the most sophisticated thing on the table and it’s mid.
SES wins, and it isn’t close. Four twenty-seven against a benchmark of 973 — less than half the error. The simplest model on the list, the one that only tracks the level, beat everything.
Now compare that to what you wrote down. If you predicted Holt-Winters would win because it models the most structure, you are in good company and you have just learned the most useful thing in this lab: more structure is not more accuracy. Every parameter Holt-Winters estimates is a parameter that can be estimated badly, and 52 seasonal indices from 225 observations is a lot of estimating.






Try it






Pause and answer these in the discussion thread for Week 1:

Did any model beat the benchmark, and by how much?
Was the winner the model you predicted in Step 3?
Holt is worse than doing nothing. Before you watch Step 5 — what’s your hypothesis for why?

Post before you continue. The next step gives away the answer to number three, and the guess is worth more than the answer.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
section: 1.7 Step 5 — Break it, then fix it
text:
1.7 Step 5 — Break it, then fix it
Look at where Holt’s forecast goes.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
ax.plot(test.index, test.values, label="actual", lw=1.6)
ax.plot(test.index, ses_fit.forecast(N_TEST), label="SES", ls="--")
ax.plot(test.index, holt_fit.forecast(N_TEST), label="Holt (undamped)", ls="--")
ax.set_ylabel("units / week"); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout()

Lecture 1 warned that undamped linear extrapolation gets unrealistic past about six periods. You are forecasting 52.
Your turn: refit Holt with a damped trend and add it to the table. One keyword argument.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in the one keyword argument ----
# holt_damped = Holt(train, ___).fit()             # <- damped_trend=True
#
# results["Holt (damped)"] = (rmse(test, holt_damped.forecast(N_TEST)),
#                             mae(test, holt_damped.forecast(N_TEST)))
#
# print(pd.DataFrame(results, index=["RMSE", "MAE"]).T
#         .sort_values("RMSE").round(0).astype(int).to_string())
# print(f"estimated phi: {holt_damped.params['damping_trend']:.3f}")

Report the value of \(\phi\). What does it mean that it came out below 1?







Walkthrough





Here’s what went wrong. Look at where Holt’s forecast goes.
That’s a straight line, and it does not stop. Holt estimated a positive trend from the training data — correctly, the series was growing — and then extrapolated it linearly for fifty-two consecutive weeks. By the end of the horizon it’s forecasting a level the store has never reached.
Lecture 1 warned that undamped linear extrapolation stops being credible after about six periods. You are forecasting fifty-two. The model isn’t wrong about the trend; it’s wrong about the trend continuing forever.
Meanwhile SES, the dashed flat line, just says “about here” — and about-here turns out to be a much better guess than a confident straight line pointed at the ceiling.






Try it






Your turn, and it’s genuinely one keyword argument. Uncomment the block and fill in the blank:
holt_damped = Holt(train, damped_trend=True).fit()
That’s the fix. Add it to the table, print the result, and print the estimated phi. Pause here and do it — it’s thirty seconds of typing and you’ll remember it because you typed it.
Holt (damped)    426   351
SES              427   352
Phi comes out at 0.800. Two things here, and the second one is the honest one.
First: damping rescued the model completely. Eleven sixty-six down to four twenty-six. Same model, same data, same trend estimate — one parameter that says “the trend decays as you forecast further out” moved it from worst on the table to best. Phi of 0.8 means each step ahead gets eighty percent of the previous step’s trend, so the forecast bends toward flat instead of running off. That is what phi below 1 means, and it’s the answer to the question in the lab.
Second — and don’t let this slide past — damped Holt beat SES by one unit of RMSE. Four twenty-six against four twenty-seven. That is not a win. On a different held-out year it could easily flip. If you report “the damped model is best” you’re reporting noise as a finding.
What actually happened is that damped Holt and SES are the same answer arrived at two ways. Damping the trend hard enough is close to not having a trend. The honest summary is: on this series, models that keep the forecast near the current level beat models that extrapolate, and the two ways of doing that tie.

title: 1  Lab 1: Benchmarks and Exponential Smoothing
section: 1.8 Step 6 — Same store. Different aisle. Opposite answer.
text:
1.8 Step 6 — Same store. Different aisle. Opposite answer.
Change one word — HOUSEHOLD becomes FOODS. Same store, same code, same horizon.

y2 = get_series("TX_1", "FOODS")
train2, test2 = y2.iloc[:-N_TEST], y2.iloc[-N_TEST:]

sn2 = y2.shift(52).iloc[-N_TEST:].values
ses2 = SimpleExpSmoothing(train2).fit()

print(f"TX_1 FOODS   seasonal naive RMSE {rmse(test2, sn2):,.0f}")
print(f"TX_1 FOODS   SES            RMSE {rmse(test2, ses2.forecast(N_TEST)):,.0f}")

Notice: the ranking flips. On the household aisle an exponential smoother won comfortably. On the food aisle of the same store, the benchmark wins and SES is about 13% worse.
The reason is visible in one number. For TX_1 HOUSEHOLD the test year sits about 15% above the year before it, so seasonal naive carries a stale level forward and loses badly. For TX_1 FOODS the level barely moves — about 1.5% down — and last year is an excellent guess.
So it is not the store, and it is not the method. It is whether the level moved.







Walkthrough





Change one word. HOUSEHOLD becomes FOODS. Same store, same code, same horizon, same fifty-two weeks held out.
TX_1 FOODS   seasonal naive RMSE 1308
TX_1 FOODS   SES            RMSE 1474
The ranking flips.
On the household aisle, SES beat the benchmark by more than half. On the food aisle of the same store, the benchmark wins and SES is about thirteen percent worse. Nothing changed except which shelf we’re looking at.
So what’s different? It isn’t the store. It isn’t the method — the code is character-for-character identical apart from one string.
It’s visible in one number. For household, the test year sits about fifteen percent above the year before it. The level moved, so seasonal naive carried a stale level forward and lost badly — and a method that tracks the level won.
For foods, the level barely moved — about one and a half percent down. When the level doesn’t move, last year is an excellent guess, and there’s nothing for a level-tracking model to add. It is not the store, and it is not the method. It is whether the level moved.
That’s the sentence to leave with. And notice what it does to the claim we opened with — “always beat a benchmark first” isn’t process hygiene. It’s the only thing that told us the answer was different on these two series. If you’d fit SES on household, seen it win, and rolled it out across the store, you’d have shipped a model that’s thirteen percent worse than doing nothing on the food aisle, and nothing in your workflow would have told you.

text:
1.9 Before you leave

Discuss: You now have two series where the best method is different. You are responsible for all 30 series in this dataset and you have to pick one approach to run in production every month.
What do you actually do — and what would you need to measure to decide? “Fit everything and pick the winner per series” is an answer, but say what it costs you.


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough











Try it






Here’s the question, and it’s the one that shows up in your job rather than in your homework.
You now have two series where the best method is different. You are responsible for all thirty series in this dataset, and you have to pick one approach to run in production every month. What do you actually do — and what would you need to measure to decide?
“Fit everything and pick the winner per series” is a legitimate answer. But say what it costs you: thirty model selections a month, each one a chance to overfit the held-out year; a pipeline that can silently switch methods between runs; and no single story to tell the person who asks why the forecast changed.
Post your answer in the Week 1 thread before the next lecture. Two or three sentences. There isn’t a key for this one — I want to see how you reason about it, and we’ll pick it up in Lecture 2 when the methods get more complicated and the temptation gets worse. Solutions for the coded parts go up on Canvas after the deadline. See you in Lecture 2.

title: 2  Lab 2: Stationarity, ARIMA, and Granger Causality
text:
2.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Lecture 2 gave you a rule — test for stationarity before you read an ACF — and a caveat: Granger causality is not structural causality. In the next 35 minutes you will do both, on data where each one actually bites.
The business question: you are forecasting weekly HOUSEHOLD demand at store CA_1, and you want to know whether watching the food aisle helps you predict it. Then, in Step 6, you run the same test on the macro question from the lecture slide — does unemployment predict retail sales? — and find that the answer depends on which years you include.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels, and two prepared files: data/processed/m5_weekly.csv (prep_m5.py) and data/processed/fred_monthly.csv (prep_fred.py).

title: 2  Lab 2: Stationarity, ARIMA, and Granger Causality
text:
2.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, grangercausalitytests
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
import io
from contextlib import redirect_stdout

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    """Find the processed data file whether you render from the repo root or from
    this file's own folder."""
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run the matching prep script from the repository root first: "
        "`prep_m5.py` for m5_*.csv, `prep_fred.py` for fred_monthly.csv."
    )

weekly = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])

def get_series(store, cat):
    return (weekly[(weekly.store_id == store) & (weekly.cat_id == cat)]
            .set_index("week_start")["units"].sort_index().astype(float))

y = get_series("CA_1", "HOUSEHOLD")
N_TEST = 52
train, test = y.iloc[:-N_TEST], y.iloc[-N_TEST:]
print(f"{len(y)} weeks — train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}")








Walkthrough





Same pattern as Lab 1 — imports, a path helper, a series accessor, a split.
277 weeks — train 225, test 52
Same store dataset, different store and same category as Lab 1: CA_1 household. Fifty-two weeks held out.
The one new import worth noticing is redirect_stdout from contextlib, and io. That’s not statistics — that’s damage control, and I’ll show you why in Step 5.

title: 2  Lab 2: Stationarity, ARIMA, and Granger Causality
text:
2.3 Step 1 — Look, then test

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.2))
ax.plot(y.index, y.values, lw=1.3)
ax.set_title("CA_1 HOUSEHOLD — weekly units"); plt.tight_layout()

Notice: the level wanders. Your eye says non-stationary. Now make the test agree.

def report_adf(series, label):
    stat, p, lags, nobs, crit, _ = adfuller(series.dropna(), autolag="AIC")
    print(f"{label:<28} ADF {stat:>7.2f}   p {p:>6.3f}   lags {lags:>2}   "
          f"{'stationary' if p < 0.05 else 'UNIT ROOT'}")

report_adf(y, "levels")

Now difference it and re-test.

dy = y.diff().dropna()
report_adf(dy, "first difference")

You should see the statistic move decisively. Write down both numbers — you will be asked to justify a choice of \(d\) in the homework, and this is what a clean case looks like.







Walkthrough





Look first. Always look first.
The level wanders. It drifts up, it drifts back, there’s no fixed value it returns to. Your eye says non-stationary. Now make the test agree — because your eye is not evidence you can put in a report.
levels                       ADF   -1.33   p  0.614   lags 12   UNIT ROOT
first difference             ADF   -5.00   p  0.000   lags 11   stationary
Read those two lines carefully, because this is what a clean case looks like and you want it in your memory for comparison later.
In levels: ADF statistic minus one point three three, p-value point six one. Nowhere near significance. We fail to reject the null of a unit root — the series is non-stationary, exactly as your eye said. First difference: minus five point zero zero, p-value effectively zero. Decisive. One difference was enough.
That tells you d equals one, and you now have an evidence trail for that choice rather than a hunch. You’ll be asked to justify a d in the homework. This is what the justification looks like.

title: 2  Lab 2: Stationarity, ARIMA, and Granger Causality
section: 2.4 Step 2 — Now you are allowed to read the ACF
text:
2.4 Step 2 — Now you are allowed to read the ACF
Lecture 2’s rule: the ACF of a non-stationary series decays slowly no matter what the underlying process is. Run both and see it.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
plot_acf(y, lags=30, ax=axes[0,0]);  axes[0,0].set_title("ACF — levels (uninformative)")
plot_pacf(y, lags=30, ax=axes[0,1]); axes[0,1].set_title("PACF — levels")
plot_acf(dy, lags=30, ax=axes[1,0]);  axes[1,0].set_title("ACF — differenced")
plot_pacf(dy, lags=30, ax=axes[1,1]); axes[1,1].set_title("PACF — differenced")
plt.tight_layout()

Compare the top row against the bottom. The top ACF crawls down — that is the signature of an undifferenced series, and it tells you nothing about \(p\) or \(q\). The bottom row is interpretable.
Your turn: using the bottom row and the four reference patterns from Lecture 2, propose a \((p, d, q)\).
In the room: say your proposed order out loud to a classmate and defend it in one sentence.
On your own: type it into a comment before you fit anything, in this form:
# (p, d, q) = (_, _, _) — PACF cuts off after lag ____, ACF cuts off after lag ____
Naming the lag that decided each term is what turns a guess into a reading you can be wrong about — and being wrong about a specific lag is something you can learn from.
Either way the point is committing to an order before you see how it scores.







Walkthrough





Four panels. Top row is the raw series, bottom row is differenced.
Look at the top ACF. It crawls down — a long slow decay, bar after bar, staying well above the significance band for twenty-plus lags.
Here’s the trap. That pattern looks like enormously strong autocorrelation, and a reasonable person reads it as “there’s a lot of structure here to model.” It isn’t. That slow decay is the signature of an undifferenced series, and it appears no matter what the underlying process is. A random walk produces it. An AR(1) with a unit root produces it. White noise plus a trend produces it. It tells you nothing about p or q. It tells you only that you skipped a step.
Now the bottom row, after differencing. That is interpretable. The bars drop into the band quickly and you can actually read structure off it.






Try it






Pause the video. Using the bottom row and the four reference patterns from Lecture 2, propose a .
Write it down before you continue, and write down why — which panel, which lags. Then post it in the Week 2 thread. I want to see the range of proposals, because there genuinely is one, and that’s part of the lesson.

section: 2.6 Step 4 — Break it: the horizon trap
text:
2.6 Step 4 — Break it: the horizon trap
Now the same model, evaluated a different way.

errs = []
vals = y.values
for i in range(104, len(vals) - 1):
    m = ARIMA(vals[:i+1], order=order).fit()
    errs.append(vals[i+1] - float(m.forecast(1)[0]))

wf = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.array(errs) ** 2)))
print(f"walk-forward 1-step RMSE : {wf:,.0f}   ({len(errs)} origins)")
print(f"single-split 52-step RMSE: {rmse:,.0f}")

Notice how much smaller the walk-forward number is. It is tempting to quote it — it makes your model look better.
Do not. They answer different questions. One-step-ahead, knowing everything up to last week, is a fundamentally easier problem than forecasting a year out from a fixed origin. If a planner is ordering inventory twelve months ahead, the 52-step number is the honest one.







Walkthrough





Same model. Different evaluation. Watch what happens to the number.
walk-forward 1-step RMSE : 352   (172 origins)
single-split 52-step RMSE: 569
Three fifty-two against five sixty-nine. The walk-forward number is nearly forty percent smaller, and it is computed from a hundred and seventy-two separate forecasts instead of one — so it even looks more rigorous. More origins, more evaluation, smaller error. It is enormously tempting to quote it. Do not.
They are not two estimates of the same thing. They answer different questions. One-step-ahead — knowing everything up to last week, forecasting next week — is a fundamentally easier problem than standing at a fixed origin and forecasting fifty-two weeks out. Of course the error is smaller. It would be alarming if it weren’t.
The question is which one matches the decision. If a planner is ordering inventory twelve months ahead, the 52-step number is the honest one, and quoting 352 to that person is not optimistic — it’s wrong.
This is the most common way I see forecast accuracy overstated in practice, and almost nobody does it dishonestly. They compute the number that’s easy to compute, and it happens to be the flattering one.

text:
2.7 Step 5 — Granger causality, and the trap in it
Does the food aisle help predict the household aisle?
grangercausalitytests prints four test variants for every lag up to maxlag — a wall of output you did not ask for. The helper below silences it and pulls out the single F-test.

food = get_series("CA_1", "FOODS")

pair = pd.concat([y.rename("household"), food.rename("food")], axis=1).diff().dropna()

def granger(effect, cause, lag=4):
    """F-test for: do lags of `cause` help predict `effect`?"""
    with redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):        # statsmodels prints 4 variants per lag
        res = grangercausalitytests(pair[[effect, cause]], maxlag=lag)
    F, p = res[lag][0]["ssr_ftest"][0], res[lag][0]["ssr_ftest"][1]
    verdict = "significant" if p < 0.05 else "not significant"
    print(f"{cause:>10} -> {effect:<10}  F = {F:5.2f}   p = {p:.4f}   {verdict}")

granger("household", "food")

Note the argument order: the second argument is the candidate cause. Getting this backwards is the single most common mistake with this function.
Your turn: run the other direction and report both F-statistics.

# ---- your turn: uncomment, then swap the two arguments ----
# granger(___, ___)








Walkthrough





Does the food aisle help predict the household aisle?
First, the practical note. grangercausalitytests prints four test variants for every lag up to maxlag — for lag 4, that’s a screen and a half of output nobody asked for. The helper swallows it with redirect_stdout and pulls out the single F-test we want. That’s what those imports were for.
      food -> household  F =  3.83   p = 0.0048   significant
Now the argument order, and please write this down: the second argument is the candidate cause. granger("household", "food") asks whether food helps predict household. Getting this backwards is the single most common mistake with this function, and it is silent — you get a perfectly reasonable-looking result to the wrong question.






Try it






Your turn. Run the other direction and report both F-statistics. It’s one line — uncomment and swap the arguments.
 household -> food        F =  2.80   p = 0.0263   significant
Both directions are significant. Food predicts household, and household predicts food.
Sit with how strange that is. Household goods do not cause groceries. Groceries do not cause household goods. Nobody buys paper towels because they bought bananas. And yet the test says each helps predict the other, at conventional significance, in both directions. We’ll come back to what’s generating that. Hold the question.

text:
2.8 Step 6 — The same test on macro data, and why the sample matters
Step 5 used two aisles of one store. Now the question from the lecture slide: does unemployment Granger-cause retail sales?
Run python scripts/prep_fred.py once before class — it caches three FRED series to data/processed/fred_monthly.csv, so this step needs no network and no API key.

fred = pd.read_csv(data_path("fred_monthly.csv"), parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")

# Both series are already stationary transforms:
#   retail_growth = monthly % change in retail sales (log-differenced)
#   unrate_diff   = monthly change in the unemployment rate
macro = fred[["retail_growth", "unrate_diff"]].dropna()

def granger_macro(effect, cause, data, lag=4):
    with redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
        res = grangercausalitytests(data[[effect, cause]], maxlag=lag)
    F, p = res[lag][0]["ssr_ftest"][0], res[lag][0]["ssr_ftest"][1]
    print(f"  {cause:>12} -> {effect:<14} F = {F:6.2f}   p = {p:.4f}"
          f"   {'significant' if p < 0.05 else 'NOT significant'}")

print(f"Full sample: {macro.index.min():%Y-%m} to {macro.index.max():%Y-%m} ({len(macro)} months)")
granger_macro("retail_growth", "unrate_diff", macro)
granger_macro("unrate_diff", "retail_growth", macro)

Both directions are significant, and unemployment looks like the stronger driver. That matches the story everyone expects: people lose jobs, people stop spending.
Now drop the COVID window and run it again.

ex_covid = macro[(macro.index < "2020-02-01") | (macro.index > "2021-06-01")]

print(f"Excluding Feb 2020 - Jun 2021 ({len(ex_covid)} months)")
granger_macro("retail_growth", "unrate_diff", ex_covid)
granger_macro("unrate_diff", "retail_growth", ex_covid)

Your turn: restrict the sample to everything before February 2020 and run both directions once more.

# pre_covid = macro[___]                     # <- rows with index < "2020-02-01"
#
# granger_macro("retail_growth", "unrate_diff", pre_covid)
# granger_macro("unrate_diff", "retail_growth", pre_covid)








Walkthrough





Now the question from the lecture slide, on real macro data. Does unemployment Granger-cause retail sales?
Both series arrive already stationary — retail growth is log-differenced monthly percent change, unemployment is the monthly change in the rate. So we can test directly.
Full sample: 1992-02 to 2026-06 (412 months)
   unrate_diff -> retail_growth   F =  18.22   p = 0.0000   significant
 retail_growth -> unrate_diff     F =  12.80   p = 0.0000   significant
Both directions significant, and unemployment is the stronger of the two — F of eighteen against thirteen. That matches the story everybody expects. People lose jobs, people stop spending. You could write that paragraph without running anything, which is exactly why you should be suspicious of how satisfying it is.
Now drop the COVID window.
Excluding Feb 2020 - Jun 2021 (395 months)
   unrate_diff -> retail_growth   F =   2.91   p = 0.0214   significant
 retail_growth -> unrate_diff     F =   6.74   p = 0.0000   significant
Seventeen months removed out of four hundred and twelve — four percent of the sample. The unemployment-to-retail F-statistic falls from 18.22 to 2.91. It’s still significant, barely, but it has lost about six-sevenths of its strength. The reverse direction went from 12.80 to 6.74. Weaker, but still overwhelming.






Try it






Your turn. Restrict to everything before February 2020 — no COVID period at all, no recovery either — and run both directions.
Pre-COVID, before Feb 2020 (336 months)
   unrate_diff -> retail_growth   F =   1.85   p = 0.1196   NOT significant
 retail_growth -> unrate_diff     F =   9.67   p = 0.0000   significant
Eighteen point two two. Two point nine one. One point eight five.
On twenty-eight years of pre-pandemic data, unemployment does not Granger-cause retail sales. The intuitive direction — the one everybody expects, the one that has a mechanism, the one you’d put in a slide without checking — is gone.
And the direction nobody leads with, retail predicting unemployment, survives every single cut: 12.80, then 6.74, then 9.67. Never above a p-value of point zero zero zero one.

2.9 Before you leave
You should have found, in Step 5, that the relationship runs both ways, at least in part.

Discuss (Step 5): Household goods do not cause groceries, and groceries do not cause household goods. So what is generating a two-way predictive relationship between two aisles of the same store?
And the question that matters commercially: given what you found, is there anything a planner is entitled to do with it? Name one legitimate use and one thing they must not conclude.

In Step 6 the intuitive direction — unemployment driving retail — is strong on the full sample, weak once COVID is removed, and gone entirely before 2020. The reverse direction survives every cut.

Discuss (Step 6): One analyst runs the full sample and reports that unemployment predicts retail sales. Another runs 1992–2019 and reports it does not. Neither has made an error.
What actually happened here — and what does it tell you about a Granger result computed on a sample containing one enormous shared shock?
Retail sales are a coincident-to-leading indicator and unemployment is a lagging one. Does that help explain which direction survived?


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough





Two questions, and I want both in the Week 2 thread before Lecture 3.






Try it






First, the aisles. You found a two-way relationship between household goods and groceries. Neither causes the other. So what is generating it?
And the commercial half, which is the one that matters: given what you found, is there anything a planner is entitled to do with it? Name one legitimate use and one thing they must not conclude.






Try it






Second, the macro result. One analyst runs the full sample and reports that unemployment predicts retail sales. Another runs 1992 to 2019 and reports that it does not.
Neither of them has made an error. Both ran the correct test, correctly, on a defensible sample. That’s what makes this worth twenty minutes of your attention rather than being a cautionary tale about sloppy work.
What actually happened — and what does it tell you about a Granger result computed on a sample containing one enormous shared shock?
One hint worth using: retail sales are a coincident-to-leading indicator, and unemployment is a lagging one. Firms cut hours and stop hiring after demand falls, not before. Does that help explain which direction survived every cut?

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
text:
3.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Lecture 3 made a claim: a GAM earns its keep when a series has several cycles running at once, because each one gets its own smooth term and you can still read the model.
Retail sales cannot show you that — they have essentially one season. So today we leave M5 and use electricity demand, which has three large cycles simultaneously, and an annual shape that will break the first model we try.
The business question: you are forecasting daily demand for a grid operator. Being wrong is expensive in both directions — under-forecast and you buy power at spot prices, over-forecast and you have paid to keep generation spinning for nothing.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, prophet, pygam, and data/processed/electricity_daily.csv + electricity_hourly.csv (run python scripts/prep_electricity.py once).

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
text:
3.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
logging.getLogger('cmdstanpy').setLevel(logging.ERROR)   # Prophet is chatty; silence it

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    """Find the processed data file whether you render from the repo root or from
    this file's own folder."""
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_electricity.py` from the repository root first."
    )

daily = pd.read_csv(data_path("electricity_daily.csv"), parse_dates=["date"])
hourly = pd.read_csv(data_path("electricity_hourly.csv"), parse_dates=["datetime"])

# Five and a half years is plenty of yearly cycles and keeps every fit under a second.
daily = daily[daily.date >= "2013-01-01"].reset_index(drop=True)

SPLIT = "2017-08-01"
train, test = daily[daily.date < SPLIT], daily[daily.date >= SPLIT]

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))
mae  = lambda a, b: float(np.mean(np.abs(np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b))))
results = {}

print(f"{len(daily)} days — train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}")
print(f"test window: {test.date.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {test.date.max():%Y-%m-%d}")








Walkthrough





2041 days — train 1673, test 368
test window: 2017-08-01 to 2018-08-03
Two notes. We trim to 2013 onward — five and a half years, which is plenty of annual cycles and keeps every fit under a second, because you’re going to fit several. And we hold out just over a year, August 2017 through August 2018, so the test window contains a full summer and a full winter. That’s deliberate. Holding out only six months of an annual cycle tells you almost nothing.
The logging line silences Prophet, which is otherwise extremely chatty on every fit.

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
text:
3.3 Step 1 — Three cycles, one series
Before any model, look at the three periodicities separately.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))

hourly.groupby("hour").mw.mean().plot(ax=axes[0], marker="o", ms=3)
axes[0].set_title("hour of day"); axes[0].set_xlabel("hour")

daily.groupby("dow").mw_mean.mean().plot(ax=axes[1], marker="o", ms=4)
axes[1].set_title("day of week (0=Mon)"); axes[1].set_xlabel("")

daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean().rolling(7, center=True).mean().plot(ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("day of year (7d smoothed)"); axes[2].set_xlabel("")

for a in axes: a.set_ylabel("MW")
plt.tight_layout()


for label, g in [("hour of day", hourly.groupby("hour").mw.mean()),
                 ("day of week", daily.groupby("dow").mw_mean.mean()),
                 ("day of year", daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean())]:
    swing = 100 * (g.max() - g.min()) / g.mean()
    print(f"{label:<14} swing {swing:5.1f}%   min {g.idxmin():>3}   max {g.idxmax():>3}")

Notice: all three cycles are large — none is a rounding error you could ignore. This is the situation Lecture 3 said GAMs are for.







Walkthrough





Before any model, look at the three periodicities separately.
Hour of day: demand bottoms out around four in the morning and peaks in the early evening, around hour nineteen. People wake up, go to work, come home, turn things on. Day of week: Monday highest, Sunday lowest. Commercial and industrial load.
Day of year: and this one is a strange shape, which is the whole point of Step 2.
hour of day    swing  33.3%   min   4   max  19
day of week    swing  11.6%   min   6   max   1
day of year    swing  44.7%   min 116   max 200
All three are large. The annual swing is forty-five percent of mean demand, the daily swing is thirty-three percent, and even the weakest — day of week — is nearly twelve percent. None of these is a rounding error you could ignore and still have a usable forecast.
That is the situation Lecture 3 said GAMs are for. Not one dominant season with noise around it. Three real cycles, all worth modeling, all on different time scales.

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
section: 3.4 Step 2 — The annual cycle has two peaks
text:
3.4 Step 2 — The annual cycle has two peaks
Look again at the third panel. It does not look like a wave.

doy = daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean()
print(f"January  (days 1-31)    {doy.loc[1:31].mean():,.0f} MW   <- heating")
print(f"April    (days 95-115)  {doy.loc[95:115].mean():,.0f} MW   <- mild, nothing running")
print(f"July     (days 180-200) {doy.loc[180:200].mean():,.0f} MW   <- air conditioning")

Two peaks and two troughs per year, because heating and cooling are both electricity demand and they happen at opposite ends of the calendar.
Now the consequence. Fit the annual shape with a single sine wave, then with two.

t = np.arange(len(doy))
one = np.c_[np.ones_like(t), np.sin(2*np.pi*t/365), np.cos(2*np.pi*t/365)]
two = np.c_[one,             np.sin(4*np.pi*t/365), np.cos(4*np.pi*t/365)]

for label, X in [("one harmonic", one), ("two harmonics", two)]:
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, doy.values, rcond=None)
    print(f"{label:<15} in-sample RMSE {rmse(doy.values, X @ beta):,.0f} MW")

This is the whole argument for a flexible term. One harmonic can put its peak in summer or in winter — not both. Adding the second harmonic (a cycle that repeats twice a year) cuts the error by about a factor of two and a half.
Prophet’s yearly_seasonality is exactly this idea with more terms: a Fourier series of order 10 by default, so 10 sine/cosine pairs. A pyGAM spline gets there differently — by bending freely — but solves the same problem.







Walkthrough





Look at that annual panel again. It does not look like a wave. It looks like a letter M.
January  (days 1-31)     34,403 MW   <- heating
April    (days 95-115)   26,945 MW   <- mild, nothing running
July     (days 180-200)  37,043 MW   <- air conditioning
There it is. High in January, low in April, high again in July. Two peaks and two troughs per year — because heating and cooling are both electricity demand, and they happen at opposite ends of the calendar. April is the month when nobody needs either.
Now the consequence, and this is the argument for the whole lecture. Fit that annual shape with a single sine wave. Then with two.
one harmonic     in-sample RMSE 3,428 MW
two harmonics    in-sample RMSE 1,348 MW
A single sine wave has one peak per cycle. It can put that peak in summer or in winter — it cannot do both. Whichever it picks, it is badly wrong for half the year. Three thousand four hundred megawatts of error on a series averaging around thirty thousand.
Add a second harmonic — a cycle that repeats twice a year — and the error drops to thirteen forty-eight. Two and a half times better, from one extra pair of terms, because that second harmonic is exactly the shape the physics needs.
That’s the mechanism. Prophet’s yearly_seasonality is this idea with more terms — a Fourier series of order ten by default, so ten sine-cosine pairs. A pyGAM spline gets there differently, by bending freely rather than by summing waves, but it’s solving the same problem: the annual shape is not a wave, so don’t fit it with one.
crumbs: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
section: 3.5 Step 3 — Prophet, and an honest benchmark
text:
3.5 Step 3 — Prophet, and an honest benchmark
Prophet wants two columns named ds and y. That is most of the API.

from prophet import Prophet

# Benchmark first, always: same day last year (364 days keeps the weekday aligned).
lookup = daily.set_index("date").mw_mean
sn = [lookup.get(t - pd.Timedelta(days=364), np.nan) for t in test.date]
results["Seasonal naive (364d)"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, sn), mae(test.mw_mean, sn))

m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True, daily_seasonality=False)
m.fit(train.rename(columns={"date": "ds", "mw_mean": "y"})[["ds", "y"]])

fc = m.predict(test.rename(columns={"date": "ds"})[["ds"]])
results["Prophet"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, fc.yhat), mae(test.mw_mean, fc.yhat))

for k, (r, a) in results.items():
    print(f"{k:<24} RMSE {r:7,.0f}   MAE {a:7,.0f}")

We turned daily_seasonality off deliberately — the data is one row per day, so there is no within-day variation left to model. Leave it on and Prophet will happily fit noise.







Walkthrough





Prophet wants two columns named ds and y. That is genuinely most of the API.
But benchmark first — always. Same day last year, and note it’s 364 days rather than 365, which keeps the weekday aligned. Comparing a Tuesday to a Wednesday would hand the benchmark an error that isn’t really about seasonality.
Seasonal naive (364d)    RMSE   4,608   MAE   3,333
Prophet                  RMSE   3,935   MAE   3,001
Prophet beats the benchmark — about fifteen percent better on RMSE.
One deliberate choice: daily_seasonality=False. The data is one row per day, so there is no within-day variation left to model. Leave it on and Prophet will happily fit a daily cycle to noise, and report it to you with a straight face.

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
text:
3.6 Step 4 — The components plot
This is the payoff, and the reason Prophet gets used by people who will be questioned about their forecast.

m.plot_components(fc);

Three panels, one per additive term, each on the scale of the original series. The trend, the weekly cycle, the yearly cycle — separately readable.
Notice the yearly panel reproduces the double peak from Step 2. Nobody told Prophet about heating and cooling; the Fourier series had enough terms to find the shape.







Walkthrough





(Screen: run m.plot_components(fc).)
This is the payoff, and it’s why Prophet gets used by people who have to defend a forecast in a meeting.
Three panels, one per additive term, each on the scale of the original series. The trend. The weekly cycle. The yearly cycle. Separately readable, and each one is a sentence you can say to a non-technical person: “demand is drifting down slightly, Mondays run about a thousand megawatts above Sundays, and there are two annual peaks.”
And look at the yearly panel — it reproduces the double peak from Step 2. Nobody told Prophet about heating and cooling. Nobody coded a January term and a July term. The Fourier series simply had enough flexibility to find the shape that was in the data.
That combination — flexible enough to find it, structured enough to show you what it found — is the entire case for additive models.

# fc1 = m1.predict(test.rename(columns={"date": "ds"})[["ds"]])
# results["Prophet (yearly order=1)"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, fc1.yhat),
#                                        mae(test.mw_mean, fc1.yhat))
#
# print(f"single harmonic RMSE {rmse(test.mw_mean, fc1.yhat):,.0f}")

Report both numbers. Does the holdout agree with what Step 2 predicted in-sample?







Walkthrough





Step 2 made this argument in-sample, on the averaged annual profile. That’s suggestive, not evidence. Test it properly, on the holdout. yearly_seasonality takes an integer — the Fourier order — instead of True.






Try it






Pause here. Fit a Prophet with the yearly order forced to 1 — a single harmonic — and add it to the results table. Everything else stays the same.
single harmonic RMSE 4,269
Four thousand two hundred and sixty-nine, against three thousand nine hundred and thirty-five for the full-order model. The holdout agrees with Step 2 — crippling the annual term costs you real accuracy out of sample, not just in-sample fit.
But look where it lands relative to the benchmark. Seasonal naive was 4,608. The single-harmonic Prophet is 4,269 — it beats the benchmark by about seven percent, and that is all it beats it by.
And here’s the part worth stopping on. On MAE, it loses to the benchmark outright — 3,358 against 3,333. Same two models, same holdout, opposite verdict depending on which error measure you quote.
That is not a trick and it is not a bug. RMSE squares errors, so it punishes the occasional large miss; MAE treats all errors proportionally. A model can be better on one and worse on the other, and when a ranking flips between them the honest move is to say so rather than to quote the metric that flatters you.

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
section: 3.8 Step 6 — pyGAM, and reading the smooth directly
text:
3.8 Step 6 — pyGAM, and reading the smooth directly
Prophet is a GAM with the time-series decisions made for you. pyGAM makes you state the terms, which is more work and more control.

from pygam import LinearGAM, s, f

# s(0) = cyclic spline on day-of-year (basis="cp" makes Dec 31 join Jan 1)
# f(1) = day-of-week as a categorical factor
X_tr, X_te = train[["doy", "dow"]].values, test[["doy", "dow"]].values

gam = LinearGAM(s(0, n_splines=20, basis="cp") + f(1)).fit(X_tr, train.mw_mean.values)
results["pyGAM (doy + dow)"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, gam.predict(X_te)),
                                mae(test.mw_mean, gam.predict(X_te)))

print(f"effective degrees of freedom: {gam.statistics_['edof']:.1f}")
print(pd.DataFrame(results, index=["RMSE", "MAE"]).T
        .sort_values("RMSE").round(0).astype(int).to_string())

Now the partial dependence — the GAM equivalent of the components plot.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
for i, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["day of year", "day of week"])):
    XX = gam.generate_X_grid(term=i)
    pdep, ci = gam.partial_dependence(term=i, X=XX, width=0.95)
    ax.plot(XX[:, i], pdep)
    ax.plot(XX[:, i], ci, c="grey", ls="--", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_ylabel("effect on MW")
plt.tight_layout()

Read the left panel and say what it means in words, the way you would to a grid operator. The confidence band widens where the data is thin — say that too.







Walkthrough





Prophet is a GAM with the time-series decisions already made for you. pyGAM makes you state the terms yourself — more work, more control.
Two terms only. A cyclic spline on day-of-year — basis="cp" is what makes December 31st join back up with January 1st, so the smooth doesn’t have a discontinuity at the year boundary — and day-of-week as a categorical factor. That’s it. No trend term. No hourly anything.
effective degrees of freedom: 22.5

                          RMSE    MAE
pyGAM (doy + dow)         3444   2550
Prophet                   3935   3001
Prophet (yearly order=1)  4269   3358
Seasonal naive (364d)     4608   3333
Every model beat the benchmark. The single-harmonic Prophet is the worst of the three, as Step 2 predicted.
And pyGAM wins. Thirty-four forty-four against Prophet’s thirty-nine thirty-five — about twelve percent better, on both RMSE and MAE, using two terms against Prophet’s three, with no trend component at all. That should bother you slightly, and we’ll come back to it in the closing question.
Now the partial dependence — the GAM equivalent of the components plot.
Say what the left panel means in words, the way you’d say it to a grid operator: demand is high in January, falls through spring to a minimum around mid-April, climbs to an annual peak in mid-July, and falls again into autumn. The model learned the M shape directly from the data by bending, without being given a single Fourier term.
And say the other thing too: the confidence band widens where the data is thin. Look at the edges. That widening is the model telling you where it is guessing, and a forecast that comes with an honest statement of its own uncertainty is worth more than a point estimate that doesn’t.
crumbs: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once

title: 3  Lab 3: GAMs, Prophet, and Several Seasons at Once
text:
3.9 Before you leave
You should have found that every method beat the seasonal-naive benchmark on RMSE, and that the single harmonic was the worst of the three models.
Look at the MAE column before you move on. The single-harmonic Prophet has a worse MAE than the benchmark it beat on RMSE. Same two models, same holdout, opposite verdict depending on which error measure you quote — because RMSE squares errors and so punishes the occasional large miss, while MAE treats every error proportionally.

Discuss: pyGAM was given only day-of-year and day-of-week — no trend term at all. Prophet was given a trend, a weekly cycle, and a yearly cycle with ten harmonics. Yet on this holdout the simpler model won, by roughly 12% on both RMSE and MAE.
Give one reason a more flexible model can lose on a held-out year, and name the thing you would check before concluding that pyGAM is genuinely the better choice here.
And the operational question: your forecast is for a grid operator who must buy generation in advance. Under-forecasting and over-forecasting cost different amounts. Which of these models would you actually ship, and what would you need to know first?


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough











Try it






Post these in the Week 3 thread before Lecture 4.
First, the awkward result. pyGAM was given two things: day of year and day of week. Prophet was given a trend, a weekly cycle, and a yearly cycle with ten harmonics. Prophet has strictly more machinery — and it lost by twelve percent.
Give me one reason a more flexible model can lose on a held-out year. And name the thing you would check before concluding that pyGAM is genuinely the better choice here, rather than luckier on this particular holdout.
Second, the operational question. Your forecast is for a grid operator who must buy generation in advance, and the two directions of error cost different amounts. Under-forecast and you buy at spot during a peak. Over-forecast and you’ve paid for spinning reserve you didn’t need.
Which of these models would you actually ship — and what would you need to know before you could answer that at all?
Notice that nothing in the table we just built answers the second question. RMSE and MAE are both symmetric — they charge you the same for being a thousand megawatts high as a thousand low. If the costs aren’t symmetric, neither metric is measuring the thing you care about.
That’s not a flaw in this lab. It’s the gap between forecast accuracy and forecast value, and it’s worth carrying into the rest of the course.
Solutions for the coded parts go up on Canvas after the deadline. See you in Lecture 4, where we start on trees.

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
text:
4.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Today the course changes character. Everything so far specified a structure and estimated it. A tree is handed a pile of features and finds the structure itself.
We use the same series you just forecast in Homework 2 — daily units for CA_1 FOODS. Same store, same aisle, same target. Last week you fitted a GAM to it. Today you fit a tree, and the comparison is the point: you will be able to say what each method bought you on identical data.
By the end you will have done four things: read a fitted tree out loud, watched the bias–variance tradeoff happen in a table, discovered why a single tree is unstable, and found the one place trees reliably fail.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scikit-learn, and data/processed/m5_daily.csv (run python scripts/prep_m5.py if it is missing).
crumbs: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
text:
4.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text, plot_tree
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    """Find the processed data file whether you render from the repo root or from
    this file's own folder."""
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42

daily = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_daily.csv"), parse_dates=["date"])
daily["dow"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofweek        # 0 = Monday
daily["doy"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofyear

FEATURES = ["units_lag1", "units_lag7", "units_lag14", "units_lag28", "units_lag365",
            "snap", "is_event", "dow", "doy", "avg_price"]

df = daily.dropna(subset=FEATURES).copy()

N_TEST = 365
train, test = df.iloc[:-N_TEST], df.iloc[-N_TEST:]
X_train, y_train = train[FEATURES].values, train["units"].values
X_test,  y_test  = test[FEATURES].values,  test["units"].values

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

print(f"{len(df)} usable days — train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}")
print(f"benchmark (same day last year): RMSE {rmse(y_test, test.units_lag365.values):,.0f}")

Notice what just happened to the data. There is no date index in X_train. Every row is an independent example, and everything the model knows about time is sitting in the lag columns. That reframing — a time series becomes a flat table — is what lets every method from here to Lecture 9 be applied to forecasting at all.







Walkthrough





1576 usable days — train 1211, test 365
benchmark (same day last year): RMSE 625
Just over four years of daily data, holding out the final year — May 2015 through May 2016.
The benchmark is the same one you have used since Lecture 1: predict today with the same day last year. 625 units. Write it down. Every number today gets measured against it.
Now look at what we handed the model, because this is the important part of the setup.
Ten columns: five lags, a SNAP flag, an event flag, day of week, day of year, and price. And no date index. There is no time in X_train at all. Every row is an independent example, and everything the model knows about when it is, is sitting in those columns because we put it there.
That reframing — a time series flattened into an ordinary table — is what lets everything from here to Lecture 9 be applied to forecasting at all. Trees, forests, boosting, neural networks: none of them know what a time series is. They all consume this table.

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
section: 4.3 Step 1 — Fit a tree and read it out loud
text:
4.3 Step 1 — Fit a tree and read it out loud
Start deliberately shallow, because a depth-3 tree is small enough to read.

tree3 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train, y_train)

print(export_text(tree3, feature_names=FEATURES, decimals=0))
print(f"\ntest RMSE: {rmse(y_test, tree3.predict(X_test)):,.0f}")


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 5))
plot_tree(tree3, feature_names=FEATURES, filled=True, rounded=True, fontsize=7, ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()

Put the root split into business language — not dow <= 4.50 but what that means about this store.
In the room: read it aloud to the person next to you. Saying it to someone is what exposes a sentence you do not actually understand.
On your own: write the sentence in a comment, then add a prediction you can check immediately:
# the root split separates ____ from ____
# I expect the higher-sales side to be dow <= 4.50 / dow > 4.50, because ____
Then read the two node values off the tree plot above and see whether you were right. A guess you wrote down and checked teaches you more than a split you merely read.
Then look at the importances:

imp = pd.Series(tree3.feature_importances_, index=FEATURES).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(imp[imp > 0].round(3).to_string())







Compare this with the lecture slide



Lecture 4’s importance table was computed on weekly CA_1 FOODS, and there the four-week lag dominated. Here, on daily data for the same store and aisle, something else wins outright.
Same store. Same product. Different frequency, different answer. Say why before moving on.









Walkthrough





Depth 3, deliberately. Eight leaves is small enough to read in full, and you should read it in full, because being able to do that is most of what a tree is for.
|--- dow <= 4
|   |--- units_lag28 <= 2596
...
|--- dow >  4
|   |--- units_lag1 <= 3351
...

test RMSE: 337
The root split is dow <= 4. That is Monday-through-Friday on one side, Saturday and Sunday on the other — and the tree found it without being told that a week has a weekend in it.






Try it






Pause here and say the whole path out loud, in business language rather than in inequalities. Not “dow less than or equal to 4.5, then units_lag28 above 2596.” Something closer to: it’s a weekday, and four weeks ago was already busy, and last week was busy too, so predict about 2,950.
If you can do that for one leaf, you can do it for a store manager, and that is a thing no model in Lectures 1 through 3 could offer you.
One branch worth reading before we move on. On the weekend side, on days when yesterday was already very busy, the tree splits on is_event — and it predicts 4,041 when there is no event and 3,583 when there is. The event lowers the forecast by about 450 units. Events in M5 include days like Christmas, when the store is shut or nearly so. The tree has no idea what Christmas is. It found the hole in the data anyway.
And the accuracy: 337 against a benchmark of 625. Roughly a 46% improvement, from eight leaves you can print on a slide.
dow            0.789
units_lag28    0.106
units_lag1     0.064
units_lag7     0.030
is_event       0.011
Day of week takes seventy-nine percent of the importance. On its own, day-of-week means explain about 66% of the variance in training units — weekday average 2,632, weekend average 3,773, a gap of 43%. There is no mystery about why the tree grabbed it first.






Try it






Lecture 4’s importance table, on the weekly version of this same store and aisle, had units_lag4 at 0.62 and day-of-week nowhere — it isn’t in the table at all. Here, on daily data, dow wins outright with 0.79 and the four-week lag drops to 0.11. Same store. Same product. Opposite answer. Pause and work out why before I say it.
Because weekly data has no day-of-week variation left in it. Aggregating to a week averages the weekend and the weekdays together and destroys the largest single signal in the series. It was never that the four-week lag mattered more; it was that the thing that mattered most had already been summed away.
That is worth more than it looks. Feature importance is a statement about the table you built, not about the business. Change the frequency and the ranking inverts.

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
section: 4.4 Step 2 — Watch the bias–variance tradeoff happen
text:
4.4 Step 2 — Watch the bias–variance tradeoff happen
Lecture 4 drew this as a curve. Now produce it.

rows = []
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train, y_train)
    rows.append({"depth": str(depth),
                 "leaves": t.get_n_leaves(),
                 "train_RMSE": round(rmse(y_train, t.predict(X_train))),
                 "test_RMSE":  round(rmse(y_test,  t.predict(X_test)))})

sweep = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(sweep.to_string(index=False))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.plot(range(len(sweep)), sweep.train_RMSE, marker="o", label="train")
ax.plot(range(len(sweep)), sweep.test_RMSE,  marker="o", label="test")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(sweep))); ax.set_xticklabels(sweep.depth)
ax.set_xlabel("max_depth"); ax.set_ylabel("RMSE"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

Two things to say out loud. What does the training error do as depth increases, and what number does it reach at the end? And where does the test error bottom out?
The gap between those two curves is overfitting, drawn to scale.







Walkthrough





Lecture 4 drew this as a curve on a slide. Here it is as an actual table on your own data.
depth  leaves  train_RMSE  test_RMSE
    1       2         443        413
    2       4         388        369
    3       8         354        337
    5      32         284        303
    8     179         184        313
   12     698          84        385
 None    1200           0        406
Read the two columns separately.
Training error falls the whole way down and ends at zero. Not near zero — zero. Look at the leaf count on that row: 1,200 leaves for 1,211 training days. The tree has given almost every single day its own leaf and memorized the answer. A model that has memorized the training set has a training error of zero by construction, and that number tells you nothing whatsoever.
Test error does something else. It falls to 303 at depth 5, and then turns around and climbs back to 406 — worse than the depth-2 tree with four leaves.
The gap between the two columns is overfitting, drawn to scale. At depth 5 it’s 284 against 303, almost nothing. At full depth it’s 0 against 406.
Two things to carry out of this table.
First, the model that fits the training data best is the worst model in the table on data it has not seen. That is not a subtlety, that is the whole lesson, and it will repeat in every lecture for the rest of the course.
Second — and this is the practical one — the depth-5 tree beats the fully grown tree, and the only thing separating them is one keyword argument. Nothing about the data changed. max_depth is the entire difference between 303 and 406.
crumbs: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
section: 4.5 Step 3 — Why one tree is not enough
text:
4.5 Step 3 — Why one tree is not enough
Lecture 4 claimed a tree is unstable: change the data slightly and the structure changes. Test it properly, using bootstrap resamples — draw a sample of the same size with replacement, refit, and repeat.

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
roots, preds = {}, []

for b in range(20):
    idx = rng.choice(len(X_train), len(X_train), replace=True)
    t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=5, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train[idx], y_train[idx])
    root = [l.strip() for l in export_text(t, feature_names=FEATURES).split("\n")
            if l.startswith("|---")][0]
    roots[root] = roots.get(root, 0) + 1
    preds.append(t.predict(X_test))

P = np.array(preds)
print("root splits across 20 bootstrap trees:")
for k, v in sorted(roots.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    print(f"  {v:2d} x  {k}")
print(f"\nper-day spread of predictions across the 20 trees:")
print(f"  average sd {P.std(0).mean():,.0f} units   worst day {P.std(0).max():,.0f} units")

The root may well be stable — one feature can be dominant enough that every resample finds it first. That is not the same as the tree being stable. Look at the spread of predictions: on a typical day the twenty trees disagree by a meaningful margin, and on the worst day they disagree enormously. All that disagreement lives below the root.
Now the payoff, and it is one line:

single = np.mean([rmse(y_test, p) for p in P])
averaged = rmse(y_test, P.mean(0))

print(f"average RMSE of a single bootstrap tree : {single:,.0f}")
print(f"RMSE of the 20 trees averaged together  : {averaged:,.0f}")
print(f"improvement: {100*(single-averaged)/single:.0f}%")

You just built a bagged ensemble by hand — bootstrap aggregating, in three lines. Nothing was tuned and no new information was added; the gain came entirely from averaging away the disagreement you measured above. It is not yet a Random Forest: a forest adds one more idea, which is to stop every tree from looking at dow first. Twenty trees that agree perfectly on their root are twenty trees making correlated mistakes. That is next week.







Walkthrough





Lecture 4 claimed a tree is unstable — nudge the data and the structure changes. Let’s test that properly rather than take it on faith.
Twenty bootstrap resamples: draw 1,211 rows with replacement, refit a depth-5 tree, record what it split on first, and keep its test predictions.
root splits across 20 bootstrap trees:
  20 x  |--- dow <= 4.50

per-day spread of predictions across the 20 trees:
  average sd 160 units   worst day 1,137 units
Now, that first result looks like it refutes the lecture. Twenty out of twenty found the same root. The root is perfectly stable.
It is stable because day-of-week is overwhelming — a 43% gap survives any resample you can draw. A stable root is not a stable tree. Look at the second number: on a typical test day the twenty trees disagree by 160 units, and on the worst day they are spread over 1,137 units — about a third of an average day’s sales. Every bit of that disagreement lives below the root, in the splits you cannot see from this printout.
That is the instability the lecture was talking about, and you can only see it by looking at predictions, not at structure.
average RMSE of a single bootstrap tree : 324
RMSE of the 20 trees averaged together  : 266
improvement: 18%
Eighteen percent. No tuning, no new features, no extra data — the twenty trees saw less data than the original fit, since a bootstrap sample leaves out about a third of the rows each time.
And note where 266 sits against Step 2’s table: the best single tree you found by sweeping depth was 303. Averaging twenty individually worse trees — 324 on average — produced something better than the best one of them and better than the best tree in the whole sweep.
That is the result the next lecture is built on, and it is worth being precise about the mechanism. Nothing here reduced any individual tree’s bias. What fell was the variance you measured two cells ago: the disagreement averages out, the signal does not.
What you have built is called bagging — bootstrap aggregating. It is not yet a random forest. A forest adds one more idea, which is to stop the trees from all looking at day-of-week first, and you can already see why that might matter: twenty trees that agree perfectly on their root are twenty trees making correlated mistakes. That is Lecture 5, and it is one keyword argument.
crumbs: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks

title: 4  Lab 4: Decision Trees — Reading One, and Finding Where It Breaks
text:
4.6 Step 4 — Where trees reliably fail
A tree predicts the mean of the training rows in a leaf. So every prediction it can ever make is an average of values it has already seen.

full = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train, y_train)
p = full.predict(X_test)

print(f"training target range : [{y_train.min():,.0f}, {y_train.max():,.0f}]")
print(f"prediction range      : [{p.min():,.0f}, {p.max():,.0f}]")

The predictions cannot leave the training range — not “usually do not,” cannot. Now watch what that does at the extremes.

hi = y_test > np.percentile(y_test, 90)
lo = y_test < np.percentile(y_test, 10)

print(f"busiest 10% of test days  (n={hi.sum()}): actual {y_test[hi].mean():,.0f}"
      f"   predicted {p[hi].mean():,.0f}   under by {y_test[hi].mean()-p[hi].mean():,.0f}")
print(f"quietest 10% of test days (n={lo.sum()}): actual {y_test[lo].mean():,.0f}"
      f"   predicted {p[lo].mean():,.0f}   over by  {p[lo].mean()-y_test[lo].mean():,.0f}")

Your turn: the two errors above point in opposite directions. Plot predicted against actual for the test set, add the 45-degree line, and see the shape this produces.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in the two blanks ----
# fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4.5))
# ax.scatter(___, ___, s=6, alpha=0.4)          # <- actual on x, predicted on y
# lims = [y_test.min(), y_test.max()]
# ax.plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
# ax.set_xlabel("actual units"); ax.set_ylabel("predicted units")
# plt.tight_layout()








Walkthrough





Every lecture in this course should end by telling you where the method breaks. Here is where a tree breaks, and it follows from one sentence: a tree predicts the mean of the training rows in a leaf. Every prediction it will ever make is an average of values it has already seen.
training target range : [0, 5,016]
prediction range      : [0, 4,527]
The prediction range sits inside the training range, and it has to — not “usually does,” cannot. A tree can never forecast a value above the largest one in its training data, because there is no arithmetic in it that could produce one. No trend term, no extrapolation, nothing. If this store grows 20% next year, the tree will predict last year’s ceiling forever.
busiest 10% of test days  (n=37): actual 4,115   predicted 3,929   under by 186
quietest 10% of test days (n=37): actual 2,030   predicted 2,237   over by  207
Both ends are wrong, and — this is the point — they are wrong in opposite directions. The busy days are under-forecast by 186 units. The quiet days are over-forecast by 207. The model is pulling everything toward the middle.
Be precise about what this is and is not. The hard ceiling did not bite this year: the busiest test day was 4,717 units and the training set had a 5,016-unit day, so nothing was clipped. What you are seeing is the softer, more common version — leaf averaging shrinks the extremes inward. It is not a large effect in absolute terms next to a full tree’s RMSE of 406. It is a systematic one, which is worse, because it will not average out over the year and it is exactly the days you care most about.






Try it






Uncomment the scatter block and fill in the two blanks — actual on x, predicted on y, with the 45-degree line. Pause the video, run it, and come back when you can describe the shape.
You should be looking at a cloud that is flatter than the 45-degree line. Below the line on the right, above it on the left, hinged in the middle. Once you have seen that shape you will recognize it everywhere, in every method that predicts by averaging.

4.7 Before you leave
You should have found that the tree systematically under-predicts the busiest days and over-predicts the quietest ones, and that averaging twenty unstable trees beat any one of them.

Discuss (the failure): A tree pulls its predictions toward the middle at both ends. Give the mechanical reason — think about what a leaf prediction actually is.
Then the operational version: this store is planning inventory. Which of those two errors costs more, and does your answer change if the product is milk rather than canned goods?
Discuss (the comparison): You forecast this exact series with a GAM last week. Which method would you rather hand to a store manager, and what specifically would each one let you say that the other would not?


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough











Try it






Two questions on the discussion board before the next session.
First, the failure. You have just seen a tree pull its predictions toward the middle at both ends. Give me the mechanical reason — and I mean mechanical, in terms of what a leaf prediction literally is, not “the model is conservative.”
Then the operational half. This store is planning inventory. One of those two errors costs more than the other: under-forecasting a busy day means an empty shelf and a lost sale; over-forecasting a quiet day means stock sitting in the back. Which is worse — and does your answer change if the product is milk rather than canned goods?
Second, the comparison. You fitted a GAM to this exact series in Homework 2, and a tree to it today. Which one would you actually hand to a store manager, and what specifically would each let you say that the other would not?
Be concrete. The GAM gives you a smooth curve per feature and a partial-dependence plot you can show someone. The tree gives you a path — weekday, four weeks ago was busy, yesterday was busy, predict 2,950 — that a manager can follow and argue with. Those are genuinely different kinds of explanation, and one of them will suit an audience better than the other.
One last thing before you close the file. Look back at Step 2’s table and notice what is not in this lab: we chose depth 5 by looking at the test set. Every number in that column was computed on the year we held out, and then we picked the winner from it. Lecture 1 told you what that is worth. Fixing it properly needs walk-forward validation on the training data alone, and that is Homework 3’s job.
