title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
At the end of Lab 4 you built a bagged ensemble by accident. You drew twenty bootstrap samples, fitted a tree to each, averaged the predictions, and the RMSE fell from about 324 to 266 — with nothing tuned and no new information added. What you did not do is the one thing that turns bagging into a Random Forest.
Today we do that properly, then find out what else the real algorithm does, then replace averaging with something better.
Same series throughout: daily units for CA_1 FOODS. You have now fitted a GAM to it (Homework 2) and a single tree (Lab 4), so every number today lands on a scale you already know.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scikit-learn, xgboost, and data/processed/m5_daily.csv.
crumbs: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
import xgboost as xgb
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42

daily = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_daily.csv"), parse_dates=["date"])
daily["dow"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofweek
daily["doy"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofyear

FEATURES = ["units_lag1", "units_lag7", "units_lag14", "units_lag28", "units_lag365",
            "snap", "is_event", "dow", "doy", "avg_price"]

df = daily.dropna(subset=FEATURES).copy()
N_TEST = 365
train, test = df.iloc[:-N_TEST], df.iloc[-N_TEST:]
X_train, y_train = train[FEATURES].values, train["units"].values
X_test,  y_test  = test[FEATURES].values,  test["units"].values

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

scoreboard = {
    "Benchmark (same day last year)": rmse(y_test, test.units_lag365.values),
    "Single tree (Lab 4)": 324,
    "20 trees averaged by hand (Lab 4)": 266,
}
for k, v in scoreboard.items():
    print(f"{k:<36} {v:>6,.0f}")








Walkthrough





Benchmark (same day last year)          625
Single tree (Lab 4)                     324
20 trees averaged by hand (Lab 4)       266
The scoreboard carries forward. 625 is the benchmark we have used since Lecture 1. 324 was a single tree. 266 was your hand-built bagging, and those two numbers are hard-coded here deliberately — they are last week’s measured results, not refitted.
Everything today gets added to this list, and at the end you will read it as one table.

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.3 Step 1 — The real thing

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

scoreboard["Random Forest (300 trees)"] = rmse(y_test, rf.predict(X_test))
print(f"Random Forest: {scoreboard['Random Forest (300 trees)']:,.0f}")

Better than your hand-built version, and much better than one tree. Two differences account for it: more trees, and a second source of randomness we are about to meet.







Walkthrough





Random Forest: 248
Three hundred trees, no tuning, two lines of code.
248 against your hand-built 266, and against 324 for a single tree. So the library version buys about 7% over what you built yourself in three lines last week.
Sit with how small that is for a moment. Most of the gain was already yours. The idea — resample, refit, average — is where the improvement came from; the professional implementation adds a useful but modest amount on top. Two things account for that remainder: three hundred trees instead of twenty, and a second source of randomness we meet in Step 3.
That is worth saying because the reverse impression is common — that the value is in the library. It isn’t. It’s in the idea, and you already had it.

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
section: 5.4 Step 2 — How many trees is enough?
text:
5.4 Step 2 — How many trees is enough?
The usual worry about a big model is overfitting. Adding trees to a forest is the rare knob where that worry does not apply — but it does stop paying.

counts = [5, 20, 50, 100, 300, 600]
curve = []
for n in counts:
    r = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train)
    curve.append(rmse(y_test, r.predict(X_test)))

for n, v in zip(counts, curve):
    print(f"  n_estimators={n:<4} test RMSE {v:,.0f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.plot(counts, curve, marker="o")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("n_estimators (log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel("test RMSE")
plt.tight_layout()

Say what the curve does after about fifty trees, and what that means for how you would spend a compute budget. More trees never hurt accuracy — but every one costs time to fit and to predict.







Walkthrough





  n_estimators=5    test RMSE 288
  n_estimators=20   test RMSE 257
  n_estimators=50   test RMSE 251
  n_estimators=100  test RMSE 249
  n_estimators=300  test RMSE 248
  n_estimators=600  test RMSE 248






Try it






Pause and describe this curve in one sentence, then say what it implies for a compute budget.
It drops hard to about fifty trees, and then it is flat. Fifty trees gets you 251; six hundred gets you 248. You paid twelve times the compute for three units of RMSE — on a series where a typical day is around 2,900 units.
Now the property that makes this curve unusual, and please notice it, because Step 6 breaks it: the curve never turns up. More trees never made the forest worse. That is not the normal behavior of a model knob. Usually “more” eventually means overfitting, and here it simply does not, because each tree is fitted independently and averaging more independent things cannot make the average worse.
So n_estimators in a forest is not really a tuning parameter — it is a budget question. Pick the point where the curve goes flat, spend nothing beyond it, and never worry that you have chosen badly. Hold that thought for twenty minutes.
crumbs: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.5 Step 3 — The “random” in Random Forest
Bagging alone gives every tree a different sample of rows. A Random Forest also gives each split a different random subset of columns — max_features. Lecture 5 argued this decorrelates the trees, so their errors cancel more completely when averaged.
Test it.

for mf in [None, 0.6, "sqrt", 0.2]:
    r = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=mf,
                              random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train)
    label = "all features" if mf is None else str(mf)
    print(f"  max_features={label:<13} test RMSE {rmse(y_test, r.predict(X_test)):,.0f}")







The textbook rule does not win here, and you should know why



max_features="sqrt" is the standard recommendation, and on this dataset it is worse than using every feature. That is not a bug — it is the rule meeting its own boundary condition.
You have 10 features, and one of them (dow) carries most of the signal. sqrt(10) is about 3, so at any given split most trees are not even allowed to look at day-of-week. Decorrelation is only a bargain when you have enough redundant, correlated features that losing a few at each split costs you little.
In Homework 3 you will run a forest on 27 features with no single dominant one. Check whether the ranking flips there. The lesson is the condition, not the default.









Walkthrough





Here is the second randomness. Bagging gives every tree a different sample of rows. A random forest also gives every split a different random subset of columns. That is the entire difference between the two algorithms — and it is why what you built last week was bagging and not a forest.
The argument from Lecture 5: if one feature is strongly predictive, every bagged tree splits on it first, so the trees are near-copies and their errors do not cancel. Deny each split most of the columns and the trees are forced to be different.
You have already seen that failure mode. Last week, twenty out of twenty bootstrap trees found dow at the root.
  max_features=all features  test RMSE 248
  max_features=0.6           test RMSE 247
  max_features=sqrt          test RMSE 254
  max_features=0.2           test RMSE 257
max_features="sqrt" is the textbook default. It is the third-best of four here, six units worse than simply using every column. And 0.2 — aggressive decorrelation — is worse still.
This is not a bug and it is not a bad dataset. It is the rule meeting its own boundary condition, and the condition is stated in the callout: you have ten features, one of which carries most of the signal. The square root of ten is about three, so at a typical split most trees are not allowed to look at day-of-week — and day-of-week, as you measured last week, is roughly two thirds of the variance in this series.
Decorrelation is a trade. You give up some accuracy per tree to gain independence between trees. That trade is a bargain when you have many partly-redundant features and no single dominant one. It is a bad trade when you have ten features and one of them is the answer.
Notice the honest middle of the table: 0.6 is the best row, at 247. Mild subsampling helps by a hair. So the finding is not “decorrelation is wrong here,” it is “the standard dose is too strong for this feature set.”
In Homework 3 you run a forest on twenty-seven features with no single dominant one. Check whether this ranking flips. It should — and that difference between the lab and the homework is the actual lesson. What you are learning is the condition, not the default.
crumbs: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.6 Step 4 — Validation for free
Each bootstrap sample leaves out about a third of the rows. Those out-of-bag rows never trained that tree, so they can score it — a validation estimate with no holdout set.

rf_oob = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True,
                               random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_train, y_train)

oob_rmse = rmse(y_train, rf_oob.oob_prediction_)
print(f"OOB R²   : {rf_oob.oob_score_:.3f}")
print(f"OOB RMSE : {oob_rmse:,.0f}")
print(f"test RMSE: {rmse(y_test, rf_oob.predict(X_test)):,.0f}")

Compare the two numbers and account for the gap. The OOB estimate is computed on training-period rows scattered through 2012–2015; the test RMSE is a solid block of the final year. Which one would you quote to someone asking how the model will do next month, and why?







Walkthrough





A bootstrap sample of n rows drawn with replacement leaves out about a third of them. Those rows never trained that tree, so they can score it — for free, with no holdout.
OOB R²   : 0.809
OOB RMSE : 297
test RMSE: 248






Try it






Pause. The OOB estimate is 297 and the test RMSE is 248, so OOB is pessimistic by about 20%. Work out why before I tell you, and then decide which of the two you would quote to someone asking how this model will do next month.
Two reasons, and they pull in the same direction.
First, an OOB prediction for a given row comes from only the third of trees that did not see it — about a hundred trees rather than three hundred. Step 2 told you exactly what a smaller forest costs. So OOB is scoring a systematically smaller forest than the one you are going to ship.
Second, the rows are different. OOB rows are scattered across 2012 to 2015, the whole training period, including the earlier, noisier stretch. The test set is one solid block of the final year.
So which do you quote? Neither, uncritically. OOB is the cheap sanity check you can compute without giving up any data — genuinely valuable when data is scarce. But it is scoring the wrong model on the wrong period for a forecasting question, and it is not a walk-forward estimate. If someone asks how this does next month, the only honest answer comes from evaluating on time you held out, in order — which is what the test column is, and what Homework 3 makes you do properly.

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
section: 5.7 Step 5 — Two importances, two different answers
text:
5.7 Step 5 — Two importances, two different answers

mdi = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=FEATURES)

perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10,
                              random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1,
                              scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
perm_imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=FEATURES)

comp = pd.DataFrame({"MDI": mdi.round(3), "permutation_ΔRMSE": perm_imp.round(1)})
comp["MDI_rank"] = comp.MDI.rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
comp["perm_rank"] = comp["permutation_ΔRMSE"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
print(comp.sort_values("MDI", ascending=False).to_string())

Permutation importance is in units of RMSE: shuffle that column on the test set, and this is how much worse the forecast gets. That is directly interpretable in a way MDI is not.
Find the disagreements. Three are worth naming before you read on:

one lag that MDI ranks above units_lag1, while permutation ranks it far below
snap, which MDI places near the bottom and permutation places near the top
avg_price against is_event: MDI ranks the price column above the event flag, while permutation scores price at exactly zero and the event flag at 22 units of RMSE

Your turn: plot the two rankings side by side as horizontal bar charts so the disagreements are visible at a glance.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in the two blanks ----
# fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
# mdi.sort_values().plot.barh(ax=axes[0], title="MDI (impurity)")
# ___.sort_values().plot.barh(ax=axes[1], title="Permutation (ΔRMSE)")   # <- which Series?
# plt.tight_layout()








Walkthrough





                MDI  permutation_ΔRMSE  MDI_rank  perm_rank
dow           0.583              284.2         1          1
units_lag28   0.119               36.8         2          4
units_lag1    0.086              116.9         3          2
units_lag7    0.053               35.6         4          5
units_lag365  0.036               10.2         5          8
doy           0.036               18.1         5          7
units_lag14   0.031                7.7         7          9
snap          0.027               40.4         8          3
avg_price     0.017                0.0         9         10
is_event      0.012               22.3        10          6
First, the units, because they change what the numbers mean. MDI is a share of impurity reduction — it sums to one and it is computed on the training data by the fitting process. Permutation importance is measured in RMSE: shuffle that column in the test set and see how much worse the forecast gets. So dow at 284 means “destroy day-of-week and you lose 284 units of accuracy.” You can say that sentence to a manager. You cannot say “0.583” to anyone.






Try it






Pause and find the three disagreements before I name them.
One. units_lag28 is second on MDI and fourth on permutation, at 36.8 — while units_lag1, which MDI ranks below it, is worth 116.9. Three times as much. MDI counts how often a feature was used for splitting; permutation measures what happens when you take it away. A feature used constantly for small refinements can lose to one used rarely for large ones.
Two, and this is the one that matters commercially. snap is eighth on MDI and third on permutation, worth 40 units of RMSE. SNAP benefits land on fixed days of the month and this is a food aisle: SNAP days average 3,201 units against 2,839 otherwise, about 13% higher, on 400 of 1,211 training days. MDI nearly buried a real, actionable effect.
Three. Look at avg_price against is_event. MDI ranks price above the event flag — 0.017 to 0.012. Permutation says price is worth exactly zero and the event flag is worth 22.
That inversion has a known mechanism, and Lecture 4’s footnote named it: MDI is biased toward high-cardinality features. avg_price takes 173 distinct values in the training set, so it offers 172 candidate split points, and with that many chances some will reduce impurity by luck alone. is_event is binary — one possible split, no opportunity to get lucky. MDI rewards opportunity; permutation rewards contribution.
The practical rule: MDI is free and permutation is honest. MDI comes out of the fit at no cost and is fine for a quick screen. Anything you are going to act on — or say out loud to a category manager — gets checked with permutation, on held-out data.






Try it



— fill in the one blank and plot the two rankings side by side. The blank is the permutation series. Come back when you can see the snap bar jump.

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.8 Step 6 — Stop averaging. Start correcting.
A forest builds many trees in parallel and averages them. Boosting builds them in sequence, each one fitted to what the previous ones got wrong.
The first four rows hold the learning rate fixed and add rounds — the same experiment you ran on the forest in Step 2. The last two change the rate instead.

for lr, n in [(0.1, 100), (0.1, 300), (0.1, 1000), (0.1, 3000),
              (0.3, 100), (0.05, 1000)]:
    m = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=n, learning_rate=lr, max_depth=4,
                         subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
                         random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"  lr={lr:<5} n={n:<5} train {rmse(y_train, m.predict(X_train)):5,.0f}"
          f"   test {rmse(y_test, m.predict(X_test)):5,.0f}")


best = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=4,
                        subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
                        random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_train, y_train)
scoreboard["XGBoost (lr=0.1, 100 trees)"] = rmse(y_test, best.predict(X_test))

print(pd.Series(scoreboard).round(0).astype(int).sort_values(ascending=False).to_string())

Read the first four rows as a curve, then compare it with Step 2. Training error falls to zero. Test error bottoms out around 300 rounds and then climbs back up — 3,000 rounds is worse than 100. In Step 2 you added trees to a forest all the way to 600 and it never once hurt.
That is the practical difference between the two ensembles. A forest’s trees are fitted independently and averaged, so extra ones can only sharpen the average. Boosting’s trees are fitted to the previous ensemble’s residuals, so extra ones keep going — eventually correcting noise. n_estimators is a free choice in a forest and a tuning parameter in boosting.
The last two rows say the obvious complement: a big rate with few rounds and a small rate with many land in much the same place, because roughly it is the product that sets the budget. What you cannot do is set a rate and then let the rounds run.
Note which configuration we put on the scoreboard below — lr=0.1, n=100, the conventional default, not the row with the best test RMSE. Picking the winner out of a column computed on the test set is the mistake Lecture 1 warned about, and it does not stop being a mistake because the grid is small.







Walkthrough





Everything so far today has been the same idea: build many trees independently, average them. Boosting is a different idea. Trees are built in sequence, and each new one is fitted to what the ensemble so far got wrong. Nothing is averaged. Every tree is a correction.
  lr=0.1   n=100   train   171   test   244
  lr=0.1   n=300   train    95   test   243
  lr=0.1   n=1000  train    19   test   250
  lr=0.1   n=3000  train     0   test   253
  lr=0.3   n=100   train    95   test   238
  lr=0.05  n=1000  train    54   test   239
Read the first four rows as a curve — the learning rate is fixed, only the number of rounds changes. That is the identical experiment you ran in Step 2 on the forest.
Training error goes 171, 95, 19, zero. Test error goes 244, 243, 250, 253. It bottoms out around three hundred rounds and then turns up.
Now put that next to Step 2, where you took a forest from five trees to six hundred and it never got worse once.
Same data, same features, same family of base learner. Opposite behavior on the same knob. The reason is structural, and it is worth stating carefully: a forest’s trees are fitted independently of one another, so an extra one only adds to an average and cannot corrupt what is already there. A boosted tree is fitted to the residuals of everything before it — so once the real signal is used up, the next tree fits noise, and it is added to the ensemble anyway, with nothing to average it away.
So: n_estimators in a forest is a budget. n_estimators in boosting is a tuning parameter, and getting it wrong costs you accuracy in a way no amount of forest-tuning ever will. That is also why boosting has a learning rate — it is the knob that decides how much damage each additional tree is allowed to do.
The last two rows are the complement. A big rate with few rounds (238) and a small rate with many (239) end up in much the same place: roughly, the product sets the budget. What you cannot do is fix a rate and let the rounds run.
Benchmark (same day last year)       625
Single tree (Lab 4)                  324
20 trees averaged by hand (Lab 4)    266
Random Forest (300 trees)            248
XGBoost (lr=0.1, 100 trees)          244
Now, look at which XGBoost row we put on that scoreboard. lr=0.1, n=100 — 244. Not the lr=0.3 row at 238, which was the best number in the grid.
That is deliberate, and it is not modesty. Every test-RMSE number in the grid above was computed on the year we held out. If I pick the winner out of that column and then report it as my result, I have used the test set to choose the model and I no longer have an honest estimate of anything. Lecture 1 said this about forecast evaluation and it does not stop being true because the grid has only six rows. So the scoreboard gets the conventional default, and the way to actually choose here is walk-forward validation inside the training period — Homework 4.

title: 5  Lab 5: Tree Ensembles — Averaging, Then Boosting
text:
5.9 Before you leave
Your scoreboard should run from a benchmark near 625 down to roughly 245, across five models fitted to one series.

Discuss (the ranking): Boosting beat the forest here. Name one property of this dataset that favors boosting, and one situation where you would still reach for the forest first — thinking about tuning effort and about what happens when nobody retunes the model for a year.
Discuss (the importances): You have two importance tables that disagree about snap. A category manager asks whether SNAP timing matters for stocking. Which table do you show them, what do you say, and what would you want to check before committing to an answer?
Discuss (the whole arc): Across Labs 4 and 5 the RMSE fell from 324 to about 245 on the same series with the same features. What was actually purchased with that improvement, and what was given up along the way? Be specific about the thing you can no longer do that you could do in Step 1 of Lab 4.

Walkthrough





Read the scoreboard as one object. 625 to 244 — a 61% reduction against the benchmark, on one series, with the same ten features throughout. Almost all of it arrived in two jumps: a single tree over the benchmark, and averaging over the single tree. The last two steps, the forest and boosting, bought 22 units between them.






Try it






Three questions on the discussion board.
The ranking. Boosting won, 244 to 248 — by about one and a half percent. Name one property of this dataset that favours it. Then name a situation where you would still reach for the forest first, thinking about two things specifically: how much tuning each one needed today, and what happens to each when nobody retunes it for a year. was fire-and-forget, and boosting’s best setting is a live decision that can go stale.*
The importances. You have two tables that disagree about snap — eighth on one, third on the other. A category manager asks whether SNAP timing matters for stocking. Which table do you show them, what exactly do you say, and what would you check before committing to an answer? Be concrete about that last part.
The arc. Across Labs 4 and 5 the error fell from 324 to 244 on the same series with the same features. What was purchased with that, and what was given up? Be specific about the thing you could do in Step 1 of Lab 4 that you cannot do now.
I’ll say the shape of that last answer, because it is the through-line of the whole course and I do not want it to be missed. In Lab 4, Step 1, you printed a tree and read a path out loud — weekday, four weeks ago was busy, yesterday was busy, predict 2,950. You cannot do that now. There is no path to read. Three hundred trees, or a hundred sequential corrections, and the best account you can give of the model is a permutation importance table.
You bought 25% accuracy with the entire explanation. Sometimes that is obviously right. Sometimes you are standing in front of a category manager and it is obviously wrong. Knowing which is which is the actual skill.

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
text:
6.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Lecture 6 claimed that ordinary least squares breaks when you have many predictors relative to observations — coefficient variance grows with \(k\), correlated predictors produce wild offsetting estimates, and past \(k > n\) there is no unique solution at all.
Today you will break it on purpose, watch exactly how it fails, and then fix it with one line.
Same series as Labs 4 and 5: daily units for CA_1 FOODS. But we now engineer the feature set an analyst would actually build — 28 consecutive lags, weekly and annual lags, rolling statistics, Fourier terms, day-of-week dummies — which is how you end up with more predictors than you meant to have.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scikit-learn, and data/processed/m5_daily.csv.
crumbs: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
text:
6.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Lasso, Ridge
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42

daily = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_daily.csv"), parse_dates=["date"]).sort_values("date")
u = daily.set_index("date")["units"]

for L in list(range(1, 29)) + [35, 42, 49, 56, 364, 365, 366]:
    daily[f"lag{L}"] = u.shift(L).values
for W in (7, 14, 28, 91, 364):
    daily[f"roll{W}_mean"] = u.shift(1).rolling(W).mean().values
    daily[f"roll{W}_std"]  = u.shift(1).rolling(W).std().values

daily["dow"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofweek
daily["doy"] = daily["date"].dt.dayofyear
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    daily[f"sin{k}"] = np.sin(2*np.pi*k*daily.doy/365)
    daily[f"cos{k}"] = np.cos(2*np.pi*k*daily.doy/365)
daily = pd.concat([daily, pd.get_dummies(daily.dow, prefix="dow")], axis=1)

FEATURES = ([c for c in daily.columns if c.startswith(("lag", "roll", "sin", "cos", "dow_"))]
            + ["snap", "is_event", "doy", "avg_price"])

df = daily.dropna(subset=[c for c in FEATURES if c.startswith(("lag", "roll"))]).copy()
N_TEST = 365
train, test = df.iloc[:-N_TEST], df.iloc[-N_TEST:]
X_train, y_train = train[FEATURES].values.astype(float), train["units"].values
X_test,  y_test  = test[FEATURES].values.astype(float),  test["units"].values

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

print(f"k = {len(FEATURES)} features, n_train = {len(X_train)}, n/k = {len(X_train)/len(FEATURES):.1f}")

Note how easily 62 predictors appeared. Nobody set out to build a 62-parameter model; it is what routine feature engineering produces.







Walkthrough





Look at what the setup does, because nothing in it is unreasonable.
Twenty-eight consecutive lags, because you don’t know which one matters. A few weekly lags — 35, 42, 49, 56. Last year’s lags, 364, 365, 366. Rolling means and standard deviations at five windows. Three Fourier pairs for annual seasonality. Day-of-week dummies. Then SNAP, events, day-of-year and price.
k = 62 features, n_train = 1210, n/k = 19.5
Sixty-two predictors. Thirty-five lags, ten rolling statistics, six Fourier terms, seven day-of-week dummies, four others.
Nobody sat down and decided to fit a sixty-two-parameter model. Every one of those columns was a defensible small decision, and the total is what routine feature engineering produces. That is the honest version of how this problem arrives: not from ambition, from diligence.
Right now the ratio is comfortable — about twenty observations per parameter. Hold onto that number, because Step 1 is going to take it apart.
crumbs: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
text:
6.3 Step 1 — Break it
With 1,210 training rows and 62 features, OLS is fine. Now shrink the training window and watch.

rows = []
for n in (1210, 400, 200, 120, 80):
    sub = train.iloc[-n:]
    sc = StandardScaler().fit(sub[FEATURES].values.astype(float))
    Xs = sc.transform(sub[FEATURES].values.astype(float))
    Xt = sc.transform(X_test)
    y  = sub["units"].values

    ols = LinearRegression().fit(Xs, y)
    rid = Ridge(alpha=100).fit(Xs, y)

    rows.append({"n": n, "n/k": round(n/len(FEATURES), 1),
                 "OLS_max_coef": f"{np.abs(ols.coef_).max():,.0f}",
                 "OLS_test_RMSE": f"{rmse(y_test, ols.predict(Xt)):,.0f}",
                 "Ridge_test_RMSE": f"{rmse(y_test, rid.predict(Xt)):,.0f}"})

print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Read that table across, then down. As the training window shrinks, the largest OLS coefficient grows from about 150 to the hundreds of thousands, and the test RMSE from 280 into the millions. Nothing about the problem changed — same features, same target, same test set. Only the ratio of observations to parameters.
Ridge, with a one-line change, degrades gracefully across the entire range.
That is Lecture 6’s opening argument, and you just measured it.







Walkthrough





We keep the features and the test set fixed and shrink only the training window. Four years, then about one, then two hundred days, then a hundred and twenty, then eighty. Same problem throughout. Only the ratio changes.
   n  n/k OLS_max_coef OLS_test_RMSE Ridge_test_RMSE
1210 19.5          153           280             278
 400  6.5          636         2,071             323
 200  3.2        1,364         5,874             363
 120  1.9    1,049,739     3,578,141             621
  80  1.3      355,629     2,072,167             770
Read across the OLS columns. At twenty observations per parameter, the largest coefficient is 153 and the test RMSE is 280 — a perfectly respectable model. At six observations per parameter, the coefficient is 636 and the error has multiplied by seven. At three, it is 1,364 and 5,874.
And then the bottom two rows stop being a degradation and become an explosion. The largest coefficient is over a million. The test RMSE is three and a half million — on a series where a busy day is four thousand units.
Now here is the part I want you to take away, and it is not in the printed table.
At n = 120, that model’s training RMSE is about 145. It looks fine. If you fitted it and looked only at how it fits the data you gave it, you would ship it. It is the best-fitting model on this slide and it is wrong by a factor of a thousand on data it has not seen.
One technical point, because a careful student will ask. We never crossed the line the lecture warned about. Sixty-two features and eighty rows — there are still more observations than parameters, so OLS has a unique solution the whole way down this table. You do not need k greater than n to get this. Twenty-eight consecutive lags of a smooth series are nearly collinear with one another, and near-collinearity is enough. The matrix does not have to be singular, only close to it.
Now the right-hand column. Same data, same features, same rows — Ridge(alpha=100) instead of LinearRegression(). One word changed. 278, 323, 363, 621, 770.
It gets worse as data gets scarcer, which it should. But it degrades gracefully, and at the row where OLS is out by three and a half million, Ridge is at 621 — roughly the benchmark. Not good, but the model is still a model. That is Lecture 6’s opening argument, and you just measured it.

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
text:
6.4 Step 2 — Two penalties, two behaviors
Back to the full training set. Fit Ridge and LASSO at a comparable penalty and count what survives.

sc = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
Xs, Xts = sc.transform(X_train), sc.transform(X_test)

for name, model in [("OLS",   LinearRegression()),
                    ("Ridge", Ridge(alpha=100)),
                    ("LASSO", Lasso(alpha=20, max_iter=50000))]:
    m = model.fit(Xs, y_train)
    nz = int(np.sum(m.coef_ != 0))
    print(f"  {name:<6} test RMSE {rmse(y_test, m.predict(Xts)):5,.0f}   non-zero coefficients {nz:3d}/{len(FEATURES)}")

Ridge keeps every coefficient and shrinks them. LASSO sets most of them to exactly zero. Neither is “better” — they encode different beliefs about how many predictors genuinely matter.







Walkthrough





Back to the full training set, where OLS was fine, and now compare the two penalties.
  OLS    test RMSE   280   non-zero coefficients  62/62
  Ridge  test RMSE   278   non-zero coefficients  62/62
  LASSO  test RMSE   286   non-zero coefficients  21/62
I want you to notice the disappointing thing first, because if I skip it you will notice it anyway and trust me less.
On the full training set, regularization buys essentially nothing. Ridge is two units better than OLS. LASSO is six units worse. With nineteen observations per parameter there was no problem to solve, and the penalty solved it.
That is the correct lesson, not a failed demo. Regularization is insurance, and Step 1 is the fire. You do not judge insurance by what it pays out in a year when the house doesn’t burn down.
But look at the last column, because that is where the two penalties differ in kind and not just in degree.
Ridge keeps all sixty-two coefficients and shrinks them toward zero. LASSO sets forty-one of them to exactly zero and keeps twenty-one.
So for six units of RMSE — about two percent — LASSO handed you a model with a third as many moving parts. That is not an accuracy trade, it is a communicability trade. Twenty-one coefficients is a model you can print and discuss. Sixty-two is a model you can only run.
Neither penalty is better. They encode different beliefs: Ridge believes many predictors each matter a little, LASSO believes a few matter and the rest are noise. Which belief is right is a question about your data, and in Step 3 you get to see which one this series votes for.

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
section: 6.5 Step 3 — The path, and the order features die in
text:
6.5 Step 3 — The path, and the order features die in
Lecture 6 argued that the order predictors leave is a more stable finding than any single coefficient table. Produce that ordering.

alphas = np.logspace(-1, 3, 60)
paths = []
for a in alphas:
    paths.append(Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000).fit(Xs, y_train).coef_)
paths = np.array(paths)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
axes[0].plot(np.log10(alphas), paths, lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("log10(alpha)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient"); axes[0].set_title("regularization path")
axes[1].plot(np.log10(alphas), (paths != 0).sum(1), marker=".", ms=3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("log10(alpha)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("non-zero coefficients"); axes[1].set_title("model size")
plt.tight_layout()


survivors, order = set(FEATURES), []
for a, coefs in zip(alphas, paths):
    nz = set(np.array(FEATURES)[coefs != 0])
    for gone in survivors - nz:
        order.append(gone)
    survivors = nz

print("the last 8 features standing, in reverse order of elimination:")
for f in reversed(order[-8:]):
    print(f"   {f}")







Look at what survived



Read that list of survivors and find the pattern in the lag numbers before reading on.
Almost all of them are multiples of 7. Nobody told the model this series has a weekly cycle, and there is no explicit “week” feature among the lags. Under increasing penalty the LASSO independently kept the lags that align with day-of-week and discarded the ones that do not.
That is what makes the dropout ordering worth reporting: it recovered the structure of the series, not just a ranking of columns.









Walkthrough





Sixty LASSO fits along a grid of penalties, from 0.1 up to 1,000, and we plot every coefficient’s trajectory.
Each line is one feature. At the left, weak penalty, everything is alive. Move right and lines collapse onto zero one after another. By the right-hand edge — and I checked this — every single coefficient is zero. The model at alpha = 1,000 predicts the mean and nothing else.
The right panel is the same thing counted: model size against penalty. It is a staircase down from 62 to 0. At alpha = 100, nine features are left.
Lecture 6 argued that the order features leave is a more stable finding than any one coefficient table — coefficients wobble under resampling, the elimination order mostly does not. So let’s read the order.
the last 8 features standing, in reverse order of elimination:
   lag28
   lag7
   lag35
   lag364
   lag14
   lag21
   lag1
   lag56






Try it






Pause here. Read those eight lag numbers and find the pattern before I say it.







Every one of them is a multiple of seven except lag1.







Now think about what was available to be chosen. The feature set had twenty-eight consecutive lags — 1, 2, 3, all the way to 28. There is no “week” feature. Nothing in the data told the model that seven days is a meaningful interval. The day-of-week dummies were there as an alternative route to the same information, and the LASSO dropped those too.
Under increasing penalty, forced to give things up, it kept exactly the lags that align with day-of-week and discarded the ones that do not. It also kept lag364 — which is fifty-two weeks, so the same-day-last-year lag that is also a multiple of seven, rather than lag365.
That is why the dropout ordering is worth reporting to someone. It did not just rank your columns. It recovered the structure of the series — a weekly cycle plus an annual echo — from a pile of undifferentiated lags. And it agrees with what the tree found on its own in Lab 4, when day-of-week took 79% of the importance. Two completely different model families, same finding.

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
section: 6.6 Step 4 — Choosing alpha, and the one-standard-error rule
text:
6.6 Step 4 — Choosing alpha, and the one-standard-error rule

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
grid = np.logspace(-1, 2.5, 30)

means, ses = [], []
for a in grid:
    s = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=50000)),
                        X_train, y_train, cv=tscv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    means.append(-s.mean()); ses.append(s.std()/np.sqrt(len(s)))
means, ses = np.array(means), np.array(ses)

i_min = int(means.argmin())
threshold = means[i_min] + ses[i_min]
i_1se = int(np.where(means <= threshold)[0].max())

for label, i in [("CV minimum", i_min), ("one-SE rule", i_1se)]:
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=grid[i], max_iter=50000)).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"  {label:<12} alpha {grid[i]:7.2f}   CV {means[i]:5,.0f}   "
          f"test {rmse(y_test, m.predict(X_test)):5,.0f}   non-zero {int(np.sum(m[-1].coef_ != 0)):3d}")

Your turn: plot the CV curve with its one-standard-error band, and mark both chosen alphas.

The one-SE rule roughly halves the number of surviving features. Decide whether that trade is worth it here — and say what you would need to know about how the model will be used before you could answer properly.







Walkthrough





So far I have been picking penalties by hand. Now do it properly: five-fold TimeSeriesSplit, thirty candidate alphas, and — this matters — the scaler goes inside the pipeline, so it is refitted on each fold’s training rows and never sees the validation fold.
  CV minimum   alpha   19.64   CV   323   test   286   non-zero  21
  one-SE rule  alpha   59.68   CV   346   test   309   non-zero  11
Two ways to read the same CV curve.
The CV minimum takes the alpha with the best cross-validated score. Standard, and it lands on 21 features.
The one-standard-error rule takes the largest alpha — the simplest model — whose CV score is still within one standard error of the best. The argument is that the CV curve is itself an estimate with noise on it, so a model that is statistically indistinguishable from the best but much simpler is the better bet.
Here that means going from 21 features to 11, and paying 23 units of test RMSE for it — 286 up to 309, about eight percent.






Try it






Two things to do. First, uncomment the plot and fill in the blank — the one-SE index — so you can see the band and both verticals. Then answer the question the lab asks: is that trade worth it here?
I’ll give you the shape of the answer rather than the answer, because the honest reply is that the lab has not told you enough to decide.
If this model is going into a dashboard that a person reads and questions, eleven coefficients against twenty-one is a real gain, and eight percent is cheap. If it is one component inside an automated replenishment system that nobody reads, you just paid eight percent for a property nobody consumes.
It is worth knowing what the eleven survivors are: lag1, lag7, lag14, lag21, lag27, lag28, lag35, lag56, lag364, the 364-day rolling mean, and snap. Nine lags, a level, and the SNAP flag. That is a model you could describe out loud in one sentence — and notice snap survived to the very end, which is the same feature permutation importance rescued in Lab 5.

title: 6  Lab 6: Regularization — Breaking OLS, Then Rescuing It
section: 6.7 Step 5 — Why your CV number looks worse than the truth
text:
6.7 Step 5 — Why your CV number looks worse than the truth
The CV RMSE above is noticeably higher than the test RMSE. That is not a mistake, and the reason is sitting in Step 1.

for i, (tr_idx, va_idx) in enumerate(tscv.split(X_train), 1):
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Lasso(alpha=20, max_iter=50000)).fit(X_train[tr_idx], y_train[tr_idx])
    print(f"  fold {i}: train n={len(tr_idx):4d} (n/k={len(tr_idx)/len(FEATURES):4.1f})   "
          f"val n={len(va_idx):3d}   RMSE {rmse(y_train[va_idx], m.predict(X_train[va_idx])):5,.0f}")

Fold 1 trains on about 200 rows — the same data-starved regime that wrecked OLS in Step 1. The final model trains on all 1,210. So walk-forward CV on an expanding window is structurally pessimistic: it averages in early folds that are trained on far less data than the model you actually ship.
That is a reason to read the CV number as a conservative estimate, not a reason to abandon it — and emphatically not a reason to switch to random folds, which fix the pessimism by letting the model see the future.







Walkthrough





One loose end from Step 4 that you should not let pass. The CV score at the minimum was 323. The test RMSE of that same model was 286. Cross-validation was pessimistic by about 13%.
If those had gone the other way you would be worried. This direction has a specific cause, and it is sitting in Step 1.
  fold 1: train n= 205 (n/k= 3.3)   val n=201   RMSE   433
  fold 2: train n= 406 (n/k= 6.5)   val n=201   RMSE   294
  fold 3: train n= 607 (n/k= 9.8)   val n=201   RMSE   325
  fold 4: train n= 808 (n/k=13.0)   val n=201   RMSE   257
  fold 5: train n=1009 (n/k=16.3)   val n=201   RMSE   308
Look at fold 1. It trains on 205 rows — three observations per parameter. That is the row from Step 1’s table where OLS was already at 5,874, and it is scored as though it were the model you are going to ship. It comes in at 433, far worse than any other fold. The model you actually ship trains on all 1,210 rows. No fold ever saw that much data.
So expanding-window cross-validation is structurally pessimistic: it averages in early folds fitted on a fraction of your data. And you can put a number on how much that costs. The five folds average to 323. Drop fold 1 alone and the remaining four average to 296 — against a test RMSE of 286. Almost the entire gap was that one starved fold. Two conclusions, and the second is the one that gets violated in practice.
First: read a walk-forward CV number as a conservative estimate. It is a lower bound on your model’s quality, not an unbiased estimate of it, and being conservative is a fine property in a forecast you are going to stake inventory on.
Second, and please do not do this: the pessimism is not a reason to switch to random k-fold splits. Random folds would fix the number, and they would fix it by training on Thursday to predict the previous Tuesday. The optimistic number you get back would be measuring your model’s ability to interpolate inside a period it has already seen, which is not the job. A pessimistic estimate of the right quantity beats an accurate estimate of the wrong one.

Then the counterpoint, which matters for Homework 4: on the weekly, 30-series panel the ranking may not look the same. What is different about that problem that could change the answer?
And the one to argue about: you have now fitted five model families to this one series. If you had to hand exactly one of them to a store manager who will not be retrained, and who will not retune anything for a year, which do you choose — and is it the one with the lowest RMSE?

Benchmark (same day last year)    625
Single tree (Lab 4)               324
LASSO, 62 features (today)        286
Random Forest (Lab 5)             248
XGBoost (Lab 5)                   244
Today’s model, with six times as many features as the tree ensembles had, lands third.
Say that plainly rather than skating past it. Sixty-two engineered features, a properly cross-validated penalty, and a careful pipeline produced 286 — comfortably better than one tree, and comfortably worse than a Random Forest you fitted in two lines with no feature engineering at all in Lab 5.






Try it






Three questions for the board.
Why trees win here. Name one property of daily store sales that favours a tree ensemble over an additive linear model, however many lags you feed it. It is in the tree you read out loud in Lab 4 — think about what happens on a weekend when yesterday was already busy, and whether a model that adds up separate effects can express that.
The counterpoint, and this one matters for Homework 4. In Homework 4 you run this comparison on the weekly, thirty-series panel with forty-six features. The ranking may not come out the same. What is different about that problem that could change the answer? Think about how many observations per series you get at weekly frequency, and what pooling thirty series does to the noise.
The one to argue about. You have now fitted five model families to this one series — a GAM in Homework 2, a tree, a forest, boosting, and a regularized linear model. Hand exactly one of them to a store manager who will never retune it and will not be retrained. Which, and is it the one with the lowest RMSE?
Notice the two properties this lab measured that RMSE does not see. The eleven-feature LASSO is the only model of the five you could write on a whiteboard. And Step 1 showed you which models fail loudly versus quietly — OLS at n=120 had a beautiful training fit and was wrong by a factor of a thousand. In a year, if this store’s data collection changes and the model quietly gets less data than it used to, which of your five would you rather be running unattended?

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
text:
7.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Two things today, and the second matters more than the first.
First, you will build the machinery Homework 5 needs: turning a panel of 30 series into windowed training examples, and training a feedforward network on them. That scaffolding is the part of Homework 5 most likely to eat an evening, so we do it together.
Second, you will train the same model several times and discover that it gives you a different answer every time. Then you will find out how large that variation is, and what it means for every neural network result you will ever read — including your own.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, torch, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv.

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
text:
7.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))

CHANNELS = ["units", "snap_days", "event_days", "avg_price"]
WINDOW   = 26
CUTOFF   = np.datetime64("2015-05-17")

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))
print(f"{weekly.groupby(['store_id','cat_id']).ngroups} series, {len(weekly):,} rows")

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
section: 7.3 Step 1 — From a panel to windows
text:
7.3 Step 1 — From a panel to windows
A network cannot read a dataframe. It needs a stack of fixed-size examples.
For each series, slide a 26-week window along the history: the window is the input, the units in the following week is the target.

X, Y, D = [], [], []
for _, g in weekly.groupby(["store_id", "cat_id"]):
    arr = g[CHANNELS].values.astype("float32")
    dates = g.week_start.values
    for i in range(len(g) - WINDOW):
        X.append(arr[i:i+WINDOW])      # (26, 4)
        Y.append(arr[i+WINDOW, 0])     # next week's units
        D.append(dates[i+WINDOW])      # the target's date decides train/test

X = np.stack(X); Y = np.array(Y, dtype="float32"); D = np.array(D)
train_mask, test_mask = D < CUTOFF, D >= CUTOFF

print(f"X shape {X.shape}  (windows, weeks, channels)")
print(f"train {train_mask.sum():,}   test {test_mask.sum():,}")

Notice the window count is far larger than the row count. Every week is the end of one window and the interior of twenty-five others, so 8,310 rows become ~7,500 overlapping examples. That overlap is why the effective sample size is much smaller than it looks.
Now standardize — using training statistics only.

mu = X[train_mask].mean(axis=(0, 1), keepdims=True)
sd = X[train_mask].std(axis=(0, 1), keepdims=True) + 1e-8
y_mu, y_sd = Y[train_mask].mean(), Y[train_mask].std()

Xn, Yn = (X - mu) / sd, (Y - y_mu) / y_sd

# flatten each window for a feedforward network: (26, 4) -> 104 features
X_tr = torch.tensor(Xn[train_mask].reshape(train_mask.sum(), -1))
y_tr = torch.tensor(Yn[train_mask])
X_te = torch.tensor(Xn[test_mask].reshape(test_mask.sum(), -1))

print(f"flattened to {X_tr.shape[1]} features per example")

This block is what Homework 5 Part 1 Q1 asks for. Keep it.







Walkthrough





30 series, 8,310 rows
X shape (7530, 26, 4)  (windows, weeks, channels)
train 5,940   test 1,590
Here is the reframing that every method from here to the end of the course depends on.
A network cannot read a dataframe. It needs a stack of identically-shaped examples. So for each series we slide a 26-week window along the history: those 26 weeks are the input, the units in week 27 are the target, and the target’s date decides whether the example is training or test.
Four channels — units, SNAP days, event days, average price. Twenty-six weeks. So each example is a 26-by-4 block.
Now notice the count, because it is a trap dressed as good news. 8,310 rows became 7,530 examples. It looks like you have seven and a half thousand independent observations. You do not. Every week appears in twenty-six different windows — once as a target, twenty-five times as interior context. The examples overlap almost completely with their neighbors.
So the effective sample size is far smaller than 7,530, and that matters for how much you should trust anything this network tells you. Half of Homework 5’s difficulty is remembering this.
flattened to 104 features per example
Two details, both of which are graded in Homework 5.
The statistics come from training data only. mu and sd are computed under train_mask and then applied to everything. Standardizing with statistics computed over the full dataset leaks test-period information into training, and it will not raise an error — it will just quietly make your results better than they are.
And then we flatten. Twenty-six weeks by four channels becomes 104 numbers in a row. A feedforward network has no notion of sequence; it sees 104 unordered features. Hold that thought — it is the answer to one of the closing questions, and it is what Lecture 8 exists to fix. This block is Homework 5 Part 1 Question 1. Keep it.

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
text:
7.4 Step 2 — Train a network

def make_model(n_features, seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(n_features, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2),
        nn.Linear(128, 64),         nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2),
        nn.Linear(64, 1))

def train(model, epochs=60, lr=5e-4, weight_decay=0.0):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=64, shuffle=False)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            opt.zero_grad()
            lossfn(model(xb).squeeze(-1), yb).backward()
            opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return rmse(Y[test_mask], model(X_te).squeeze(-1).numpy() * y_sd + y_mu)

model = make_model(X_tr.shape[1], seed=1)
print(f"parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
print(f"test RMSE:  {train(model):,.0f}")

Note shuffle=False. Almost every PyTorch tutorial sets it True. For a time series it destroys the ordering, and nothing warns you.
Compare that RMSE against your records. XGBoost managed 781 on this panel in Homework 4, and a 46-coefficient LASSO managed 744. Your network has around 22,000 parameters.







Walkthrough





parameters: 21,761
test RMSE:  1,109
Three layers — 104 in, 128, 64, one out — with ReLU and dropout between them. Twenty-one thousand seven hundred and sixty-one parameters, trained on 5,940 overlapping examples.
One line deserves attention. shuffle=False in the DataLoader. Almost every PyTorch tutorial you will find sets it to True, because for images it is right. For a time series it destroys the ordering, and — this is the theme of the lab — nothing warns you. No error, no warning, just a number that is wrong in a way you cannot see.
Now the result. 1,109 on the test weeks, against a seasonal-naive benchmark of 2,152. So the network is roughly twice as good as the benchmark. On a panel where a typical week is about 9,300 units, that is an error of about 12%.
And now the comparison you should not skip. On this same panel, in Homework 4, XGBoost managed 781 and a 46-coefficient LASSO managed 744. Twenty-two thousand parameters lost to forty-six coefficients. Not narrowly — by about 45%.
I am not going to soften that, and you should not expect the rest of the lab to rescue it. It is the honest result on this dataset, and why is one of your discussion questions. But hold the number 1,109 loosely for about ninety seconds, because Step 3 is going to tell you how much that particular number is worth.

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
text:
7.5 Step 3 — Run it again
Same code, same data, same settings. Only the random seed changes.

for seed in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f"seed {seed}:  test RMSE {train(make_model(X_tr.shape[1], seed)):,.0f}")

Say out loud what just happened, because it is the point of the lab. Nothing about the problem changed. The differences you see come entirely from random weight initialization and dropout.







Walkthrough





Same code. Same data. Same settings. Same machine. The only thing that changes is the random seed — which controls the initial weights and which units dropout switches off.
seed 1:  test RMSE 1,109
seed 2:  test RMSE 1,176
seed 3:  test RMSE 946






Try it






Pause the video and say what just happened, in one sentence, before I do. Nothing about the problem changed and the answer moved by 230 RMSE — from 946 to 1,176.
Sit with the size of that. 230 is not a rounding error. It is about 20% of the result. It is larger than most differences you will ever see quoted between two competing architectures in a blog post.
And notice which seed won. Seed 3 gives 946 — the best number anywhere in this lab. If I had run seed 3 first and stopped there, I would have reported 946 and believed it. If I had run seed 2 first, I would have reported 1,176 and believed that. The reported number would depend entirely on an integer nobody thinks of as part of the experiment. That is the whole lab. Everything from here is working out the consequences.

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
section: 7.6 Step 4 — So how would you compare two settings?
text:
7.6 Step 4 — So how would you compare two settings?
Here is the trap. Suppose you want to know whether weight decay helps. You try three values, train once each, and pick the winner.

single = {wd: train(make_model(X_tr.shape[1], seed=1), weight_decay=wd)
          for wd in (0.0, 1e-4, 1e-2)}
for wd, r in single.items():
    print(f"weight_decay={wd:<7} test RMSE {r:,.0f}")

Now do it honestly — five seeds per setting, and look at the spread as well as the mean.

rows = []
for wd in (0.0, 1e-4, 1e-2):
    runs = [train(make_model(X_tr.shape[1], s), weight_decay=wd) for s in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)]
    rows.append({"weight_decay": f"{wd:g}", "mean": round(np.mean(runs)),
                 "sd": round(np.std(runs)), "min": round(min(runs)), "max": round(max(runs))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))







Compare the two tables before you go on



When this was run while writing the lab, the single-seed experiment made 1e-4 look like the winner — about 100 RMSE better than no weight decay at all. On five seeds the two means differed by 4.
That 100-point advantage was not a small effect measured imprecisely. It did not exist.
The five-seed table also shows something the single run cannot: 1e-2 is not just worse on average, its spread is three times wider. A setting that sometimes returns 1,050 and sometimes 1,792 is a different kind of bad from one that reliably returns 1,240 — and you would never learn that from one run.


Your turn: using your own two tables, state the smallest RMSE difference you would be willing to call real.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in ----
# spread = ___                      # <- a number from your five-seed table
# print(f"differences smaller than about {spread:,.0f} RMSE are not evidence")








Walkthrough





Here is the trap, and it is the single most common mistake in applied deep learning. You want to know whether weight decay helps. Three values, one training run each, pick the winner.
weight_decay=0.0     test RMSE 1,109
weight_decay=0.0001  test RMSE 1,007
weight_decay=0.01    test RMSE 1,142
Clear result. 1e-4 wins by 102 RMSE over no weight decay at all. Nine percent. You would write that down, you would put it in a slide, and honestly most people would put it in a paper.
Now do it honestly. Five seeds per setting, and report the spread as well as the mean.
weight_decay  mean  sd  min  max
           0  1084  86  946 1176
      0.0001  1088 134  991 1343
        0.01  1241 278 1050 1792
The two means differ by four.
Not “the effect was smaller than we thought.” Not “the advantage was modest.” The 102-point advantage that the single-seed experiment found did not exist. Seed 1 happened to be a good draw for 1e-4 and an average draw for zero, and that is the entire finding.
Look closer and it is worse than that. On min and on max, no weight decay is better than 1e-4 — 946 against 991, 1,176 against 1,343. The setting with the worse spread has the marginally better mean, by four. There is no effect here in any direction.
Now the column the single run could never have produced: sd.
1e-2 is worse on average — 1,241 — but the important number is 278, more than three times the spread of no weight decay at all. It returned 1,050 once and 1,792 another time. That is a different kind of bad from a setting that reliably lands at 1,240. One is a model that is mediocre; the other is a model you cannot make promises about. You cannot see that in one run. Ever.






Try it






Fill in the blank and answer the question in your own words: what is the smallest RMSE difference you would be willing to call real on this problem?
There is no single right answer, but there is a defensible way to reason. The run-to-run standard deviation at your best setting is about 86. Two single runs differing by less than that are telling you nothing at all. If you want to claim a difference of that size is real, you need several seeds per setting and you need to compare the distributions, not the winners.
Which means: a difference under roughly 100 RMSE, from single runs, is not evidence. And you will notice that this disqualifies almost every architecture comparison you have ever read.

title: 7  Lab 7: Your First Network — and Why One Run Proves Nothing
text:
7.7 Step 5 — Break it on purpose
One line, no error message.

def train_broken(model, epochs=60, lr=5e-4):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=64, shuffle=False)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            # opt.zero_grad()        <-- deleted
            lossfn(model(xb).squeeze(-1), yb).backward()
            opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return rmse(Y[test_mask], model(X_te).squeeze(-1).numpy() * y_sd + y_mu)

print(f"with    zero_grad():  {train(make_model(X_tr.shape[1], 1)):,.0f}")
print(f"without zero_grad():  {train_broken(make_model(X_tr.shape[1], 1)):,.0f}")

Without zero_grad(), PyTorch accumulates gradients across batches instead of replacing them, so every update uses a sum of all gradients seen so far in that epoch.
No exception. No warning. Just a model that trains badly — and note how badly. The broken version lands at 7,325, which is more than three times worse than the seasonal-naive benchmark of 2,152. A one-line omission turned a working model into something far worse than predicting last year’s value.







Walkthrough





One last thing, and it is the same theme in a different costume.
Look at train_broken. One line is commented out — opt.zero_grad(). Everything else is identical.
with    zero_grad():  1,109
without zero_grad():  7,325
PyTorch accumulates gradients by default. It does not replace them. If you never zero them, every update is driven by the sum of every gradient seen so far in that epoch — so the steps get larger and larger and increasingly unrelated to the batch in front of you.
The result is 7,325. The seasonal-naive benchmark is 2,152. The broken model is three and a half times worse than predicting last year’s value.
And the point is not the number, it is everything that did not happen. No exception. No warning. No NaN. The loop ran to completion in the normal amount of time and returned a float. If you had not had a benchmark to compare against, you would have had no way to know.
That is why Lecture 1 spent a whole session on benchmarks, and it is why every scoreboard in this course starts with seasonal naive. A benchmark is not there to flatter your model. It is the only thing standing between you and a silent bug.

Three questions for the board.
The seeds. You now know a single run tells you very little. But papers, blog posts, and vendor benchmarks routinely report exactly one. When you read “our model achieves RMSE 1,050”, what do you need to know before believing it beats a baseline at 1,100? Be specific about what you would ask for — and notice that today, a 50-point gap is well inside one standard deviation.

title: 8  Lab 8: Convolutions — What the Filter Can Actually See
text:
8.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Last week you flattened a 26-week window into a vector of 104 numbers and fed it to a network. That model had no idea the window was ordered — week 1 and week 26 were just positions in a list.
A convolution does know. It slides a filter along the time axis and looks for local shapes.
Today you will build one, and then find out how far back it can actually see — which is considerably less than the window you hand it, and is the single most useful thing to understand about this architecture.
You will also use last week’s lesson: every comparison here runs on three seeds, because one run tells you nothing.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, torch, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv.

title: 8  Lab 8: Convolutions — What the Filter Can Actually See
text:
8.2 Setup
Same windowing as Lab 7, with one change that matters.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first.")

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))
CHANNELS = ["units", "snap_days", "event_days", "avg_price"]
CUTOFF   = np.datetime64("2015-05-17")
rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

def build(W):
    X, Y, D = [], [], []
    for _, g in weekly.groupby(["store_id", "cat_id"]):
        arr, dates = g[CHANNELS].values.astype("float32"), g.week_start.values
        for i in range(len(g) - W):
            X.append(arr[i:i+W]); Y.append(arr[i+W, 0]); D.append(dates[i+W])
    X = np.stack(X); Y = np.array(Y, dtype="float32"); D = np.array(D)
    tr, te = D < CUTOFF, D >= CUTOFF
    mu, sd = X[tr].mean((0,1), keepdims=True), X[tr].std((0,1), keepdims=True) + 1e-8
    ym, ys = Y[tr].mean(), Y[tr].std()
    Xn, Yn = (X - mu)/sd, (Y - ym)/ys
    # Conv1d wants (batch, channels, time) -- the transpose is the whole point
    return (torch.tensor(Xn[tr].transpose(0, 2, 1)), torch.tensor(Yn[tr]),
            torch.tensor(Xn[te].transpose(0, 2, 1)), Y[te], ym, ys)

DATA = {W: build(W) for W in (13, 26, 52)}
print("shapes at W=26:", DATA[26][0].shape, "(batch, channels, time)")







The transpose that bites everyone



Your DataLoader naturally yields (batch, time, channels). Conv1d demands (batch, channels, time).
Get it backwards and nothing crashes. The model convolves across the four channels instead of along time, learns something meaningless, and returns a number. Same failure mode as forgetting zero_grad() last week: no exception, just a wrong answer.









Walkthrough





shapes at W=26: torch.Size([5940, 4, 26]) (batch, channels, time)
Same windowing as Lab 7, wrapped in a build() function so we can rebuild it at three window lengths. Same panel, same cutoff, same train/test split, statistics from training rows only. One change matters, and it is in the last line of build.
Conv1d wants . Your natural windowing produces (batch, time, channels)**. So there is a transpose, and the comment calls it “the whole point.”
Read this callout properly, because it is the same species of bug as last week’s missing zero_grad().
Get the transpose backwards and nothing crashes. The shapes are still valid — you have four of one thing and twenty-six of another, and Conv1d will happily convolve across the four channels as though they were the time axis. It will slide a filter over “units, SNAP days, event days, price” in that order, learn something with no meaning at all, and return a number that looks like an RMSE.
That is the third time this course has shown you the same shape of failure: shuffle=True on a time series, a missing zero_grad(), and now a transposed axis. None of them raise. All of them return a plausible number. This is what makes deep learning code different from regression code — the language cannot tell you that your tensor means the wrong thing.

title: 8  Lab 8: Convolutions — What the Filter Can Actually See
section: 8.3 Step 1 — How far back can the filter see?
text:
8.3 Step 1 — How far back can the filter see?
Before building anything, work this out on paper.
Our network is Conv1d(4, 32, kernel_size=5) then Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=3).

A neuron in layer 1 sees 5 consecutive weeks.
A neuron in layer 2 sees 3 layer-1 neurons — which between them span \(3 + (5 - 1) = \mathbf{7}\) weeks.


def receptive_field(kernels):
    rf = 1
    for k in reversed(kernels):
        rf = rf + (k - 1)
    return rf

print(f"kernels (5, 3)      -> receptive field {receptive_field([5,3])} weeks")
print(f"kernels (5, 3, 3)   -> receptive field {receptive_field([5,3,3])} weeks")
print(f"kernels (5, 3, 3, 3)-> receptive field {receptive_field([5,3,3,3])} weeks")

Seven weeks. Not 26 — seven. Hand this model a 52-week window and each output neuron still sees only seven consecutive weeks of it.
Hold that fact. Step 4 tests what it costs.







Walkthrough





Before we build anything, we do the arithmetic on paper. This is the calculation that decides whether the architecture can possibly work, and it takes ten seconds. Our network is Conv1d(4, 32, kernel_size=5) and then Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=3).
A neuron in the first layer sees five consecutive weeks — that is what kernel size 5 means.
A neuron in the second layer sees three first-layer neurons. But those three overlap: each sees five weeks, shifted by one. So between them they span 3 + (5 − 1) = seven weeks.
kernels (5, 3)      -> receptive field 7 weeks
kernels (5, 3, 3)   -> receptive field 9 weeks
kernels (5, 3, 3, 3)-> receptive field 11 weeks
Seven weeks. Not twenty-six. Seven.
And look at what stacking buys: each extra kernel-3 layer adds two weeks. Two. You go from seven to nine to eleven, one whole convolutional layer at a time.
Hand this network a 52-week window and every output neuron still sees seven consecutive weeks of it. The annual cycle — the thing that actually drives a retail series — is not merely hard for this model to find. It is outside what any neuron in it can look at. Hold that. Step 4 measures what it costs.

title: 8  Lab 8: Convolutions — What the Filter Can Actually See
text:
8.4 Step 2 — Build the CNN

def conv_out_len(W):
    return W - 4 - 2          # kernel 5, then kernel 3, no padding

def make_cnn(W, head, seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    body = [nn.Conv1d(4, 32, 5), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv1d(32, 64, 3), nn.ReLU()]
    if head == "flatten":
        tail = [nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * conv_out_len(W), 1)]
    elif head == "avgpool":
        tail = [nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64, 1)]
    else:
        tail = [nn.AdaptiveMaxPool1d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64, 1)]
    return nn.Sequential(*body, *tail)

def train(model, W, epochs=40):
    Xtr, Ytr, Xte, Yte, ym, ys = DATA[W]
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr), batch_size=128, shuffle=False)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            opt.zero_grad(); lossfn(model(xb).squeeze(-1), yb).backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return rmse(Yte, model(Xte).squeeze(-1).numpy() * ys + ym)

m = make_cnn(26, "flatten", seed=1)
print(f"parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()):,}")
print(f"test RMSE:  {train(m, 26):,.0f}")








Walkthrough





parameters: 8,161
test RMSE:  980
Two convolutional layers, then a head that flattens and maps to one output.
Compare that parameter count with last week: 8,161 against 21,761. The CNN is about a third the size of the feedforward network — because the filters are shared across all time positions instead of every input getting its own weight. And on this single seed it scores 980, against the FFN’s 1,109.
Smaller model, better number. That is the convolutional bargain: weight sharing buys you efficiency, as long as the thing you are looking for is local. Which — per Step 1 — means seven weeks local. Keep that qualifier attached.

title: 8  Lab 8: Convolutions — What the Filter Can Actually See
text:
8.5 Step 3 — Does pooling belong here?
Lecture 8 argued that pooling buys translation invariance — an image classifier should not care where in the frame the cat is — and that a forecaster usually should care where the spike was.
Test it. Three heads, three seeds each, because of last week.

head_runs = {}
rows = []
for head in ("flatten", "maxpool", "avgpool"):
    head_runs[head] = [train(make_cnn(26, head, s), 26) for s in (1, 2, 3)]
    rows.append({"head": head, "mean": round(np.mean(head_runs[head])),
                 "sd": round(np.std(head_runs[head])),
                 "runs": [round(r) for r in head_runs[head]]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

Read the spread before the means. The run-to-run sd is around 50–80. The gap between flatten and avgpool is several hundred. That difference is real in a way last week’s weight decay comparison was not.
Flatten keeps all 64 channels at all 20 remaining time positions, so the final layer knows where each pattern was found. AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) averages across time and throws that away.

Say it in one sentence: why would averaging over time be the right thing to do for classifying photographs and the wrong thing for forecasting demand?








Walkthrough





Lecture 8 argued that pooling buys translation invariance. An image classifier should not care where in the frame the cat is; pooling throws away position and keeps the presence of the pattern. That is exactly right for photographs.
The claim was that a forecaster usually should care where the spike was. A demand spike three weeks ago and a demand spike twenty weeks ago are different facts about next week.
Three heads, three seeds each.
   head  mean  sd               runs
flatten  1032  80   [980, 1145, 972]
maxpool  1418  47 [1433, 1354, 1467]
avgpool  1534  81 [1643, 1448, 1509]
Read the spread before you read the means — that is the habit last week was for.
Run-to-run standard deviation is 47 to 81. The gap between flatten and avgpool is 502. That is six to ten times the noise. Unlike last week’s weight decay comparison, this difference is unambiguously real, and you can say so with three runs precisely because you measured the spread.
The mechanism is worth stating exactly. Flatten keeps all 64 channels at all 20 surviving time positions and hands the final layer 1,280 numbers — so the model knows where each pattern was found. AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) collapses the time axis to a single average per channel: 64 numbers. It keeps “this pattern occurred” and discards “it occurred in week 22.”






Try it






Pause and answer: why is averaging over position right for classifying photographs and wrong for forecasting demand?
Because in a photograph, position is nuisance — the cat is a cat wherever it sits, and a model that has to learn “cat in the top left” and “cat in the middle” separately is wasting capacity. In a forecast, position is the signal. Recency is the single most informative thing about a lag, and average pooling deletes it.
Note that max pooling is less bad than average pooling — 1,418 against 1,534 — which fits: max at least preserves the strongest response rather than diluting it across the window. Both are far behind keeping the positions.
