section: 8.6 Step 4 — A longer window, the same receptive field
text:
8.6 Step 4 — A longer window, the same receptive field
Now the experiment Step 1 set up. Keep the architecture fixed and vary only the window.

rows = []
for W in (13, 26, 52):
    # W=26 was already fitted in Step 3 -- reuse those three rather than paying twice
    runs = head_runs["flatten"] if W == 26 else [train(make_cnn(W, "flatten", s), W) for s in (1, 2, 3)]
    n_par = sum(p.numel() for p in make_cnn(W, "flatten", 1).parameters())
    rows.append({"window": W, "receptive_field": receptive_field([5,3]),
                 "parameters": n_par, "mean_RMSE": round(np.mean(runs)),
                 "sd": round(np.std(runs)), "runs": [round(r) for r in runs]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))







The result runs the wrong way, and that is the lesson



A longer window does not help. Read the ends of the table, not the middle.
13 weeks and 26 weeks sit inside each other’s run-to-run spread — a 52-point gap against a standard deviation of 80. That is exactly the kind of difference Lab 7 taught you not to trust, and you should not trust it here either. But 52 weeks is 123 RMSE worse than 13 weeks, a gap no seed accounts for: the worst 13-week run still beats the best 52-week run.
The receptive field is stuck at seven weeks no matter how much history you supply. What a longer window does add is parameters — the flatten layer grows with W, from 7,329 to 9,825 — so you get more capacity to overfit and no additional context to justify it.
More data into the model is not more information out of it, unless the architecture can reach it.


Your turn: using receptive_field(), find how many kernel-3 layers you would need to stack after the first kernel-5 layer to actually span 52 weeks.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in ----
# k = [5]
# while receptive_field(k) < 52:
#     k.append(___)               # <- what kernel size?
# print(f"{len(k)} layers needed: kernels {k} -> {receptive_field(k)} weeks")








Walkthrough





Now the experiment Step 1 set up, and it is the reason this lab exists.
Keep the architecture completely fixed — same two layers, same kernels, same seven-week receptive field — and vary only how much history you hand it. Thirteen weeks, twenty-six, fifty-two. Three seeds each, and we reuse Step 3’s three flatten runs for the 26-week row rather than paying for them twice.
 window  receptive_field  parameters  mean_RMSE  sd               runs
     13                7        7329        980  42   [1039, 960, 943]
     26                7        8161       1032  80    [980, 1145, 972]
     52                7        9825       1103  26  [1111, 1068, 1131]
Quadrupling the window made the forecast worse.
Now let me show you how to read this table honestly, because there are two different claims in it and only one of them is safe.
The middle comparison is not evidence. Thirteen weeks against twenty-six is 980 against 1,032 — a gap of 52, when the 26-week row’s own standard deviation is 80. Last week you decided that differences smaller than about 100 RMSE, from a handful of runs, are not findings. That rule applies to results you like as much as results you don’t. Those two windows are indistinguishable.
The ends are evidence. Thirteen weeks against fifty-two is 980 against 1,103 — 123 RMSE, and the spreads do not touch: the worst 13-week run, 1,039, still beats the best 52-week run, 1,068. Three seeds each, no overlap. That one you can report.
So the finding is: giving this architecture four times the history made it measurably worse, and giving it twice the history did nothing at all.
Why? Look at the two columns either side of the RMSE. The receptive field is 7 on every row — it does not move, because nothing about the architecture changed. The parameter count goes 7,329, 8,161, 9,825 — because the flatten layer’s input grows with the window.
So a longer window adds capacity and adds no reach. Every extra week you supply becomes more weights to fit and not one additional week that any neuron can actually look at. That is a recipe for overfitting, and the 52-week column is what it looks like.
More data into the model is not more information out of it, unless the architecture can reach it.






Try it






Fill in the blank in the next cell and find out how many kernel-3 layers you would have to stack after that first kernel-5 layer to span a full 52 weeks.
The answer is 24 — twenty-five convolutional layers in total, for a receptive field of 53 weeks. Twenty-three is not enough; it reaches 51.
Sit with that for a second. To let this architecture see one year, you would need a twenty-five-layer network — on 5,940 training examples that overlap almost completely. Nobody is going to do that, and if they did it would overfit spectacularly.
That is the honest limit of a plain 1D CNN for this problem, and it is why the next lecture is about a different mechanism rather than a deeper stack of the same one. Real practitioners reach for dilated convolutions here — filters with gaps in them, so the receptive field grows multiplicatively instead of by two per layer. That is a genuine third option and worth knowing the name of.

XGBoost (HW4)                     781

Say the honest version of this table.
The CNN at 1,032 and the FFN at 1,084 differ by 52 — and you measured the run-to-run spread at 80. So the correct statement is not “the CNN beat the feedforward network.” It is: the two are indistinguishable on this problem. One-third the parameters, a genuinely better inductive bias, ordering preserved — and it bought nothing measurable.
Both are well behind a 46-coefficient LASSO at 744.
That is not a failure of the lab and it is not a bad implementation. It is a result about the problem. The useful signal in weekly store sales sits at lags a seven-week filter cannot reach — last year’s same week, the annual shape — and no amount of care inside this architecture will recover something the receptive field excludes.
Which is the honest reason to move on to Lecture 9, and not a reason to conclude that convolutions are bad.

title: 9  Lab 9 Part 1: Recurrence — and When Gates Are Not Worth It
text:
9.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Labs 7 and 8 gave you two models that could not properly use a window. The feedforward network flattened it and lost the ordering; the CNN kept ordering but could only see seven weeks at a time.
A recurrent network has neither limit. It reads the sequence in order and carries a hidden state, so in principle nothing stops it using the whole window.
Today you build two of them — a plain RNN and an LSTM — and find that at the training budget anyone would have used, the more sophisticated one loses badly. Then you vary the budget and the result changes. Working out which claim the evidence actually supports, and why, is the point of the lab, and it is the most transferable thing in it.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, torch, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv. Most fits are quick — about six seconds each. The exception is Step 4, which trains four models to 100 epochs and takes two to three minutes; start it and read the text underneath while it runs.

title: 9  Lab 9 Part 1: Recurrence — and When Gates Are Not Worth It
text:
9.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first.")

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))
CHANNELS = ["units", "snap_days", "event_days", "avg_price"]
CUTOFF   = np.datetime64("2015-05-17")
rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

def build(W):
    X, Y, D = [], [], []
    for _, g in weekly.groupby(["store_id", "cat_id"]):
        arr, dates = g[CHANNELS].values.astype("float32"), g.week_start.values
        for i in range(len(g) - W):
            X.append(arr[i:i+W]); Y.append(arr[i+W, 0]); D.append(dates[i+W])
    X = np.stack(X); Y = np.array(Y, dtype="float32"); D = np.array(D)
    tr, te = D < CUTOFF, D >= CUTOFF
    mu, sd = X[tr].mean((0,1), keepdims=True), X[tr].std((0,1), keepdims=True) + 1e-8
    ym, ys = Y[tr].mean(), Y[tr].std()
    Xn, Yn = (X - mu)/sd, (Y - ym)/ys
    # recurrent layers want (batch, time, channels) -- NOT the Conv1d layout
    return (torch.tensor(Xn[tr]), torch.tensor(Yn[tr]), torch.tensor(Xn[te]), Y[te], ym, ys)

DATA = {W: build(W) for W in (13, 26, 52)}
print("shape at W=26:", DATA[26][0].shape, "(batch, time, channels)")







The layout flips back



Conv1d wanted (batch, channels, time). nn.RNN and nn.LSTM with batch_first=True want (batch, time, channels) — the transpose you added in Lab 8 must come out again here.
Neither library will complain. Both will train on nonsense.









Walkthrough





Same build() function as Lab 8, same panel, same cutoff, same standardization from training rows only. Three window lengths again — 13, 26, 52. One line is different from last week, and it is the one the callout is about.
The layout flips back. Conv1d wanted (batch, channels, time). nn.RNN and nn.LSTM with batch_first=True want (batch, time, channels) — so the transpose you carefully added last week has to come out again this week.
And as always: neither library complains. Feed an RNN the Conv1d layout and it will read your four channels as a four-step sequence, treat the 26 weeks as features, train to convergence, and hand you a number.
That is now the fourth instance of the same failure mode in this course — shuffle=True, missing zero_grad(), transposed axes for the convolution, and now transposed back for the recurrence. None of them raise. I keep pointing at it because it is the single biggest practical difference between this material and the regression you did in Lecture 6, where a shape error is an error.

title: 9  Lab 9 Part 1: Recurrence — and When Gates Are Not Worth It
text:
9.3 Step 1 — A plain RNN
One recurrent layer, then a linear layer on the final hidden state — the summary after reading the whole window.

class Recurrent(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, kind, n_channels=4, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        layer = nn.RNN if kind == "rnn" else nn.LSTM
        self.rnn = layer(n_channels, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.fc  = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        out, _ = self.rnn(x)          # nn.LSTM returns out, (h, c) -- the _ absorbs both
        return self.fc(out[:, -1, :]).squeeze(-1)

def train(kind, W, seed, epochs=30):
    Xtr, Ytr, Xte, Yte, ym, ys = DATA[W]
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = Recurrent(kind)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr), batch_size=128, shuffle=False)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            opt.zero_grad()
            lossfn(model(xb), yb).backward()
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)   # see below
            opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        score = rmse(Yte, model(Xte).numpy() * ys + ym)
    return score, sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

score, n_par = train("rnn", 26, seed=1)
print(f"vanilla RNN — {n_par:,} parameters, test RMSE {score:,.0f}")

clip_grad_norm_ is not decoration. Backpropagating through 26 steps multiplies gradients repeatedly, and the product can explode. Clipping caps the update size. It is one line, it costs nothing, and recurrent models are the place you need it.







Walkthrough





One recurrent layer, then a linear layer on the final hidden state — the summary after the model has read the whole window.
vanilla RNN — 4,545 parameters, test RMSE 860
Four and a half thousand parameters. Hold that against Lab 7’s feedforward network, which had 21,761, and Lab 8’s CNN at 8,161. This is the smallest model in the entire neural section, and on this seed it is already the best.
One line deserves a word. clip_grad_norm_ is not decoration. Backpropagating through 26 steps multiplies gradients together 26 times, and that product can explode as easily as it can vanish. Clipping caps the size of the update. It costs nothing, and recurrent models are exactly where you need it.

title: 9  Lab 9 Part 1: Recurrence — and When Gates Are Not Worth It
text:
9.4 Step 2 — An LSTM
Identical code, one word changed.

score_lstm, n_par_lstm = train("lstm", 26, seed=1)
print(f"LSTM        — {n_par_lstm:,} parameters, test RMSE {score_lstm:,.0f}")
print(f"\nparameter ratio: {n_par_lstm / n_par:.1f}x the RNN")

Account for that ratio before reading the RMSE. An LSTM has a forget gate, an input gate, an output gate and a candidate — four sets of weights where the RNN has one. Same hidden size, four times the parameters.

LSTM        — 17,985 parameters, test RMSE 1,004

parameter ratio: 4.0x the RNN

9.5 Step 3 — Which wins, and does it hold?
One comparison at one window is not evidence. Vary the window and use two seeds.

rows = []
for W in (13, 26, 52):
    r = [train("rnn",  W, s)[0] for s in (1, 2)]
    l = [train("lstm", W, s)[0] for s in (1, 2)]
    rows.append({"window": W,
                 "RNN": round(np.mean(r)),  "RNN_sd": round(np.std(r)),
                 "LSTM": round(np.mean(l)), "LSTM_sd": round(np.std(l)),
                 "winner": "RNN" if np.mean(r) < np.mean(l) else "LSTM"})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))







Read the columns in this order



The winner column first. At this training budget, on this panel, the plain RNN wins at every window length. That part is not a seed artifact — the run-to-run spreads (3 to 33) are tiny next to the gaps (112 to 193).
Then the parameter count. The model that lost has four times as many parameters as the model that won.
Then be suspicious. Both models trained for exactly 30 epochs, because that is what train() defaults to. Nothing above establishes that 30 epochs is enough for both of them — and a model with four times the parameters is not obviously finished learning at the same point as the smaller one. Step 4 checks, and the answer is not the one this table implies.

section: 9.6 Step 4 — Was that a fair fight?
text:
9.6 Step 4 — Was that a fair fight?
Step 3 compared two models at one training budget. Lab 7 taught you not to trust a comparison run at one seed; this is the same objection one level up. An LSTM has four times the parameters, and bigger models generally take longer to converge.
So train both to 100 epochs, and record the test RMSE along the way instead of only at the end.

CKPT = [10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 80, 100]

def curve(kind, W, seed):
    """Train once to 100 epochs, scoring the test set at each checkpoint."""
    Xtr, Ytr, Xte, Yte, ym, ys = DATA[W]
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = Recurrent(kind)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(Xtr, Ytr), batch_size=128, shuffle=False)
    out = {}
    for ep in range(1, max(CKPT) + 1):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            opt.zero_grad(); lossfn(model(xb), yb).backward()
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
        if ep in CKPT:
            model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                out[ep] = rmse(Yte, model(Xte).numpy() * ys + ym)
    return out

paths = {}
for kind in ("rnn", "lstm"):
    runs = [curve(kind, 26, s) for s in (1, 2)]        # fit each seed ONCE
    paths[kind] = [np.mean([r[e] for r in runs]) for e in CKPT]

table = pd.DataFrame({"epochs": CKPT,
                      "RNN":  [round(v) for v in paths["rnn"]],
                      "LSTM": [round(v) for v in paths["lstm"]]})
table["gap"] = table.LSTM - table.RNN
print(table.to_string(index=False))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ax.plot(CKPT, paths["rnn"],  marker="o", label="vanilla RNN")
ax.plot(CKPT, paths["lstm"], marker="o", label="LSTM")
ax.axvline(30, ls="--", lw=1, color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("epochs"); ax.set_ylabel("test RMSE"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Step 3 measured at the dashed line", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()







The gap is largest at exactly the budget we used



Read the gap column downwards. It is negative at 10 epochs — the LSTM is ahead early — then peaks at 30, the setting Step 3 used, and shrinks at every checkpoint after until the two models are level.
Look at the shapes, not just the endpoint. The RNN is finished by about epoch 45 and flat thereafter. The LSTM is still improving at 100 epochs; its curve has not turned over. We ran out of patience, not the model.
So the honest verdict is not “the LSTM loses.” It is:

at a fixed 30-epoch budget the RNN is far ahead — and 30 epochs is the point of its maximum advantage anywhere in this range;
given enough epochs the two are tied;
the RNN reaches its best score about three times faster, on a quarter of the parameters.

That last line is a real advantage and worth having. It is simply a different claim from the one the Step 3 table appears to make — and you could not have told the two apart without varying the budget.


Your turn: the run-to-run spread in Step 3 was roughly 20 RMSE. From which checkpoint on is the gap smaller than that?

# print(table[table.gap.abs() < noise].epochs.tolist())








Walkthrough





This is the step the lab is really about, and I want to be honest that it was added after the fact. The first version of this lab stopped at Step 3.
Lab 7 taught you not to trust a comparison run at one seed. This is the same objection one level up: not one seed, one budget. So train both models to 100 epochs and record the test RMSE at seven checkpoints along the way, instead of only at the end.
 epochs  RNN  LSTM  gap
     10 1099  1002  -97
     20  922  1033  111
     30  842   987  145
     45  834   953  119
     60  828   926   98
     80  833   885   52
    100  830   821   -9
Read the gap column down. At ten epochs it is negative — the LSTM is ahead. At thirty it is plus one forty-five. Then 119, 98, 52, and at a hundred epochs it is minus nine.
The gap is largest at exactly the budget we used in Step 3. Not near the largest — the largest anywhere in the range.
And look at the shapes, because they are different. The RNN goes 834, 828, 833, 830 from epoch 45 onward. Flat. Finished. The LSTM goes 953, 926, 885, 821 — still falling at epoch 100, and its curve has not turned over. We ran out of patience, not the model.
So the honest verdict is not “the LSTM loses.” It is three separate statements, and you need all three.
At a fixed 30-epoch budget, the RNN wins by a wide margin — that is true and it is what Step 3 measured. Given enough epochs, the two tie. And the RNN reaches its best score roughly three times faster on a quarter of the parameters.
That third one is a real advantage and worth having. Convergence speed matters when you are tuning, when you are retraining nightly, when compute is billed. But it is an optimization advantage, not a verdict on gating — and those are different claims that the Step 3 table cannot tell apart.






Try it






The run-to-run spread in Step 3 was about 20. From which checkpoint on is the gap smaller than that? Fill the blank in and find out.
One more thing before we move on, and it is the transferable part. Nobody thinks of the epoch count as part of an experiment. It is boilerplate — you set it once, you copy it between projects, you stop seeing it. That is precisely what made it dangerous here: a number that felt like configuration turned out to be the thing determining the answer. Seeds in Lab 7. Windows in Lab 8. Budget here. Same mistake, three costumes.

title: 9  Lab 9 Part 1: Recurrence — and When Gates Are Not Worth It
section: 9.7 Step 5 — Why the gates buy nothing here
text:
9.7 Step 5 — Why the gates buy nothing here
The LSTM’s gates exist to solve one problem: in a plain RNN, gradients shrink as they propagate backward, so signal from far in the past never reaches the weights. Put a number on it.

for factor in (0.7, 0.9):
    print(f"gradient shrink factor {factor} per step:")
    for steps in (1, 5, 10, 26, 52):
        print(f"   {steps:>3} steps back -> {factor**steps:,.6f}")
    print()

At 0.7 per step the signal is essentially gone by 26 steps. That is the problem gating fixes.
Two things about that table before we go on. At a shrink factor of 0.7 the signal is gone by 26 steps. At 0.9 it is still 0.065 at 26 steps and 0.004 at 52 — small, but not zero. Vanishing gradients are a matter of degree and of sequence length, and 26 weeks is short.
Now stop asserting and go measure whether this dataset has the problem gating solves. Three questions, three numbers.

w = weekly.assign(series=weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id)
w["level"] = w.groupby("series").units.transform("mean")
w["dev"]   = w.units - w.level

grand = w.units.mean()
btw = ((w.level - grand) ** 2).sum() / ((w.units - grand) ** 2).sum()
print(f"1. between-series share of total variance : {btw:.1%}")

print("\n2. within-series autocorrelation of units")
for lag in (1, 4, 13, 26, 52):
    a = w.groupby("series").dev.apply(lambda x: x.autocorr(lag)).mean()
    print(f"      lag {lag:>2}: {a:+.3f}")

print("\n3. does a flag at t predict units at t+k?")
for ch in ("snap_days", "event_days"):
    cells = []
    for k in (0, 1, 2, 4):
        c = w.groupby("series").apply(lambda g: g[ch].corr(g.dev.shift(-k))).mean()
        cells.append(f"t+{k}: {c:+.3f}")
    print(f"      {ch:<11} " + "   ".join(cells))







Three reasons the gates have nothing to do



1. Most of the variance is not sequential at all. About 91% of the variation in weekly units is between series — which store, which category — and only 9% is within a series over time. The single biggest thing a model must get right is the level of the series in front of it, and that is readable from the most recent few weeks. No memory mechanism is needed for it.
2. The series are smooth, which is the opposite of needing memory. Within-series autocorrelation is 0.83 at lag 1 and still 0.43 at lag 52. That looks like long memory and is in fact the reason long memory is unnecessary: because neighboring weeks are nearly the same number, the recent past is a sufficient statistic for the distant past. Nothing has to be carried across the gap, because the gap has been filled in continuously along the way. Gating pays off when a value must survive many steps that would otherwise overwrite it — and here nothing overwrites anything.
3. Nothing in the inputs arrives early. snap_days correlates +0.14 with units in the same week and essentially zero at every lead; event_days is flat at every horizon including zero. There is no announcement structure in this data — nothing shows up at time \(t\) that must be stored until \(t+k\). That is the canonical use for a forget gate and an input gate, and this panel does not contain one instance of it.
So the gates solve something real, on data that does not have it. They charge four times the parameters and — as Step 4 showed — roughly three times the epochs for the service, and at convergence they return a tie.


The transferable part is the three questions, not the answer. Before reaching for a gated or attention-based model on your own series, ask: how much of my variance is cross-sectional rather than sequential? Is my series smooth enough that recent values already summarize old ones? Does anything in my inputs lead the target? If the answers look like this panel’s, the extra machinery has nothing to do.







Walkthrough





Step 4 told us the RNN’s margin was mostly a budget artifact. It did not tell us why the LSTM never pulls ahead — and for that you have to look at the data.
Start with the problem gating exists to solve. In a plain RNN, gradients shrink as they propagate backward, so signal from far in the past never reaches the weights.
gradient shrink factor 0.7 per step:      26 steps back -> 0.000094
gradient shrink factor 0.9 per step:      26 steps back -> 0.064611
                                          52 steps back -> 0.004175
Notice this is a matter of degree and of length. At a shrink factor of 0.7 the signal is gone by 26 steps — that is the catastrophe the textbooks draw. At 0.9 it is 0.065 at 26 steps. Small, but not zero. And 26 weeks is a short sequence. Vanishing gradients are a real phenomenon that bites hard at hundreds of steps and only bites softly here.
Now stop asserting and measure whether this dataset has the problem at all. Three questions.
1. between-series share of total variance : 91.0%

2. within-series autocorrelation of units
      lag  1: +0.828      lag 13: +0.695
      lag  4: +0.824      lag 26: +0.575
                          lag 52: +0.432

3. does a flag at t predict units at t+k?
      snap_days   t+0: +0.143   t+1: +0.030   t+2: -0.128   t+4: +0.116
      event_days  t+0: +0.004   t+1: +0.023   t+2: -0.009   t+4: -0.009
One. Ninety-one percent of the variance is not sequential at all. It is between series — which store, which category. Only nine percent is within a series over time. So the single biggest thing any model here must get right is the level of the series in front of it, and that is readable off the most recent few weeks. No memory mechanism is involved in it.
Two, and this one is counter-intuitive, so slow down. The autocorrelation is 0.83 at lag 1 and still 0.43 at lag 52. That looks like long memory — like exactly the case for an LSTM.
It is the opposite. Because neighboring weeks are nearly the same number, the recent past is a sufficient statistic for the distant past. Week 51 already tells you most of what week 40 knew. Gating earns its keep when a value must survive many steps that would otherwise overwrite it — and here nothing overwrites anything, because the series was filled in continuously the whole way along.
Three. Nothing in the inputs arrives early. SNAP correlates 0.14 with units in the same week and essentially zero at every lead. Events are flat everywhere, including at zero. There is no announcement in this data — nothing shows up at time t that must be held until t + k.
That is the textbook use for a forget gate and an input gate, and this panel does not contain a single instance of it.
And now the part to carry out of the lab, which is not the answer — it is the three questions. Before you reach for a gated model, or an attention model, on a series of your own: how much of my variance is cross-sectional rather than sequential? Is my series smooth enough that recent values already summarize the old ones? Does anything in my inputs lead the target?
If the answers look like this panel’s, the extra machinery has nothing to do. If they don’t, it might be exactly what you need — and you will know which, before you spend a week finding out.

title: 10  Lab 9 Part 2: Attention — and the Line You Cannot Forget
text:
10.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Last week’s recurrent models read the window one step at a time. Attention does not: every position looks at every other position at once, so week 3 reaches week 50 in a single operation rather than through forty-seven state updates.
Today you build a Transformer encoder, then delete one line from it and watch it fall apart. That line is the one PyTorch does not add for you, and forgetting it is the most common way this architecture fails silently.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, torch, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv.

10.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first.")

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))
CHANNELS, WINDOW = ["units", "snap_days", "event_days", "avg_price"], 52
CUTOFF = np.datetime64("2015-05-17")
rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))

X, Y, D = [], [], []
for _, g in weekly.groupby(["store_id", "cat_id"]):
    arr, dates = g[CHANNELS].values.astype("float32"), g.week_start.values
    for i in range(len(g) - WINDOW):
        X.append(arr[i:i+WINDOW]); Y.append(arr[i+WINDOW, 0]); D.append(dates[i+WINDOW])
X = np.stack(X); Y = np.array(Y, dtype="float32"); D = np.array(D)
tr, te = D < CUTOFF, D >= CUTOFF
mu, sd = X[tr].mean((0,1), keepdims=True), X[tr].std((0,1), keepdims=True) + 1e-8
ym, ys = Y[tr].mean(), Y[tr].std()
Xn, Yn = (X - mu)/sd, (Y - ym)/ys
X_tr, y_tr, X_te = torch.tensor(Xn[tr]), torch.tensor(Yn[tr]), torch.tensor(Xn[te])
print(f"{X.shape[0]:,} windows of {WINDOW} weeks — train {tr.sum():,}, test {te.sum():,}")








Walkthrough





Same panel, same cutoff, same standardization. One difference from the recurrent lab: the window is fixed at 52 weeks throughout, because a long window is where attention is supposed to earn its keep. If direct long-range paths are worth anything, a full year of history is where we should see it.
That choice is also why this lab is slow. Attention compares every position with every other position, so the cost grows with the square of the window. Fifty-two weeks means 2,704 pairwise comparisons per example per head per layer.

title: 10  Lab 9 Part 2: Attention — and the Line You Cannot Forget
section: 10.3 Step 1 — Positional encoding, before the model
text:
10.3 Step 1 — Positional encoding, before the model
Attention computes a weighted average over positions. Averaging does not care about order: shuffle the input and every attention output is unchanged.
So position has to be added to the input itself. The standard device is a set of sinusoids of different frequencies.

def sinusoidal(seq_len, d_model):
    pe = torch.zeros(seq_len, d_model)
    pos = torch.arange(seq_len).unsqueeze(1).float()
    div = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model))
    pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos * div)
    pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos * div)
    return pe.unsqueeze(0)

pe = sinusoidal(WINDOW, 64)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3))
im = ax.imshow(pe[0].T, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu")
ax.set_xlabel("week in window"); ax.set_ylabel("encoding dimension")
plt.colorbar(im); plt.tight_layout()

Read the picture. Every column — every week — has a distinct pattern down the dimensions, so the model can tell positions apart. Nearby columns look similar, so it can also learn relative distance rather than only absolute index.







Walkthrough





Start with the problem, because the solution makes no sense without it.
Attention computes a weighted average over positions. And an average does not care about order — reverse the sequence, shuffle it, deal it like a deck of cards, and every attention output is identical. The mechanism is permutation-invariant by construction.
That is a catastrophe for forecasting. “Sales were 3,000 last week and 9,000 a year ago” and “sales were 9,000 last week and 3,000 a year ago” are the same bag of numbers and completely different futures.
So position has to be put into the input itself, before attention ever sees it. The standard device is a set of sinusoids at different frequencies.






Try it






Pause on the heat map and check two properties before I name them.
One: every column is distinct. Each week has its own signature down the 64 dimensions, so the model can tell position 3 from position 47.
Two, and this is the part people miss: nearby columns look similar. Week 20 and week 21 have almost the same pattern; week 20 and week 50 do not. That means the encoding carries relative distance, not just an arbitrary label per slot. A model can learn “about four weeks apart” as a concept rather than memorizing every pair of indices — which is what makes the scheme work at positions it never saw in training.
That is why sinusoids rather than, say, just numbering the weeks 1 to 52.

10.4 Step 2 — Build the encoder

class TransformerForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_channels=4, d_model=64, nhead=4, layers=2, use_pe=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.use_pe = use_pe
        self.inp = nn.Linear(n_channels, d_model)
        self.register_buffer("pe", sinusoidal(WINDOW, d_model))
        enc_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
            d_model=d_model, nhead=nhead, dim_feedforward=128,
            dropout=0.1, batch_first=True)
        self.enc = nn.TransformerEncoder(enc_layer, num_layers=layers)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(d_model, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.inp(x)
        if self.use_pe:
            h = h + self.pe                 # <- the line in question
        return self.fc(self.enc(h)[:, -1, :]).squeeze(-1)

def train(use_pe, seed, epochs=30):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = TransformerForecaster(use_pe=use_pe)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    lossfn = nn.MSELoss()
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
        torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=128, shuffle=False)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:
            opt.zero_grad()
            lossfn(model(xb), yb).backward()
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
            opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return rmse(Y[te], model(X_te).numpy() * ys + ym), sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

score, n_par = train(use_pe=True, seed=1)
print(f"Transformer — {n_par:,} parameters, test RMSE {score:,.0f}")

Note the parameter count against last week’s models: the RNN had 4,545 and won.







Walkthrough





The whole architecture is four objects: a linear layer lifting 4 channels to 64 dimensions, the positional encoding, two TransformerEncoderLayers, and a linear head reading the final position.
That line is the subject of the lab. One addition. Everything else in this class is supplied by PyTorch.
Transformer — 67,329 parameters, test RMSE 1,013
Sixty-seven thousand parameters. Hold that against last week: the vanilla RNN had 4,545 and scored 805. So attention arrives with fifteen times the parameters of the model it needs to beat.

The Transformer beats the CNN and lands level with the LSTM, on roughly fifteen times the parameters of the RNN that beat both.
Every advantage attention has is an advantage at scale. Parallel computation across positions matters when a sequence is thousands of steps and a corpus is billions of tokens. Direct long-range paths matter when the signal genuinely sits far back. Neither describes 5,900 windows of weekly retail demand.







Walkthrough





LASSO, 46 features (HW4)     744
XGBoost (HW4)                781
Vanilla RNN (Lab 9 Pt 1)     805
Transformer (today)          990
LSTM (Lab 9 Pt 1)            998
1D CNN (Lab 8)              1032
Seasonal naive              2152
Read it honestly. The Transformer beats the CNN. It ties the LSTM — 990 against 998, a gap of 8 when the run-to-run spread is 23, so those two are indistinguishable. And it loses to the vanilla RNN by 185, on fifteen times the parameters.
Nothing here is a failed implementation. This is the architecture working correctly on a problem it was not designed for. And that is the point worth carrying. Every advantage attention has is an advantage at scale.
Parallel computation across positions is transformative when your sequence is thousands of steps and your corpus is billions of tokens — an RNN has to walk the sequence one step at a time, and a Transformer does not. Direct paths between distant positions matter when the signal genuinely sits far back and must survive the journey.
Neither describes 5,160 training windows of weekly retail demand, where the answer is mostly in the last few weeks. You are paying for a mechanism whose benefits do not exist at this size, with parameters that have to be estimated from data you do not have.

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
text:
11.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
Every model so far returned a number. Today’s returns a distribution, and the work shifts accordingly: less about fitting, more about deciding what you believe beforehand and checking whether the machinery actually worked.
The question is small on purpose so the workflow stays visible: what fraction of weeks are high-SNAP weeks at CA_1 FOODS? You will state a prior, check it before looking at the data, fit the model, verify the sampler, and then ask the posterior questions no point estimate can answer.
Suggested time: ~35 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pymc, arviz, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv. Each fit takes about ten seconds.
crumbs: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
text:
11.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
logging.getLogger('pymc').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first.")

weekly = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
ca1 = weekly[(weekly.store_id == "CA_1") & (weekly.cat_id == "FOODS")]

N_WEEKS = len(ca1)
N_HIGH  = int((ca1.snap_days >= 5).sum())
print(f"CA_1 FOODS: {N_HIGH} high-SNAP weeks out of {N_WEEKS} "
      f"({100*N_HIGH/N_WEEKS:.0f}% observed)")







ArviZ changed its default interval



az.summary(idata) now reports an 89% equal-tailed interval (eti89_lb, eti89_ub). This course uses the highest density interval, which is the shortest interval containing a given probability mass.
Always ask for it: az.summary(idata, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94).
For a symmetric posterior the two nearly coincide. For a skewed one they do not, and the HDI is the honest summary.









Walkthrough





CA_1 FOODS: 72 high-SNAP weeks out of 277 (26% observed)
Seventy-two of two hundred seventy-seven. Twenty-six percent. Hold that number — the whole lab is about how different beliefs collide with it.
Read this callout, because it will bite you in Homework 6 otherwise. ArviZ changed its default interval. az.summary now reports an 89% equal-tailed interval. This course uses the highest density interval — the shortest interval containing the mass — so you must ask for it every time: ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94.
For a symmetric posterior the two nearly coincide; here the equal-tailed 94% interval is [0.2155, 0.3141] against an HDI of [0.2144, 0.3129], so it hardly matters. For a skewed posterior they diverge, and the HDI is the honest summary. Get in the habit now, while the stakes are low.

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
section: 11.3 Step 1 — Check the prior before you use it
text:
11.3 Step 1 — Check the prior before you use it
We will model the count of high-SNAP weeks as Beta-Binomial. Start with Beta(2, 2) — weakly informative, centered at 0.5.
Before fitting anything, ask what that prior alone implies about the data.

with pm.Model() as model:
    theta = pm.Beta("theta", alpha=2, beta=2)
    obs   = pm.Binomial("obs", n=N_WEEKS, p=theta, observed=N_HIGH)
    prior_pred = pm.sample_prior_predictive(500, random_seed=42)

sim = prior_pred.prior_predictive["obs"].values.ravel()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.hist(sim, bins=40)
ax.axvline(N_HIGH, color="crimson", lw=2, label=f"observed = {N_HIGH}")
ax.set_xlabel("simulated high-SNAP weeks out of 277"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"prior predictive spans {sim.min()} to {sim.max()} weeks")

Read the plot. The prior thinks almost any count is plausible — from nearly zero to nearly every week. The observed value sits comfortably inside, so the prior is not wrong.
But is it good? SNAP is disbursed on a published calendar. We are not genuinely ignorant here, and a prior that entertains “every week is a high-SNAP week” is entertaining something we know is false.







Walkthrough





Here is the step almost everyone skips, and it costs about four seconds.
Before fitting anything, we ask what the prior alone implies about the data. Beta(2,2) — weakly informative, centered at one half. Draw five hundred values of θ from it, simulate a count of high-SNAP weeks from each, and look at what comes out.
prior predictive spans 8 to 276 weeks
Eight to two hundred seventy-six. Out of 277. The prior considers essentially every possible answer plausible — from almost never to almost always.
The observed value, 72, sits comfortably inside that. So the prior is not wrong. Nothing here is going to blow up.
But look at what it is willing to entertain. “Two hundred seventy-six of two hundred seventy-seven weeks are high-SNAP weeks” is not an uncertain belief, it is a false one. SNAP is disbursed on a published calendar. We are not genuinely ignorant about this rate, and Beta(2,2) pretends we are.
That is the difference between a prior that is defensible and one that is lazy, and the prior predictive check is what makes the difference visible. It costs one function call, and it is the single highest-value habit in this lecture.
crumbs: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
text:
11.4 Step 2 — Fit it

with model:
    idata = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, progressbar=False, random_seed=42)

summary = az.summary(idata, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(summary.round(4).to_string())

The posterior mean sits between the prior mean of 0.5 and the observed proportion — much closer to the data, because 277 observations carry far more weight than a Beta(2, 2) prior.







Walkthrough





         mean     sd hdi94_lb hdi94_ub ess_bulk ess_tail r_hat
theta  0.2628  0.026     0.22     0.31     3686     5175  1.00
Posterior mean 0.2628.
Now put three numbers side by side, because their arrangement is the lesson. The prior mean was 0.5. The observed proportion is 0.2599. The posterior mean is 0.2628.
The posterior sits between them, as it must — but look at where between them. It is three thousandths from the data and nearly a quarter away from the prior. Two hundred seventy-seven observations against a Beta(2,2) prior is not a fair fight, and the data wins almost totally.
That is what “the likelihood dominates” means, concretely, and it is the answer to half the objections people raise about Bayesian methods before they have run one.
The 94% HDI reads [0.22, 0.31] here — two decimals, because that is az.summary’s default rounding. Step 4 prints the same interval more precisely. Same numbers, different display.
crumbs: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
text:
11.5 Step 3 — Did the sampler work?
MCMC always returns samples. Whether they came from the posterior is a separate question, and one you are expected to answer every time.

n_div = int(idata.sample_stats.diverging.sum())
print(f"R-hat        {summary.r_hat.max():.3f}    (want < 1.01)")
print(f"ESS (bulk)   {summary.ess_bulk.min():.0f}      (want > 400)")
print(f"divergences  {n_div}        (want 0)")

az.plot_trace(idata, var_names=["theta"]);
plt.tight_layout()

Read the trace plot. On the right, four chains overlapping in a band with no drift and no stuck stretches — that is what convergence looks like. On the left, four densities lying on top of one another.
If the chains had separated, \(\hat{R}\) would exceed 1.01 and nothing downstream would mean anything.







Walkthrough





R-hat        1.001    (want < 1.01)
ESS (bulk)   3687      (want > 400)
divergences  0        (want 0)
MCMC always returns samples. It never fails with an error because the answer is wrong. Whether those samples came from the posterior you asked for is a separate question, and you are expected to answer it every single time before reading any result.
By now that sentence should sound familiar. It is the same shape as zero_grad(), as the transposed axis, as the missing positional encoding — the code runs, the output is plausible, and nothing tells you. Bayesian workflow just has better instruments for catching it.
Three numbers. R-hat at 1.001, comfortably under 1.01 — the four chains agree with each other. Effective sample size at 3,687, far above the 400 rule of thumb — the samples are not so autocorrelated that you have less information than it looks. Divergences at zero — the sampler never had to give up on a step.
And the picture. On the right, four chains overlapping in a flat band, no drift, no stuck stretches — that is what convergence looks like, and it is worth memorizing the shape so a bad one jumps out. On the left, four densities lying on top of each other.
If those chains had separated, R-hat would exceed 1.01 and nothing downstream would mean anything — not the mean, not the interval, not the probabilities in the next step.

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
section: 11.6 Step 4 — Ask the posterior a question
text:
11.6 Step 4 — Ask the posterior a question
The posterior is a set of samples, so any question about \(\theta\) is answered by counting.

theta = idata.posterior["theta"].values.ravel()

print(f"P(theta > 0.30)          = {(theta > 0.30).mean():.3f}")
print(f"P(0.24 < theta < 0.28)   = {((theta > 0.24) & (theta < 0.28)).mean():.3f}")
print(f"94% HDI                  = {np.round(az.hdi(theta, prob=0.94), 4)}")

Say the first line out loud as a sentence a manager would understand. Then notice you cannot say anything of that form from a confidence interval — a frequentist 94% interval is a statement about the procedure, not about \(\theta\).







Walkthrough





The posterior is a set of samples. So any question about θ is answered by counting, which is the part that feels almost too easy.
P(theta > 0.30)          = 0.080
P(0.24 < theta < 0.28)   = 0.558
94% HDI                  = [0.2132 0.3098]






Try it



— (replaces “say it out loud as a sentence a manager would understand”)


Pause and write the first line as a sentence you could say in a meeting. Then try to write the same sentence from a confidence interval.
The first one is easy: “There is an eight percent chance that more than thirty percent of weeks are high-SNAP weeks.” A claim about the world, in the units of the question.
The second is impossible, and this is the part worth being precise about rather than glib. A frequentist 94% interval is a statement about the procedure — that intervals built this way cover the true value 94% of the time. It is not a statement about θ, and “there is a 94% chance θ is in this interval” is exactly the misreading every textbook warns against and every practitioner makes anyway.
The Bayesian version means what people already thought the frequentist version meant. That is the practical appeal, and it is bought with the prior.
crumbs: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler

title: 11  Lab 10: Priors, Posteriors, and Checking the Sampler
section: 11.7 Step 5 — How much did the prior matter?
text:
11.7 Step 5 — How much did the prior matter?
The honest objection to Bayesian work is that the prior is arbitrary. Test how much it moves the answer.

rows = []
for a, b, label in [(2, 2, "Beta(2,2) — weak, centered 0.5"),
                    (5, 15, "Beta(5,15) — informed, centered 0.25"),
                    (20, 2, "Beta(20,2) — badly wrong, centered 0.91")]:
    with pm.Model():
        th = pm.Beta("theta", alpha=a, beta=b)
        pm.Binomial("obs", n=N_WEEKS, p=th, observed=N_HIGH)
        i2 = pm.sample(1000, tune=1000, chains=2, progressbar=False, random_seed=42)
    s = az.summary(i2, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
    rows.append({"prior": label, "prior_mean": round(a/(a+b), 3),
                 "posterior_mean": round(float(s["mean"].iloc[0]), 3)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))







With enough data the prior stops mattering



Three priors, including one centered on 0.91 — badly, deliberately wrong. All three posteriors land close together, because 277 observations dominate.
That is the answer to the arbitrariness objection, and it comes with a condition attached: it holds when you have enough data. With 8 observations rather than 277, the third prior would still be visible in the answer.
Which is exactly the situation Lecture 11 Part 2 is about.


Your turn: re-run the badly-wrong prior against only the first 10 weeks of data and report how far the posterior moves.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in ----
# n_small, k_small = 10, int((ca1.snap_days >= 5).head(10).sum())
# with pm.Model():
#     th = pm.Beta("theta", alpha=___, beta=___)      # <- the badly-wrong prior
#     pm.Binomial("obs", n=n_small, p=th, observed=k_small)
#     i3 = pm.sample(1000, tune=1000, chains=2, progressbar=False, random_seed=42)
# print(az.summary(i3, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94).round(3).to_string())








Walkthrough





Now the honest objection, the one you should expect from any audience: the prior is arbitrary, so the answer is arbitrary. Test it rather than argue about it.
Three priors. Weak and centered at 0.5. Informed and centered at 0.25 — roughly right. And one centered at 0.91, which is not a mild disagreement, it is a belief that nine weeks in ten are high-SNAP weeks. Deliberately, badly wrong.
                                 prior  prior_mean  posterior_mean
         Beta(2,2) — weak, centered 0.5       0.500           0.265
   Beta(5,15) — informed, centered 0.25       0.250           0.259
Beta(20,2) — badly wrong, centered 0.91       0.909           0.309
The prior means span 0.25 to 0.91 — a range of 0.66. The posterior means span 0.259 to 0.309 — a range of 0.05. The data compressed the disagreement by a factor of thirteen.
Now let me be more careful than the word “close” allows, because this is the step where it is tempting to oversell.
The badly-wrong prior did not land in the same place as the others. It landed at 0.309, and the weak prior’s 94% interval runs up to 0.313. So the wrong prior’s answer sits just inside the upper edge of what the honest analysis considered plausible — inside the range, but at the very boundary of it. And its own interval, [0.258, 0.358], barely contains the observed proportion of 0.260 at its lower edge.
So the correct claim is not “the prior did not matter.” It is: with 277 observations, even an absurd prior gets dragged to the edge of the right answer rather than away from it. That is a strong result and it does not need embellishment.
And it comes with a condition, which is the sentence to land hardest on. It holds when you have enough data. With eight observations instead of 277, that third prior would still be sitting in your answer, plainly visible.






Try it






That is your turn. Re-run the badly-wrong prior against only the first ten weeks and report how far the posterior moves. Fill in the two blanks — they are the alpha and beta of the Beta(20,2).
And that situation — a handful of observations per unit, and a prior that therefore still matters — is not a contrived exercise. It is Lecture 11 Part 2, where ten series have very different amounts of data and the thin ones borrow strength from the thick ones. Everything you just did by hand, the hierarchy will do automatically.

is easier to skip, because MCMC hands you a tidy summary table that looks authoritative whether or not it converged.*

title: 12  Lab 11 Part 1: Structural Time Series — and Two Ways to Get the Interval Wrong
text:
12.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
A structural model writes a series as parts you can name — a level that drifts, a seasonal shape, and noise — and puts a prior on each. The output is not a forecast line but a distribution for every future week.
Today you will build one, hit a failure the diagnostics catch, fix it — and then find that the correct way to forecast produces a worse-calibrated interval than the shortcut.
That last result is not a mistake in the lab. It is the model telling you something, and working out what takes the rest of the session.
Suggested time: ~40 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pymc, arviz, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv. Sampling takes about 20 seconds per fit.

title: 12  Lab 11 Part 1: Structural Time Series — and Two Ways to Get the Interval Wrong
text:
12.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
logging.getLogger('pymc').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first.")

weekly = pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
ca1 = (weekly[(weekly.store_id == "CA_1") & (weekly.cat_id == "FOODS")]
         .sort_values("week_start").reset_index(drop=True))

N_TEST = 52
train, test = ca1.iloc[:-N_TEST], ca1.iloc[-N_TEST:]
y = train.units.values.astype(float)
n = len(train)
y_mu, y_sd = y.mean(), y.std()
y_z = (y - y_mu) / y_sd          # standardize: the priors below assume unit scale

K, P = 3, 52                     # 3 Fourier pairs, annual period on weekly data
def fourier(t):
    return np.column_stack([f(2*np.pi*k*t/P) for k in range(1, K+1) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)])
t_all = np.arange(len(ca1))
X_tr, X_te = fourier(t_all[:n]), fourier(t_all[n:])

print(f"train {n} weeks, test {N_TEST} weeks | {2*K} Fourier coefficients standing in for 52")








Walkthrough





train 225 weeks, test 52 weeks | 6 Fourier coefficients standing in for 52
CA_1 FOODS again — the series you have been forecasting since Homework 2 — held out for a full final year.
One line deserves attention. Six coefficients standing in for fifty-two. Three sine-cosine pairs describe the annual shape, rather than fifty-two weekly dummies. That is a modeling choice with a cost and a benefit: you cannot represent a one-week spike, but you have six parameters to estimate instead of fifty-two, on 225 observations. Remember it — it comes back in Step 3 as a suspect.
Also note the standardization. y_z is the series in standard units, because the priors below — Exponential(10), Normal(0, 0.5) — assume unit scale. Priors are not scale-free, and this is the line that makes them defensible.

title: 12  Lab 11 Part 1: Structural Time Series — and Two Ways to Get the Interval Wrong
section: 12.3 Step 1 — Fit it the obvious way
text:
12.3 Step 1 — Fit it the obvious way
The model is a drifting level plus seasonality. PyMC has a distribution for a random walk, so the natural thing is to use it.

with pm.Model() as centered:
    sigma_level = pm.Exponential("sigma_level", 10.0)
    level = pm.GaussianRandomWalk("level", sigma=sigma_level, shape=n)
    beta  = pm.Normal("beta", 0, 0.5, shape=2*K)
    sigma = pm.Exponential("sigma", 1.0)
    pm.Normal("obs", mu=level + pm.math.dot(X_tr, beta), sigma=sigma, observed=y_z)
    idata_c = pm.sample(1500, tune=2000, chains=4, progressbar=False,
                        random_seed=42, target_accept=0.95)

s_c = az.summary(idata_c, var_names=["sigma_level", "sigma", "beta"],
                 ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(f"R-hat        {s_c.r_hat.max():.3f}   (want < 1.01)")
print(f"ESS (bulk)   {s_c.ess_bulk.min():.0f}     (want > 400)")
print(f"divergences  {int(idata_c.sample_stats.diverging.sum())}")

It did not converge. No exception, a forecast is available, and the diagnostics are the only thing telling you not to use it. Note that target_accept is already at 0.95 — this is not fixed by asking the sampler to try harder.







Walkthrough





The model is a drifting level plus seasonality. PyMC has a distribution for a random walk, so the obvious thing is to reach for it: pm.GaussianRandomWalk. It reads exactly like the maths.
R-hat        1.022   (want < 1.01)
ESS (bulk)   274     (want > 400)
divergences  0
It did not converge, and I want you to look carefully at how you know.
R-hat is 1.022, above the 1.01 threshold — the four chains do not agree with each other. Effective sample size is 274, below 400 — the draws are so autocorrelated that six thousand samples carry less information than a few hundred independent ones. And divergences are zero.
That last line matters, because divergences are the diagnostic everyone learns first, and here they are silent. The sampler never had to give up on a step; it just wandered badly. Different pathologies trip different instruments — which is precisely why you check all three, every time, rather than the one you remember.
Next week you will see the mirror image: a model where R-hat and ESS both pass and forty-three divergences are the only thing objecting.
And note this is not fixed by asking the sampler to try harder. target_accept is already at 0.95. The problem is not effort.

title: 12  Lab 11 Part 1: Structural Time Series — and Two Ways to Get the Interval Wrong
text:
12.4 Step 2 — Reparameterize
The problem is the shape of the posterior, not the model. Write the walk as a cumulative sum of standard Normal draws scaled by sigma_level, and the sampler gets a geometry it can navigate.

with pm.Model() as model:
    sigma_level = pm.Exponential("sigma_level", 10.0)
    z = pm.Normal("z", 0, 1, shape=n)                              # standard normal
    level = pm.Deterministic("level", pm.math.cumsum(z * sigma_level))
    beta  = pm.Normal("beta", 0, 0.5, shape=2*K)
    sigma = pm.Exponential("sigma", 1.0)
    pm.Normal("obs", mu=level + pm.math.dot(X_tr, beta), sigma=sigma, observed=y_z)
    idata = pm.sample(1500, tune=2000, chains=4, progressbar=False,
                      random_seed=42, target_accept=0.95)

s = az.summary(idata, var_names=["sigma_level", "sigma", "beta"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(f"R-hat        {s.r_hat.max():.3f}   (want < 1.01)")
print(f"ESS (bulk)   {s.ess_bulk.min():.0f}    (want > 400)")
print(f"divergences  {int(idata.sample_stats.diverging.sum())}")

Same model, same data, same priors. cumsum(z * sigma) and GaussianRandomWalk(sigma=sigma) describe the identical distribution — only the coordinates the sampler explores have changed.
Look at the components it recovered:

lev = idata.posterior["level"].values.reshape(-1, n).mean(0) * y_sd + y_mu
sea = (idata.posterior["beta"].values.reshape(-1, 2*K) @ X_tr.T).mean(0) * y_sd

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharex=True)
ax[0].plot(train.week_start, train.units, lw=.8, alpha=.5, label="observed")
ax[0].plot(train.week_start, lev, lw=2, label="level")
ax[0].legend(); ax[0].set_ylabel("units")
ax[1].plot(train.week_start, sea, lw=1.5, color="darkgreen")
ax[1].set_ylabel("seasonal"); ax[1].axhline(0, color="k", lw=.5)
plt.tight_layout()








Walkthrough





The problem is the shape of the posterior, not the model.
A centered random walk couples the level to sigma_level: when the scale is small, the steps must be small, so the posterior narrows into a funnel that the sampler cannot traverse at a single step size. The fix is to write the walk as a cumulative sum of standard Normal draws, scaled afterwards. Now z and sigma_level are independent in the posterior geometry.
R-hat        1.002   (want < 1.01)
ESS (bulk)   2376    (want > 400)
divergences  0
R-hat 1.022 to 1.002. Effective sample size 274 to 2,376 — nearly nine times more information out of the same number of draws.
And here is the sentence to say slowly: same model, same data, same priors. cumsum(z * sigma) and GaussianRandomWalk(sigma=sigma) describe the identical distribution. Nothing about what we believe has changed. Only the coordinate system the sampler explores.
That is worth internalising, because it is unlike everything else in this course. This is not a modeling improvement or a bias-variance trade. It is a computational fix to a computational problem, and the give-away is that the posterior it targets is unchanged.
And now the payoff of a structural model — you can look at the parts. Top panel, the level: a slow drift under the noise. Bottom panel, the seasonal shape the six Fourier coefficients recovered. Neither of those is available from XGBoost at any price.

title: 12  Lab 11 Part 1: Structural Time Series — and Two Ways to Get the Interval Wrong
text:
12.5 Step 3 — Forecast, two ways
To forecast you need the level at each future week. There are two candidates, and one of them is theoretically right.
Held constant: carry the last estimated level forward unchanged. Simple, and it asserts the level stops drifting the moment your data ends — which is not what the model says.
Propagated: let the level keep random-walking forward, exactly as it did in-sample. This is what the fitted model actually implies.

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
post = idata.posterior
lev_last = post["level"].values[:, :, -1].ravel()
sl       = post["sigma_level"].values.ravel()
b        = post["beta"].values.reshape(-1, 2*K)
sg       = post["sigma"].values.ravel()
D = len(lev_last)
actual = test.units.values

# The POINT forecast is identical for both methods, and not approximately so:
# propagating the level adds zero-mean steps, so E[level] is unchanged. Only the
# spread differs. Compute the point forecast once, from the deterministic part.
point = (lev_last[:, None] + b @ X_te.T).mean(0) * y_sd + y_mu
rmse_point = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((actual - point) ** 2)))

def score(draws, label):
    lo, hi = np.percentile(draws, [3, 97], axis=0) * y_sd + y_mu
    return {"method": label,
            "RMSE": round(rmse_point),
            "coverage_%": round(100*float(np.mean((actual >= lo) & (actual <= hi)))),
            "mean_width": round(float(np.mean(hi - lo)))}

# (a) level held constant at its last value  -- the tempting shortcut
mu_a = lev_last[:, None] + b @ X_te.T
draws_a = mu_a + rng.normal(0, 1, size=mu_a.shape) * sg[:, None]

# (b) level keeps random-walking into the future -- what the model actually says
steps = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(D, N_TEST)) * sl[:, None]
mu_b = lev_last[:, None] + np.cumsum(steps, axis=1) + b @ X_te.T
draws_b = mu_b + rng.normal(0, 1, size=mu_b.shape) * sg[:, None]

print(pd.DataFrame([score(draws_a, "level held constant"),
                    score(draws_b, "level propagated")]).to_string(index=False))







The theoretically correct choice calibrated worse. Work out why.



The two methods have the same point forecast — not nearly the same, exactly the same, because propagating the level adds steps with mean zero. So RMSE cannot distinguish them, and everything that separates them lives in the interval — which differs enormously, and not in the direction you would predict.
Propagating the walk is the defensible choice: the level genuinely does keep drifting, and freezing it asserts a certainty the model does not have. Yet the propagated interval over-covers, while the frozen one lands close to its nominal 94%.
Over-covering means too wide. Over 52 weeks the propagated level accumulates roughly \(\sqrt{52}\,\sigma_{\text{level}}\) of drift, so if \(\sigma_{\text{level}}\) is too large the interval inflates fast.
And there is good reason to think it is too large. The random walk is the most flexible part of this model. Anything the Fourier terms fail to capture — a promotion, a holiday shift, an outlier — gets absorbed into the level, inflating \(\sigma_{\text{level}}\) beyond genuine drift.
So the frozen version is not right. It is wrong in a way that happens to cancel an overestimated drift on this series and this horizon. Rely on that and it will fail elsewhere.


Your turn: check the size of the estimated drift against the noise it is competing with.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in ----
# print(az.summary(idata, var_names=[___, ___],        # <- the two scale parameters
#                  ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94).round(4).to_string())
# print("\ndrift accumulated over 52 weeks, in standardized units:")
# print(f"  {np.sqrt(52) * float(post['sigma_level'].values.mean()):.2f}")


Now split coverage by horizon, which is where the difference actually shows.

def by_horizon(draws, label):
    lo, hi = np.percentile(draws, [3, 97], axis=0) * y_sd + y_mu
    inside = (actual >= lo) & (actual <= hi)
    segs = {"wk 1-13": slice(0,13), "wk 14-39": slice(13,39), "wk 40-52": slice(39,52)}
    row = {"method": label}
    for name, sl_ in segs.items():
        row[name] = f"{100*inside[sl_].mean():.0f}% / {int((hi-lo)[sl_].mean()):,}"
    return row

print("coverage / mean width, by horizon (nominal 94%)")
print(pd.DataFrame([by_horizon(draws_a, "level held constant"),
                    by_horizon(draws_b, "level propagated")]).to_string(index=False))

Read the widths across each row. The frozen version’s interval is essentially the same width at week 50 as at week 1 — it has no mechanism to widen. The propagated version’s roughly doubles.
That is the real distinction, and it is structural rather than a matter of which scored better here: one of these models knows that forecasting further ahead is harder, and the other does not. On this series, at this horizon, that ignorance happened not to cost anything. On a series with a genuinely drifting level it would.







Walkthrough





To forecast you need the level at each future week, and there are two candidates.
Held constant. Carry the last estimated level forward unchanged. Simple — and it asserts that the level stops drifting the moment your data ends, which is not what the model says.
Propagated. Let the level keep random-walking forward exactly as it did in-sample. This is what the fitted model actually implies. It is the defensible choice.
             method  RMSE  coverage_%  mean_width
level held constant  1589          96        6340
   level propagated  1589         100       11667
The point forecasts are identical — 1,589 on both rows, and not by coincidence. Propagating the level adds steps whose mean is zero, so the expected level is unchanged and RMSE simply cannot tell these two apart. Everything separating them is in the interval, which differs by a factor of nearly two, and not in the direction you would predict.
The theoretically correct method over-covers: 100% of weeks fell inside a 94% interval. The shortcut lands at 96%, close to nominal. The defensible choice calibrated worse.






Try it






Pause and work out why before I tell you. Then do the first “your turn” — print the two scale parameters and the drift accumulated over 52 weeks.
Over 52 weeks a random walk accumulates about \(\sqrt{52}\) — call it seven — times sigma_level of drift. So if sigma_level is even somewhat too large, the interval inflates fast, and it inflates with the square root of the horizon.
And there is good reason to think it is too large, which brings back the Fourier choice from the setup. The random walk is the most flexible component in this model. Anything the six coefficients cannot represent — a promotion, a holiday that moves, a single bad week — has nowhere else to go, so it gets absorbed into the level. That inflates sigma_level beyond genuine drift, and the forecast then propagates that inflated drift for a year.
So — and this is the sentence that matters — the frozen version is not right. It is wrong in a way that happens to cancel an overestimated drift, on this series, at this horizon. Rely on that and it will fail somewhere else, silently, and you will not know which of the two errors moved.
coverage / mean width, by horizon (nominal 94%)
             method      wk 1-13      wk 14-39      wk 40-52
level held constant 100% / 6,255   92% / 6,537  100% / 6,027
   level propagated 100% / 8,081 100% / 11,974 100% / 14,637
Read the widths across each row, not the coverage.
The frozen version: 6,255 at weeks 1–13, and 6,027 at weeks 40–52. It is narrower a year out than a month out. It has no mechanism to widen, because nothing in it knows that time has passed. The propagated version: 8,081, then 11,974, then 14,637. It nearly doubles.
One of these models knows that forecasting further ahead is harder, and the other does not. That is a structural difference, not a scoring difference, and it is why the aggregate table on its own would have misled you. On this series, at this horizon, the ignorance happened to cost nothing. On a series with a genuinely drifting level it would cost a great deal.
And notice the only sub-nominal cell in the table: the frozen version drops to 92% in weeks 14–39. Its respectable 96% average is hiding a stretch where it is overconfident. Aggregates hide things; that is the third time this course has said so.

12.6 Step 4 — Calibrated is not the same as useful
Take the propagated version — the one the model implies — and ask two separate questions of it.

res = score(draws_b, "level propagated")
print(f"coverage      {res['coverage_%']}%   against a nominal 94%")
print(f"mean width    {res['mean_width']:,} units")
print(f"              = {100*res['mean_width']/ca1.units.mean():.0f}% of average weekly units")
print(f"RMSE          {res['RMSE']:,}")
print(f"seasonal naive{np.sqrt(np.mean((actual - train.units.values[-52:])**2)):>7,.0f}")

Question one: is it calibrated? Compare coverage against 94%.
Question two: is it useful? Compare the width against the size of the thing you are forecasting, and ask whether you would place an inventory order against it.
Your turn: state, in one sentence each, your answer to both — and whether passing the first excuses failing the second.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and answer in the strings ----
# calibrated = "..."
# useful     = "..."
# print(calibrated); print(useful)








Walkthrough





Take the propagated version — the one the model implies — and ask it two separate questions.
coverage      100%   against a nominal 94%
mean width    11,667 units
              = 59% of average weekly units
RMSE          1,589
seasonal naive  1,660
Question one: is it calibrated? Yes, and then some. 100% against a nominal 94% — not overconfident. Conservative. Question two: is it useful?
The interval is 11,667 units wide on a series averaging about 19,700 — call it plus or minus thirty percent. Now say that out loud as a business sentence: “I am 94% confident that next week’s demand is somewhere between roughly thirty percent below and thirty percent above average.”
Nobody places an inventory order against that. It is honest and it is useless, and those are not the same axis.






Try it






Write your one-sentence answer to each question, and then the third question the lab actually asks: does passing the first excuse failing the second?
And the point forecast: 1,589 against seasonal naive’s 1,660. About 4% better, for a model that took twenty seconds to sample, a reparameterization to converge, and a page of code.
If accuracy were the argument for this model, that number would be an embarrassment. Accuracy is not the argument. What you bought is a level and a seasonal component you can plot and defend, a full distribution for every future week, and — the thing the whole lab has been about — an interval that admits when it does not know. Whether that trade is worth 5% is a business question, and it depends entirely on whether anyone downstream will use the uncertainty you went to the trouble of producing.

12.7 Before you leave

Discuss (the two problems): The convergence failure was caught by a diagnostic. The over-wide interval was not — it needed a held-out set and a coverage calculation. What is the structural difference between the two, and what habit catches the second kind?
Discuss (the payoff): The point forecast beat seasonal naive by only a few percent. Given that, what did fitting this model actually buy — and name a business question it can answer that XGBoost from Homework 4 cannot.
Discuss (the fix): The interval is honest and too wide to act on. Propose one change to the model — not the forecasting code — that would narrow it, and say what you would be assuming in exchange.


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough











Try it






Three questions for the board.
The two problems. The convergence failure was caught by a diagnostic — R-hat and ESS, computed from the fit alone, before you looked at any data you were predicting. The over-wide interval was caught by nothing of the sort: it needed a held-out year and a coverage calculation. What is the structural difference between those two kinds of error, and what habit catches the second kind?
held-out check asks “is the model any good?” — and no amount of the first substitutes for the second. A perfectly converged sampler will happily give you a useless interval.*
The payoff. The point forecast beat seasonal naive by about four percent. Given that, what did fitting this model actually buy? Name one business question it answers that XGBoost from Homework 4 cannot.
The fix. The interval is honest and too wide to act on. Propose one change to the model — not the forecasting code — that would narrow it, and say what you are assuming in exchange.
assumes the level really does drift slowly; or more seasonal flexibility so the Fourier terms stop dumping their residual into the level. The second is the more interesting answer because it addresses the cause rather than the symptom.*

title: 13  Lab 11 Part 2: Partial Pooling — and the Question That Comes Before It
text:
13.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
A hierarchical model lets thirty series share information: each gets its own effect, drawn from a common distribution the data also estimates. Data-poor series borrow from data-rich ones, and nobody has to choose the weights.
That is genuinely powerful, and today you will watch it work. You will also watch it produce a confidently wrong answer — on the same data, with clean diagnostics, textbook shrinkage, and no warning of any kind.
The difference between the two runs is not the code. It is a decision made before any code was written: which series belong in the same hierarchy.
Suggested time: ~45 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pymc, arviz, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv. Six model fits, most under 30 seconds.

title: 13  Lab 11 Part 2: Partial Pooling — and the Question That Comes Before It
text:
13.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
RANDOM_STATE = 42

weekly = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/m5_weekly.csv", parse_dates=["week_start"])
weekly["series"] = weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id
weekly["hi_snap"] = (weekly.snap_days >= 5).astype(int)

df = weekly.dropna(subset=["units"]).copy()
df["ly"] = np.log(df.units.clip(lower=1))

print(f"{df.series.nunique()} series | {len(df):,} rows | "
      f"{df.hi_snap.mean():.1%} of weeks are high-SNAP")

Our question: does a high-SNAP week lift units, and by how much in each store?
We will need one helper repeatedly — the SNAP effect actually observed in a set of weeks, with no model involved. It is just the difference in mean log units between high-SNAP weeks and the rest.

def empirical_effect(frame, series_name):
    """Observed high-SNAP effect on log units for one series."""
    z = frame[frame.series == series_name]
    if z.hi_snap.nunique() < 2:
        return np.nan
    return z.ly[z.hi_snap == 1].mean() - z.ly[z.hi_snap == 0].mean()








Walkthrough





30 series | 8,310 rows | 22.1% of weeks are high-SNAP
The question: does a high-SNAP week lift units, and by how much in each store?
And note this helper, because it is what makes the whole lab possible. It computes the SNAP effect actually observed in a set of weeks — the difference in mean log units between high-SNAP weeks and the rest — with no model involved. Later we will hold weeks back, fit a model without them, and then use this function to ask what really happened in those weeks.
Most of the time you cannot grade a model this way. Today you can, because we are going to create the missing data ourselves.
