title: 13  Lab 11 Part 2: Partial Pooling — and the Question That Comes Before It
text:
13.3 Step 1 — Build the imbalance
Real panels are lopsided: some series have years of history, others are new stores or newly re-categorized products with a handful of usable weeks. We create that imbalance deliberately so we can check the answer later.
Thin every third series down to 8 weeks. The weeks we remove are not thrown away — they become a held-out set that the model never sees, and that we will use in Step 3 to grade it.

codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df.series)
df["idx"] = codes
J = len(uniq)

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
keep = []
for j in range(J):
    rows = df.index[df.idx == j].tolist()
    n = 8 if j % 3 == 0 else len(rows)
    keep += list(rng.choice(rows, size=min(n, len(rows)), replace=False))

train = df.loc[sorted(keep)].copy()
heldout = df.drop(index=keep).copy()
thin = np.array([j % 3 == 0 for j in range(J)])

print(f"train {len(train):,} rows | held-out {len(heldout):,} rows")
print(f"{thin.sum()} thin series (8 weeks each), {(~thin).sum()} full series")

Here is the model. It is the one from lecture, written non-centered, and it takes a flag so we can reuse it for the unpooled fit.

def fit(data, kind, n_series, centered=False, target_accept=0.9):
    """kind: 'unpooled' or 'hier'. Returns the InferenceData."""
    i = data.idx.values
    x = data.hi_snap.values.astype(float)
    y = data.ly.values
    with pm.Model():
        a = pm.Normal("a", y.mean(), 1, shape=n_series)
        s = pm.Exponential("s", 1.0)
        if kind == "unpooled":
            b = pm.Normal("b", 0, 0.5, shape=n_series)
        else:
            mu_b = pm.Normal("mu_b", 0, 0.5)
            sd_b = pm.HalfNormal("sd_b", 0.25)
            if centered:
                b = pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=n_series)
            else:
                z = pm.Normal("z", 0, 1, shape=n_series)
                b = pm.Deterministic("b", mu_b + z * sd_b)
        pm.Normal("obs", mu=a[i] + b[i] * x, sigma=s, observed=y)
        return pm.sample(1000, tune=1500, chains=4, progressbar=False,
                         random_seed=RANDOM_STATE, target_accept=target_accept)

def b_means(idata, n_series):
    return az.summary(idata, var_names=["b"], ci_kind="hdi",
                      ci_prob=0.94)["mean"].values








Walkthrough





train 5,620 rows | held-out 2,690 rows
10 thin series (8 weeks each), 20 full series
Real panels are lopsided — some series have years of history, others are new stores with a handful of weeks. We manufacture that imbalance: every third series cut down to 8 weeks.
The weeks we remove are not discarded. They go into heldout, the model never sees them, and in Step 3 they become the answer key.
Remember the rule: j % 3 == 0. Every third series. It looks arbitrary and it is about to matter enormously.

13.4 Step 2 — Fit it, and admire the shrinkage
Fit both models on all thirty series and measure how far each estimate moved.

idata_u30 = fit(train, "unpooled", J)
idata_h30 = fit(train, "hier", J)

bu30, bh30 = b_means(idata_u30, J), b_means(idata_h30, J)

def diag(idata, label):
    su = az.summary(idata, var_names=["b"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
    print(f"  {label:<14s} r_hat {su.r_hat.max():.3f}  "
          f"ess {su.ess_bulk.min():5.0f}  "
          f"divergences {int(idata.sample_stats.diverging.sum()):4d}")

print("Diagnostics")
diag(idata_u30, "unpooled")
diag(idata_h30, "hierarchical")


move_thin = np.abs(bh30[thin] - bu30[thin]).mean()
move_full = np.abs(bh30[~thin] - bu30[~thin]).mean()

print("\n              unpooled spread   after pooling   mean move")
print(f"  thin (8w)       {bu30[thin].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bh30[thin].std():.3f}          {move_thin:.3f}")
print(f"  full (277w)     {bu30[~thin].std():.3f}           "
      f"{bh30[~thin].std():.3f}          {move_full:.3f}")
print(f"\n  ratio: thin series moved {move_thin / move_full:.1f}x further")

g = az.summary(idata_h30, var_names=["mu_b", "sd_b"], ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94)
print(f"  mu_b {g.loc['mu_b','mean']:.3f}   sd_b {g.loc['sd_b','mean']:.3f}")

Everything a hierarchical model is supposed to do, it did. Diagnostics are clean. The data-poor series moved an order of magnitude further toward the group mean than the data-rich ones, and nobody told the model which was which.
The shrinkage plot makes it visual.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for j in range(J):
    c = "crimson" if thin[j] else "steelblue"
    ax.plot([0, 1], [bu30[j], bh30[j]], "-o", color=c, alpha=0.7, ms=4)
ax.axhline(g.loc["mu_b", "mean"], ls="--", c="gray", lw=1)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["unpooled", "hierarchical"])
ax.set_ylabel("estimated high-SNAP effect (log units)")
ax.set_title("Shrinkage: thin series (red) collapse onto the group mean")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Before you go on



Write down, in one sentence, what you would now tell the business. Keep it — Step 3 will ask whether it was right.









Walkthrough





Diagnostics
  unpooled       r_hat 1.004  ess  6637  divergences    0
  hierarchical   r_hat 1.001  ess  5203  divergences    0
Both models sampled cleanly. R-hat near one, effective sample sizes in the thousands, not one divergence. If you were checking your work the way Lecture 10 taught you, you would stop here satisfied.
              unpooled spread   after pooling   mean move
  thin (8w)       0.104           0.000          0.110
  full (277w)     0.012           0.001          0.010

  ratio: thin series moved 11.5x further
  mu_b 0.011   sd_b 0.008
And this is textbook. The thin series — 8 weeks each — moved 11.5 times further toward the group mean than the full series did. Nobody told the model which series were starved. It worked that out from how much each one had to say.
The picture makes it obvious: the red lines, the thin series, collapse onto the dashed group mean. The blue lines barely move.






Try it






Pause the video and write one sentence: what would you now tell the business about SNAP weeks? Keep it where you can see it. Step 3 is going to ask whether it was right. Before we grade it, look at one number I have not commented on. sd_b is 0.008.
That is the model’s estimate of how much stores differ from one another. Eight thousandths of a log unit — which is to say, the model has concluded that all thirty of these series respond to SNAP essentially identically.
Hold that up against what you know about the world. Thirty series spanning three states, three product categories, stores of different sizes. Is “they are all the same” plausible?
It is not a diagnostic. Nothing flags it. But it is a claim about the world, and claims about the world can be sanity-checked in a way that R-hat cannot.

section: 13.5 Step 3 — Grade it against the weeks it never saw
text:
13.5 Step 3 — Grade it against the weeks it never saw
We thinned those ten series ourselves. The weeks we removed are sitting in heldout, and each thinned series has hundreds of them. So we can compute the effect that actually occurred and compare.

thin_names = [uniq[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]]
truth = np.array([empirical_effect(heldout, s) for s in thin_names])
est_u = np.array([bu30[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]])
est_h = np.array([bh30[j] for j in range(J) if thin[j]])

out = pd.DataFrame({"series": thin_names, "unpooled": est_u.round(3),
                    "hierarchical": est_h.round(3), "held_out_truth": truth.round(3)})
print(out.to_string(index=False))

rmse = lambda e: np.sqrt(np.nanmean((e - truth) ** 2))
print(f"\n  RMSE vs truth:  unpooled {rmse(est_u):.3f}   "
      f"hierarchical {rmse(est_h):.3f}")
print(f"  mean held-out effect across these series: {np.nanmean(truth):.3f}")

Read that table before reading on.
The hierarchical model reported an effect near mu_b for every one of these series. The held-out weeks say the true effects average close to 0.09 — several times larger. The model did not merely lose precision on these series; it moved them all to the wrong place, and reported tight intervals around it.
And notice what the RMSE column says: pooling barely improved on the unpooled fit at all. All that shrinkage bought us essentially nothing.






The diagnostics could never have caught this



\(\hat{R}\), ESS and divergences ask whether the sampler explored the posterior of the model you wrote. They cannot ask whether that model was the right one. Every diagnostic here passed.

Read the middle column first. 0.011, ten times. The hierarchical model reported essentially the same effect for every one of these ten series.
Now read the last column. The held-out weeks — hundreds of them per series, weeks the model never saw — say the true effects average 0.089, and range from 0.011 up to 0.209.
The model was not merely imprecise. It moved all ten series to a number roughly eight times too small, and reported tight intervals around it.
And look at the RMSE line, because it takes away the last consolation. Unpooled 0.102, hierarchical 0.097. All of that shrinkage — the beautiful collapsing lines, the 11.5× ratio — bought a five percent improvement over just fitting each series separately.
Now the sentence that matters most in this lecture. The diagnostics could never have caught this. R-hat, ESS and divergences ask whether the sampler explored the posterior of the model you wrote. section: 13.6 Step 4 — Find out what went wrong
text:
13.6 Step 4 — Find out what went wrong
Two things are wrong, and one of them is invisible until you look.
First, look at which series we thinned.

print("thinned series:", thin_names)


print("\nEmpirical high-SNAP effect by category (all data, no model):")
for cat, grp in df.groupby("cat_id"):
    effs = [empirical_effect(grp, s) for s in grp.series.unique()]
    print(f"  {cat:<10s} n={len(effs):2d}  mean {np.mean(effs):+.3f}  "
          f"sd {np.std(effs):.3f}")

Two findings, and they compound.
The groups were not exchangeable. SNAP is a food assistance program. FOODS responds; HOBBIES and HOUSEHOLD barely move. Putting all thirty in one hierarchy told the model these are thirty interchangeable draws from one distribution — so it estimated a group mean near zero, dominated by the twenty series with no effect, and pulled the FOODS series down to it.
And j % 3 == 0 selected exactly the FOODS series. The series are ordered store-major with three categories each, so every third one is a FOODS series. We starved precisely the ten series that had something to say, then pooled them toward twenty that did not.






Exchangeability is a modeling assumption, and it is yours to defend



Groups are exchangeable when, before seeing the data, you have no reason to expect one to differ from another in a particular direction. Ten FOODS series in ten stores: plausible. FOODS against HOBBIES: you knew the answer before you looked.
Nothing in PyMC checks this. No diagnostic reports it. It is subject-matter knowledge, applied before the model is written.



# ---- your turn: uncomment and answer in the strings ----
# whose_fault = "..."   # <- would a bigger sample have fixed this? why or why not?
# print(whose_fault)








Walkthrough





Two things went wrong, and they compound.
thinned series: ['CA_1_FOODS', 'CA_2_FOODS', 'CA_3_FOODS', 'CA_4_FOODS', 'TX_1_FOODS',
                 'TX_2_FOODS', 'TX_3_FOODS', 'WI_1_FOODS', 'WI_2_FOODS', 'WI_3_FOODS']
Every thinned series is a FOODS series. All ten. That is not a coincidence and it is not bad luck — the panel is ordered store-major with three categories each, so j % 3 == 0 selects the same category every time.
Empirical high-SNAP effect by category (all data, no model):
  FOODS      n=10  mean +0.089  sd 0.058
  HOBBIES    n=10  mean +0.006  sd 0.010
  HOUSEHOLD  n=10  mean +0.011  sd 0.014
And there it is. SNAP is a food assistance program. FOODS responds at +0.089. HOBBIES and HOUSEHOLD are at +0.006 and +0.011 — indistinguishable from nothing. So put the two together, because neither alone is fatal.
We told the model that thirty series were thirty interchangeable draws from one distribution. They are not: twenty of them have no effect and ten do. The group mean therefore landed near zero, dominated by the twenty. And then — the second error — we starved precisely the ten series that had something to say, so those ten had almost no data with which to resist being pulled toward a mean built from series unlike them.
That is why sd_b came out at 0.008. Averaged across a group where two thirds genuinely have no effect, “stores are all the same” is the best summary of a badly-posed question.






Try it






Pause and answer the question in the code cell: would a bigger sample have fixed this?
No — and this is worth being clear about, because “get more data” is the reflex. More weeks per series would sharpen each estimate, and the hierarchy would still be pulling FOODS series toward a mean computed from HOBBIES and HOUSEHOLD. The error is in the structure we imposed, and no quantity of data corrects a structural mistake. It just makes you more confident about it.
Exchangeability is a modeling assumption and it is yours to defend. Groups are exchangeable when, before seeing the data, you have no reason to expect one to differ from another in a particular direction. Ten FOODS series across ten stores: plausible. FOODS against HOBBIES: you knew the answer before you looked.
Nothing in PyMC checks this. No diagnostic reports it. It is subject-matter knowledge, applied before the model is written.

Compare that middle column to Step 2’s. There, everything collapsed onto the group mean. Now grade it the same way.

tn = [uniq_f[j] for j in range(Jf) if thin_f[j]]
truth_f = np.array([empirical_effect(heldout_f, s) for s in tn])

      f"   ({r_u / r_h:.1f}x better)")

That is borrowing strength, and now it is real. The same code, the same priors, the same diagnostics — and the thin series are estimated well because the other five exist. The only thing that changed was which series were allowed into the hierarchy.

section: 13.8 Step 6 — The trap in the code
text:
13.8 Step 6 — The trap in the code
One more failure, and this one is mechanical. The natural way to write the hierarchy reads exactly like the equation:
b = pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=J)   # the centered form
Fit it that way and watch the diagnostics.

idata_cent = fit(train_f, "hier", Jf, centered=True)

print("Diagnostics")
diag(idata_cent, "centered")
diag(idata_hf, "non-centered")

Same model. Same data. Same answer, if you could sample it — but the centered form makes the sampler walk a funnel: when sd_b is small the b_j must crowd into a narrow neck, and a sampler tuned for the wide part cannot get in.






Which alarm fired



Look at the two columns. \(\hat{R}\) is near the threshold and ESS clears 400 — on those two numbers alone you might have shipped it. The divergence count is unambiguous.
On hierarchical models, divergences are the sensitive instrument. Do not wait for \(\hat{R}\).









Walkthrough





One more failure, and this one is mechanical rather than conceptual.
The natural way to write a hierarchy reads exactly like the equation: b = pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=J). Everybody writes it that way first. It is called the centered form.
Diagnostics
  centered        r_hat 1.044  ess   413  divergences  127
  non-centered    r_hat 1.002  ess  1728  divergences    1
Same model. Same data. The same posterior, if you could sample it — but the centered form makes the sampler walk a funnel: when sd_b is small the individual b_j must crowd into a narrow neck, and a sampler tuned for the wide part of the funnel cannot get into the neck.
Now read the three numbers as three different kinds of warning, because that is the lesson. ESS passes. 413, thirteen over the threshold. You would not look twice.
R-hat fails — 1.044 against 1.01. But be honest about what happens in practice when a number is a little over a line: people rerun it, or call it close enough, or decide the threshold is conservative.
127 divergences against a threshold of exactly zero. There is no version of “close to zero” that gets you to a hundred and twenty-seven. It admits no conversation.
So the rule: on hierarchical models, divergences fire first and least ambiguously. Do not wait for R-hat to decide for you.

title: 14  Lab 12: Elasticity — What the Coefficient Means, and What It Costs to Get Wrong
text:
14.1 What we are doing
Run this one live: the executable lab.
A Bayesian regression coefficient is a distribution, and a price elasticity is the one number a category manager will actually act on. Today you will estimate one, and then find three separate ways it can be wrong while every diagnostic still says the model is fine.
Two of the three are not statistical failures at all. One is a routine preprocessing step you have used in every lab since Lecture 6.
Suggested time: ~45 minutes · You will need: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pymc, arviz, and data/processed/m5_weekly.csv. Four model fits, most under 30 seconds.

title: 14  Lab 12: Elasticity — What the Coefficient Means, and What It Costs to Get Wrong
text:
14.2 Setup

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
RANDOM_STATE = 42

weekly = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/m5_weekly.csv", parse_dates=["week_start"])
weekly["series"] = weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id

df = weekly.dropna(subset=["units", "avg_price"]).copy()
df = df[df.avg_price > 0]
df["ly"]    = np.log(df.units.clip(lower=1))
df["lp"]    = np.log(df.avg_price)
df["snap"]  = (df.snap_days >= 5).astype(float)
df["event"] = (df.event_days > 0).astype(float)
df["yr"]    = (df.week_start - df.week_start.min()).dt.days / 365.25

codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df.series)
df["idx"] = codes
J = len(uniq)
y = df.ly.values

print(f"{len(df):,} rows | {J} series | sd(log price) = {df.lp.std():.4f}")

With units and price both in logs, the price coefficient is an elasticity: the percent change in demand per percent change in price. Hold on to that sentence — Step 3 is about the moment it stops being true.
One model function, with switches for the three things we want to vary.

def fit(price_col, controlled=True, standardize_price=False, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    x = df[price_col].values.astype(float)
    if standardize_price:
        x = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
    with pm.Model():
        s  = pm.Exponential("sigma", 1.0)
        bp = pm.Normal("b_price", 0, 1)
        bs = pm.Normal("b_snap",  0, 1)
        be = pm.Normal("b_event", 0, 1)
        if controlled:
            a  = pm.Normal("a", y.mean(), 1, shape=J)
            bt = pm.Normal("b_trend", 0, 1)
            mu = (a[df.idx.values] + bp * x + bs * df.snap.values
                  + be * df.event.values + bt * df.yr.values)
        else:
            a  = pm.Normal("a", y.mean(), 1)
            mu = a + bp * x + bs * df.snap.values + be * df.event.values
        pm.Normal("obs", mu=mu, sigma=s, observed=y)
        return pm.sample(1000, tune=1500, chains=4, progressbar=False,
                         random_seed=seed, target_accept=0.9)

def show(idata, controlled=True, label=""):
    vs = ["b_price", "b_snap", "b_event"] + (["b_trend"] if controlled else [])
    su = az.summary(idata, var_names=vs, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94, round_to=4)
    print(label)
    print(su[["mean", "hdi94_lb", "hdi94_ub", "r_hat", "ess_bulk"]].to_string())
    return su








Walkthrough





8,310 rows | 30 series | sd(log price) = 0.2444
Both units and price are in logs, and that is what makes the price coefficient an elasticity — percent per percent. Say that sentence carefully now, because Step 3 is entirely about the moment it stops being true.
And note 0.2444, the standard deviation of log price across the whole panel. Keep it in view. In Step 3 a different, much smaller number takes its place, and the gap between them is where the damage comes from.

title: 14  Lab 12: Elasticity — What the Coefficient Means, and What It Costs to Get Wrong
text:
14.3 Step 1 — The naive elasticity
Regress log units on log price, SNAP and events. Nothing else.

idata_naive = fit("lp", controlled=False)
_ = show(idata_naive, controlled=False, label="Naive")

An elasticity near \(-2.8\): a 1% price rise costs almost 3% of volume. Diagnostics are clean, \(\hat{R}\) is 1.00, ESS is in the thousands, and the interval is tight.
It is also badly wrong, and Lecture 12’s DAG says why before any model is fitted. Our thirty series are different categories in different stores. Categories differ systematically in both typical price and typical volume — HOBBIES items cost more per unit and sell fewer of them. So series identity is an arrow into price and into units: a textbook confounder.
Comparing a hobby item to a food item is not measuring a price response. It is measuring the difference between two product categories.







Walkthrough





Log units on log price, SNAP, and events. Nothing else.
Naive
           mean  hdi94_lb  hdi94_ub   r_hat   ess_bulk
b_price -2.8046   -2.8531   -2.7522  1.0010  2296.4356
An elasticity of minus 2.8. A one percent price rise costs almost three percent of volume. That is a dramatic, highly elastic result — and it would change how a category is priced.
Look at the diagnostics. R-hat 1.001. ESS 2,296. The interval runs from −2.85 to −2.75 — a width of one tenth. This model is certain. It is also badly wrong, and the useful part is that we knew that before fitting it.
Lecture 12’s DAG says why. Our thirty series are different categories in different stores, and categories differ systematically in both typical price and typical volume — hobby items cost more per unit and sell fewer of them. So series identity is an arrow into price and an arrow into units. That is the textbook shape of a confounder.
Comparing a hobby item to a food item is not measuring a price response. It is measuring the difference between two product categories, and calling it elasticity.

title: 14  Lab 12: Elasticity — What the Coefficient Means, and What It Costs to Get Wrong
text:
14.4 Step 2 — Control for the confounder
Add per-series intercepts and a trend. Center log price within each series, so the model uses only price variation inside a series over time — which is the variation a manager could actually create.

df["lpc"] = df.lp - df.groupby("series").lp.transform("mean")

idata_ctrl = fit("lpc", controlled=True)
su_ctrl = show(idata_ctrl, label="Controlled")


b_naive = idata_naive.posterior["b_price"].values.ravel()
b_ctrl  = idata_ctrl.posterior["b_price"].values.ravel()

print(f"  naive       {b_naive.mean():+.3f}   width of 94% HDI "
      f"{np.diff(az.hdi(b_naive, prob=0.94))[0]:.3f}")
print(f"  controlled  {b_ctrl.mean():+.3f}   width of 94% HDI "
      f"{np.diff(az.hdi(b_ctrl, prob=0.94))[0]:.3f}")
print(f"  the naive estimate is {b_naive.mean()/b_ctrl.mean():.1f}x too large")







Precision is not accuracy



The naive estimate is nearly six times too large and its interval is half the width. It is not noisy. It is confidently, precisely wrong.
A tight credible interval says the model is sure. It says nothing about whether the model is answering your question — and no diagnostic in ArviZ will ever tell you that it isn’t. Only the DAG does.



# ---- your turn: uncomment and answer in the string ----
# direction = "..."   # <- the naive estimate is too NEGATIVE. Which arrow in the DAG
#                     #    makes the bias run that way rather than the other?
# print(direction)








Walkthrough





Add per-series intercepts and a trend, and center log price within each series — so the model uses only price variation inside a series over time, which is the only variation a manager could actually create.
Controlled
           mean  hdi94_lb  hdi94_ub
b_price -0.4921   -0.5949   -0.3872
  naive       -2.805   width of 94% HDI 0.100
  controlled  -0.492   width of 94% HDI 0.207
  the naive estimate is 5.7x too large
Minus 0.49 rather than minus 2.8. The naive estimate was 5.7 times too large.
Now the line that matters, and it is the second column. The naive interval is 0.100 wide. The correct one is 0.207 — twice as wide.
So the wrong model was not noisy. It was more precise than the right one, by a factor of two, while being nearly six times off. It was confidently, tightly, precisely wrong.
That is worth dwelling on, because it inverts an instinct almost everybody has. A narrow credible interval feels like a good sign. All it says is that the model is sure about the answer to the question it was actually asked — and the naive model was asked “how do hobby items differ from food items?”, which the data answers very precisely indeed.
No diagnostic in ArviZ will ever tell you the question was wrong. Only the DAG does, and the DAG is drawn before any code is written.






Try it






Answer the question in the cell: the naive estimate is too negative. Which arrow in the DAG makes the bias run that way rather than the other?

title: 14  Lab 12: Elasticity — What the Coefficient Means, and What It Costs to Get Wrong
section: 14.5 Step 3 — The preprocessing step that silently destroys the answer
text:
14.5 Step 3 — The preprocessing step that silently destroys the answer
You have standardized predictors in nearly every lab since Lecture 6. It makes Normal(0, 1) priors mean the same thing across variables, and it helps samplers. It is a good habit.
Do it to log price here and watch what happens.

idata_std = fit("lpc", controlled=True, standardize_price=True)
b_std = idata_std.posterior["b_price"].values.ravel()

print(f"  unstandardized  b_price = {b_ctrl.mean():+.4f}")
print(f"  standardized    b_price = {b_std.mean():+.4f}")
print(f"  sd(centered log price)   = {df.lpc.std():.4f}")
print(f"  ratio                   = {b_ctrl.mean()/b_std.mean():.4f}")

The two fits agree perfectly — they are the same model. But the coefficient is no longer the same quantity. Standardizing divided log price by its standard deviation, so the coefficient is now the change in log units per standard deviation of log price, not per percent.
Both diagnostics are clean. Both intervals exclude zero. Nothing anywhere reports a problem. The only thing that changed is what the number means, and the model has no way to tell you.
Now watch it become a business error.

def scenario(b, pct=5.0):
    """Percent change in units, and in revenue, from a `pct` price rise."""
    units = 100 * (np.exp(b * np.log(1 + pct/100)) - 1)
    rev   = 100 * ((1 + pct/100) * np.exp(b * np.log(1 + pct/100)) - 1)
    return units, rev

for label, b in [("correct (elasticity)", b_ctrl), ("standardized", b_std)]:
    u, r = scenario(b)
    print(f"  {label:<22s} 5% price rise -> units {u.mean():+.2f}%  "
          f"revenue {r.mean():+.2f}%")







This is the lab’s point



Read the two lines. Using the standardized coefficient, a manager is told a 5% price rise costs about a tenth of a percent of volume. The truth is more than twenty times that — because the coefficient was divided by the standard deviation of centered log price, which is only 0.0455. The revenue projection is inflated too, from \(+2.5\%\) to \(+4.9\%\).
The smaller the standard deviation you divide by, the larger the distortion. Here the within-series price variation is genuinely small, which makes the error enormous — and entirely invisible.
The model was right. The sampler was right. The diagnostics were right. The error entered through a preprocessing convenience three cells earlier, and it survived all the way to a stocking decision because nothing downstream carries units.
The habit that prevents it: write down what one unit of each variable is before you rescale it, and check that the coefficient still answers the question you asked.



# ---- your turn: uncomment and fill in ----
# print("To recover the elasticity from the standardized fit, multiply it by ___")








Walkthrough





You have standardized predictors in nearly every lab since Lecture 6. It makes Normal(0,1) priors mean the same thing across variables, it helps samplers, and it is a genuinely good habit that I am not about to tell you to abandon. Do it to log price here.
  unstandardized  b_price = -0.4921
  standardized    b_price = -0.0224
  sd(centered log price)   = 0.0455
  ratio                   = 21.9384
The two fits agree perfectly — they are the same model, and both have clean diagnostics and intervals excluding zero. But the coefficient went from −0.49 to −0.022, a factor of nearly twenty-two.
Nothing is broken. Standardizing divided log price by its standard deviation, so the coefficient is now the change in log units per standard deviation of log price rather than per percent. Same model, same fit, different unit — and the number no longer means “elasticity.”
Now look at what it was divided by. 0.0455.
Remember the setup printed 0.2444 for log price across the whole panel? This is not that number. This is the standard deviation of log price within a series, after centering — and it is five times smaller, because prices move very little inside a single store-category over time.
And here is the irony worth naming. That within-series variation is small because of the good decision we made in Step 2. Centering within series is what removed the confounding. It is also what makes the standard deviation tiny, and the smaller the number you divide by, the larger the distortion. The correct modeling choice amplified the preprocessing error.
  correct (elasticity)   5% price rise -> units -2.37%  revenue +2.51%
  standardized           5% price rise -> units -0.11%  revenue +4.89%
Read those two lines as advice given to a person.
Using the standardized coefficient, a manager is told that a 5% price rise costs about a tenth of a percent of volume — essentially free. The truth is −2.37%, more than twenty times larger. And the revenue projection nearly doubles, from +2.5% to +4.9%. That is a real decision, made from a real model, that passed every check.
The model was right. The sampler was right. The diagnostics were right. The error entered through a preprocessing convenience three cells earlier, and it survived all the way to a stocking decision because nothing downstream carries units. A float is a float. -0.0224 looks exactly as authoritative as -0.4921.






Try it






Fill in the blank: to recover the elasticity from the standardized fit, what do you multiply by?
And the habit that prevents this, which is the one line to take from the lab: write down what one unit of each variable is before you rescale it, and check that the coefficient still answers the question you asked. Keep standardizing. Just know what you are holding afterwards.

section: 14.6 Step 4 — Ask the posterior a business question
text:
14.6 Step 4 — Ask the posterior a business question
The posterior is samples, so any question is answered by counting. Use the correct fit.

print(f"  P(elasticity < 0)     = {(b_ctrl < 0).mean():.3f}")
print(f"  P(elasticity < -0.5)  = {(b_ctrl < -0.5).mean():.3f}")
print(f"  P(-0.5 < e < 0)       = {((b_ctrl > -0.5) & (b_ctrl < 0)).mean():.3f}")

The first number settles the direction: every posterior sample is negative, so demand falls when price rises. There is no doubt at all.
The second is the interesting one. Elasticity \(-0.5\) is a meaningful business threshold, and the posterior puts us within a few points of a coin flip. The data cannot settle whether demand is elastic or inelastic, and that is the honest report. A significance test would have announced the direction and said nothing about the question the manager actually asked.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.hist(b_ctrl, bins=60, color="steelblue", alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(-0.5, color="crimson", ls="--", lw=1.5, label="elastic / inelastic boundary")
ax.axvline(0, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("price elasticity"); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Now the decision the manager actually faces.

u5, r5 = scenario(b_ctrl, 5.0)
print(f"  5% price rise:  units {u5.mean():+.2f}%  "
      f"[{np.percentile(u5,3):+.2f}, {np.percentile(u5,97):+.2f}]")
print(f"                  revenue {r5.mean():+.2f}%  "
      f"[{np.percentile(r5,3):+.2f}, {np.percentile(r5,97):+.2f}]")
print(f"  P(revenue rises) = {(r5 > 0).mean():.3f}")

Revenue rises with probability 1.00 across every posterior sample — even though the elasticity might well be past \(-0.5\). Both facts are true at once, and only the posterior lets you say so.

# ---- your turn: uncomment and answer in the strings ----
# recommend = "..."   # <- two sentences to the manager, with a probability attached
# caveat    = "..."   # <- name one DAG arrow that, if wrong, invalidates this
# print(recommend); print(caveat)








Walkthrough





Back to the correct fit. The posterior is samples, so any question is answered by counting.
  P(elasticity < 0)     = 1.000
  P(elasticity < -0.5)  = 0.446
  P(-0.5 < e < 0)       = 0.554
The first line settles the direction completely. Every posterior sample is negative — demand falls when price rises, with no doubt whatsoever.
The second line is the interesting one, and it is the reason to have fitted a Bayesian model at all. Minus one half is a meaningful business boundary: past it, demand is elastic and a price rise loses revenue. The posterior puts us at 0.446 — within a few points of a coin flip.
So the honest report is: the data cannot settle whether demand is elastic or inelastic. Not “it is inelastic.” Not “the effect is significant.” A significance test here would have announced the direction — which was never in question — and said nothing at all about the boundary the manager actually cares about.
  5% price rise:  units -2.37%  [-2.86, -1.87]
                  revenue +2.51%  [+2.00, +3.04]
  P(revenue rises) = 1.000
And now the resolution, which is the most useful thing in the lab.
Revenue rises with probability 1.000 — across every posterior sample — even though the elasticity may well be past −0.5. Both of those are true at once. The threshold question is genuinely unresolved; the decision question is not.
Only a posterior lets you say both. A point estimate forces you to pick one number and then argue about which side of the line it falls on. The distribution lets you answer the question that was actually asked — should we raise the price? — with a probability attached, while being honest that a different question remains open.






Try it






Write the two strings: your two-sentence recommendation to the manager with a probability attached, and one DAG arrow that, if wrong, invalidates it.

text:
14.7 Before you leave

Discuss (the three failures): This lab produced a wrong elasticity three ways — an omitted confounder, a rescaled coefficient, and a threshold question the data cannot answer. Which of the three would any ArviZ diagnostic have caught? What does your answer imply about what diagnostics are for?
Discuss (the habit): Standardizing is genuinely good practice and you should keep doing it. State the rule that lets you keep the habit without repeating Step 3’s error.
Discuss (the decision): You must advise on the 5% rise using only Step 4’s output. Write the recommendation. Then say what you would want measured before a 20% rise, and why extrapolating this elasticity that far is a different kind of claim.
Discuss (the course): You have now estimated the same kind of quantity with OLS, XGBoost, and a Bayesian regression. Only one of them naturally answers “how likely is it that revenue rises?” Explain what about the Bayesian output makes that question cheap, and name one forecasting task from this course where you would still not reach for it.


Solutions posted to Canvas after class.






Walkthrough











Try it






Four questions, and the last one closes the course.
The three failures. You produced a wrong elasticity three ways — an omitted confounder, a rescaled coefficient, and a threshold the data cannot resolve. Which would any ArviZ diagnostic have caught?
that the computation did what the code said. Everything about whether the code said the right thing is yours.*
The habit. Standardizing is good practice and you should keep doing it. State the rule that lets you keep the habit without repeating Step 3.
The decision. Advise on the 5% rise using only Step 4’s output. Then say what you would want measured before a 20% rise — and why extrapolating this elasticity that far is a different kind of claim.
that actually occurred within series, and the standard deviation of that is 0.0455 — a few percent. A 20% move is far outside the range the data has ever seen. That is extrapolation, not estimation, and it is the same limit you met in Lab 4 when a tree could not predict beyond its training range.*
The course. You have now estimated this kind of quantity with OLS, with XGBoost, and with a Bayesian regression. Only one of them naturally answers “how likely is it that revenue rises?” Explain what about the Bayesian output makes that question cheap — and name one forecasting task from this course where you would still not reach for it.
And that is the last lab. Fifteen weeks, one dataset, a dozen model families, and a scoreboard that ends with a 46-coefficient linear model at the top.
The through-line was never which method wins. It was that every one of these models will return a confident number whether or not it deserves one — a tree that cannot extrapolate, a network whose result moves 230 RMSE with the seed, a forecast interval that is honest and useless, a hierarchy pooling series that never belonged together, and today a coefficient that stopped being an elasticity three cells before anybody read it.
None of those announced themselves. Every one of them was caught by holding something out and checking. That habit is the course. Solutions go up on Canvas after the deadline. See you in Week 16 for the synthesis.

text:
18.1 Initial Prompt for Your AI Assistant
Paste the block below as the very first message in your assistant session before sending any questions. This sets the context that all subsequent prompts build on and does not count against your prompt budget.
I am working on Homework 1, Part 1 for ECON 8310: Business Forecasting at the University of Nebraska at Omaha.

Dataset: M5 / Walmart weekly sales, prepared at `data/processed/m5_weekly.csv`. Columns: store_id (10 Walmart stores across CA, TX, WI), cat_id (FOODS, HOBBIES, HOUSEHOLD), state_id, week_start, units, avg_price, snap_days, event_days, and lag features (units_lag1 through units_lag52). There are 30 store-category series, each with 277 weekly observations covering January 2011 to May 2016.

Part 1 covers exponential smoothing only (SES, Holt, Holt-Winters) using Python and statsmodels, on the CA_1 FOODS series. ARIMA and VAR come in Part 2 — do not introduce them here. I will ask you questions one at a time. For each:
1. Write clean, well-commented Python code that runs end-to-end

19.2 Q2 — Exponential Smoothing Models
(Suggested prompts: 2)
Hold out the final 52 weeks as a test set. Fit the three models below on the training portion, forecast across the test period, and compute RMSE and MAE for each.

Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES)
Holt’s linear trend model
Holt-Winters (additive seasonality, period = 52)

Also compute the same two metrics for a seasonal naive benchmark — this week last year — so you can tell whether any of the three models is earning its complexity. Present all four rows in one summary table.






Why a 52-week test set works here



Holt-Winters must estimate a seasonal index for each of the 52 weeks in a year, and it needs at least two complete cycles — \(2m = 104\) observations — before it can initialize them. This is the \(2m\) rule from Lecture 1.
Each series has 277 weeks. Holding out 52 still leaves 225 for training, comfortably above the threshold, and a one-year holdout is the horizon a demand planner actually cares about. The assertion below makes the constraint explicit rather than letting it fail deep inside statsmodels.



N_TEST = 52                                   # final year held out
train, test = ca1.iloc[:-N_TEST], ca1.iloc[-N_TEST:]

SEASONAL_PERIOD = 52
assert len(train) >= 2 * SEASONAL_PERIOD, (
    f"Training set has {len(train)} weeks but Holt-Winters with period "
    f"{SEASONAL_PERIOD} needs at least {2 * SEASONAL_PERIOD}. "
    f"Reduce N_TEST."
)
print(f"train: {len(train)} weeks   test: {len(test)} weeks")

# Fit SES, Holt, and Holt-Winters; add a seasonal naive benchmark;
# compute RMSE and MAE for all four


Your response: Which model performs best, and does it beat the seasonal naive benchmark? This series trends upward over the sample — explain what that implies for SES specifically, given that SES produces a flat forecast. Then interpret the estimated \(\alpha\): what does its value say about how quickly CA_1 food sales respond to recent weeks, and what would you tell a demand planner who wanted to know how much weight the model puts on last week?

title: 17  Homework 2: Generalized Additive Models
text:
18 Overview
Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) extend linear regression by replacing straight-line effects with flexible smooth functions — one per predictor — that are then added together to produce a forecast. This structure preserves interpretability (you can inspect each component individually) while capturing nonlinear patterns that fixed-slope models miss. Prophet, developed at Meta, applies exactly this idea to time series by decomposing a signal into trend, seasonality, and user-defined regressor effects. This assignment applies both Prophet and pyGAM to daily Walmart sales and benchmarks them against a seasonal-naive baseline and against your ARIMA/ETS results from Homework 1.
Learning objectives. By the end of this assignment you will be able to:

Why SNAP is the interesting one



SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits are disbursed on fixed calendar days that vary by state. California’s schedule puts them on roughly the first ten days of each month. This is a known, published, future-dated schedule — you always know next year’s SNAP days in advance. That is what makes it usable as a forecasting regressor, and it is the property you should look for when someone proposes a predictor.

(Suggested prompts: 2)
pyGAM fits an additive model directly on a feature matrix rather than on a time index, which makes it easy to include calendar-derived features and binary indicators side by side. Term
Predictor
Type
Purpose




s(0, basis="cp")
day_of_year (1–366)
Cyclic spline
Annual cycle, with Dec 31 joined to Jan 1


f(1)
day_of_week (0–6)
Factor
Within-week pattern


l(2)
snap
Linear
SNAP benefit-day lift


l(3)
is_event
Linear
Calendar event effect



Two of those choices are deliberate and you should be able to defend them. basis="cp" makes the spline cyclic, so the fitted curve meets itself at the year boundary instead of being free to jump between December 31 and January 1. And f(1) rather than s(1): day of week takes seven discrete values with no meaningful “between,” so a factor term is the honest choice — a smooth spline would interpolate a fractional Wednesday-and-a-half.

title: 18  Homework 3: Decision Trees and Random Forests
text:
19 Overview
This homework shifts from time series methods to machine learning approaches for forecasting. Decision trees and random forests reframe the problem as supervised learning: rather than modeling a single series through time, each store-category-week row becomes an independent training example, and lagged unit sales carry the temporal information that would otherwise live inside a model like ARIMA or ETS. These methods require no stationarity assumptions and discover nonlinear interactions automatically — for example, the effect of a SNAP benefit week may differ sharply between food and hobby categories, and a tree will split on both features without any manual interaction term.

text:
22.3 Q3 — Random Forest
(Suggested prompts: 2)
A Random Forest grows many decision trees on bootstrap samples of the data and averages their predictions. By training each tree on a different random subset of rows — and considering only a random subset of features at each split — the ensemble reduces the variance that makes individual deep trees unreliable. One by-product of bootstrap sampling is that roughly one-third of the training rows are left out of each tree: these out-of-bag (OOB) samples can be used to produce an internal validation score without touching the held-out test set.

(b) Report the test RMSE. Compare it to the depth-3 and depth-10 Decision Trees from Q2, and to the seasonal-naive benchmark from Q1.
(c) Plot the MDI feature importances as a horizontal bar chart, sorted descending, showing all features.

(Suggested prompts: 2)
MDI importance measures how much each feature reduces impurity across all trees in the forest. It is fast to compute because it is a by-product of training, but it has a known bias: features with many distinct numeric values tend to receive inflated importance scores simply because they offer the splitter more places to cut, not because they carry more information.
Permutation importance avoids this bias by directly measuring how much accuracy degrades when a single feature’s values are randomly shuffled on the test set. A feature that matters will cause a large increase in RMSE when shuffled; a redundant or spurious one will cause almost none.
(a) Plant two controls. Add two columns of pure noise to the modeling table — one continuous, one binary — and refit the forest with them included:

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
df["noise_continuous"] = rng.rand(len(df))          # uniform on [0, 1)
df["noise_binary"] = rng.randint(0, 2, len(df))     # 0 or 1

FEATURES_WITH_NOISE = FEATURES + ["noise_continuous", "noise_binary"]

# Refit the Random Forest (same settings as Q3) using FEATURES_WITH_NOISE

Neither column carries any information about units — you generated them from a random number generator. Any importance either one receives is an artifact of the method, not a finding.

(c) Build a comparison table for the two noise columns and three real features of your choice, showing MDI and permutation importance side by side. Then report where noise_continuous ranks by MDI out of all features, and where noise_binary ranks.
(d) Produce the side-by-side bar charts: top-10 features by MDI, and top-10 by permutation importance, in one figure.

# (c) comparison table for noise_continuous, noise_binary, and three real features
#     plus the MDI rank of each noise column

title: 19  Homework 4: Boosted Trees and Regularization
text:
19.1 Overview
Boosting builds trees sequentially — each new tree corrects the errors left by the previous ones. XGBoost is the dominant gradient boosting implementation for tabular data, and it often outperforms Random Forests given proper tuning. Regularized linear models (LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net) take a different approach: they shrink coefficients toward zero, performing automatic feature selection while keeping the model interpretable.
This homework applies both families to the same M5/Walmart data as Homework 3 — but with a deliberately richer feature set — and ends with a head-to-head comparison across every method tried in the course so far.

title: 19  Homework 4: Boosted Trees and Regularization
text:
19.2 Dataset and Setup
We use the same weekly M5 data and the same temporal split as Homework 3 — but we engineer many more features first, and the reason matters.
In Homework 3 you had 27 features and 5,160 training rows. With \(k\) that much smaller than \(n\), there is very little for a shrinkage penalty to do: ordinary least squares is already stable, and Ridge or LASSO will select almost no penalty. Regularization earns its keep when \(k\) is large relative to \(n\), which is exactly the situation Lecture 6 opened with.
So we build the feature set a working analyst would actually build — ten lags, rolling means and standard deviations at four windows, Fourier terms for the annual cycle, calendar variables, and one-hot identity columns — and let the penalty decide which survive.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge, ElasticNet, ElasticNetCV, RidgeCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))

# --- feature engineering, per store-category series ---------------------------
g = weekly.groupby(["store_id", "cat_id"])["units"]

for L in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 13, 26, 52):        # ten lags
    weekly[f"lag{L}"] = g.shift(L)

for W in (4, 13, 26, 52):                           # rolling stats, shifted to avoid leakage
    weekly[f"roll{W}_mean"] = g.shift(1).rolling(W).mean().values
    weekly[f"roll{W}_std"]  = g.shift(1).rolling(W).std().values

weekly["month"] = weekly["week_start"].dt.month
weekly["week_of_year"] = weekly["week_start"].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)
weekly["year"] = weekly["week_start"].dt.year

for k in (1, 2, 3):                                 # Fourier terms for the annual cycle
    weekly[f"sin{k}"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * weekly.week_of_year / 52)
    weekly[f"cos{k}"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * weekly.week_of_year / 52)

df_enc = pd.get_dummies(weekly, columns=["store_id", "cat_id", "state_id"],
                        prefix=["store", "cat", "state"])

FEATURES = ([c for c in df_enc.columns
             if c.startswith(("lag", "roll", "sin", "cos", "store_", "cat_", "state_"))]
            + ["avg_price", "snap_days", "event_days", "month", "week_of_year", "year"])
TARGET = "units"

LAGGED = [c for c in FEATURES if c.startswith(("lag", "roll"))]
df = df_enc.dropna(subset=LAGGED).copy()

cutoff = pd.Timestamp("2015-05-17")          # same split as Homework 3
train = df[df["week_start"] < cutoff]
test  = df[df["week_start"] >= cutoff]

X_train, y_train = train[FEATURES].values.astype(float), train[TARGET].values
X_test,  y_test  = test[FEATURES].values.astype(float),  test[TARGET].values

print(f"k = {len(FEATURES)} features | train {len(X_train):,} rows | test {len(X_test):,} rows")







Note the .shift(1) on the rolling features



g.shift(1).rolling(W) computes each rolling statistic from data strictly before the current week. Drop the .shift(1) and the window includes the current week’s own units — the target leaking into its own predictor. Your CV error would improve and your forecast would fail. This is the same leakage failure as random k-fold, wearing different clothes.


Compute the seasonal-naive benchmark (predict units with lag52) on the test set before going further. Every model below is measured against it.

Standardize the features using StandardScaler (LASSO is sensitive to feature scale). Fit LASSO at 30 values of alpha spaced logarithmically from 1 to 10,000. Plot the regularization path: coefficient values on the y-axis, log₁₀(alpha) on the x-axis, one line per feature labeled by name.

X_test_scaled  = scaler.transform(X_test)

# Fit LASSO at each alpha and collect coefficients

Alongside the coefficient path, plot non-zero count against log₁₀(alpha). That second plot is often the more useful one in practice: it tells you how much model you are buying at each level of penalty.

Your response: Which features are the last three standing as alpha increases? Report the ordering in which features drop out, not just the final survivors — Lecture 6 argued that this ordering is a more stable finding than any single coefficient table, and this is where you check whether that holds. Does the ordering match what XGBoost’s gain importance told you in Q1?




19.4.4 Q4 — Elastic Net vs LASSO vs Ridge (Suggested prompts: 2)
Lecture 6 gave two knobs: \(\lambda\) sets the total penalty, \(\alpha\) (sklearn’s l1_ratio) sets the mix. This question separates them properly.






Do not fix alpha across all five models



It is tempting to fit Lasso(alpha=100), ElasticNet(alpha=100, ...), and Ridge(alpha=100) and call that a fair comparison. It is not, for two separate reasons.
First, sklearn scales the two objectives differently. Lasso and ElasticNet minimize \(\frac{1}{2n}\|y - Xw\|^2 + \ldots\), while Ridge minimizes \(\|y - Xw\|^2 + \alpha\|w\|^2\) with no \(1/2n\) factor. With \(n \approx 5{,}000\) training rows, the same numeric alpha means penalties that differ by roughly four orders of magnitude.
Second, even within one family, the right total penalty depends on the mix — an \(\ell_2\)-heavy model needs a different \(\lambda\) than an \(\ell_1\)-heavy one to be equally regularized.
So tune \(\lambda\) separately for every mix, exactly as Lecture 6’s code slide does.

title: 20  Homework 5: Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
20.2 Dataset and Setup
We construct fixed-length sliding windows over each store-category series. Each input is a window of past weeks; the target is the next week’s units. Part A (FFN, CNN) uses a 26-week window; Part B (RNN, LSTM, Transformer) uses 52 weeks, so the sequence models get a full annual cycle.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42
torch.manual_seed(RANDOM_STATE)
np.random.seed(RANDOM_STATE)

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))
weekly["series"] = weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id

# The four channels every window carries through time
CHANNELS = ["units", "snap_days", "event_days", "avg_price"]

CUTOFF = pd.Timestamp("2015-05-17")     # same split as Homework 3 and 4

print(f"{weekly.series.nunique()} series | "
      f"{weekly.week_start.min().date()} to {weekly.week_start.max().date()} | "
      f"{len(weekly):,} rows")

Building the windows. For each series, slide a window of length W along the history: the window is the input, the units in week W+1 is the target. A window belongs to the training set if its target week falls before the cutoff.






Two mistakes that will not raise an error



Do not shuffle. DataLoader(..., shuffle=False) for every model here. Shuffling destroys the ordering the sequence models exist to exploit, and it will not warn you.
Standardize using training statistics only. Compute the mean and standard deviation on the training windows, then apply them to the test windows. Computing them over the full dataset leaks the test period into training — the same error as scaling outside a CV fold in Homework 4.

24.4 Part C: Pooling Across Series
The quantity of interest: the effect of a high-SNAP week on log units, store by store.

24.4.1 Q1 — What Are You Allowed to Pool? (Suggested prompts: 1)
A hierarchy says the groups are exchangeable: before seeing the data, you have no reason to expect one to differ from another in a particular direction. That is an assumption about the world, and nothing in PyMC will check it for you.
Before fitting anything, compute the raw high-SNAP effect — the difference in mean log units between high-SNAP weeks and the rest — for every one of the thirty series, and summarize it by category.

# Raw effect per series; mean and spread within each category


Your response: Report the three category means. SNAP is a food assistance program — does the table agree? State which set of series you are willing to treat as exchangeable and why, and name the specific wrong answer you would get by pooling all thirty.







This question decides the rest of the assignment



Get it wrong and every model below will fit cleanly, pass every diagnostic, and give you a confidently wrong number. The lab shows exactly that happening.





24.4.2 Q2 — Three Models (Suggested prompts: 3)
Work from here on with the series you defended in Q1. Build the information imbalance that partial pooling exists to handle: thin every other series down to 8 weeks, and keep the weeks you removed — you will need them in Q4.

foods = weekly[weekly.cat_id == "FOODS"].dropna(subset=["units"]).copy()
codes, uniq = pd.factorize(foods.series)
foods["idx"] = codes
J = len(uniq)

rng = np.random.RandomState(RANDOM_STATE)
keep = []
for j in range(J):
    rows = foods.index[foods.idx == j].tolist()
    n = 8 if j % 2 == 0 else len(rows)
    keep += list(rng.choice(rows, size=min(n, len(rows)), replace=False))

train = foods.loc[sorted(keep)].copy()      # what the models see
heldout = foods.drop(index=keep).copy()     # the grader for Q4
thin = np.array([j % 2 == 0 for j in range(J)])

print(f"{J} series, {thin.sum()} thinned to 8 weeks | "
      f"train {len(train):,} rows, held-out {len(heldout):,} rows")

Fit all three on train:

Pooled — one b shared by every series
Unpooled — b with shape=J, each estimated independently
Hierarchical — b_j ~ Normal(mu_b, sd_b), written non-centered

Each also needs a per-series intercept a with shape=J.

# Fit pooled, unpooled and hierarchical







The centered form will fail, and that is the lesson



Writing the hierarchy as pm.Normal("b", mu_b, sd_b, shape=J) produces divergences — a few dozen at target_accept=0.9. Fit it that way first, record the count, then switch to the non-centered form and record it again. Report both; your exact count will differ from mine.

Explain why that is the behavior you want, rather than a sign the model is inconsistent.

You thinned those series yourself, so the removed weeks are sitting in heldout. For each thin series compute the high-SNAP effect that actually occurred in its held-out weeks, and compare it against both estimates.

What kind of error can this held-out check catch that those three cannot — and what does that imply about shipping a model on diagnostics alone?

title: 25  Homework 7: Bayesian Linear Regression
text:
25.1 Overview
Bayesian linear regression replaces OLS point estimates with full posterior distributions over every coefficient. Instead of asking “Is beta significant at p < 0.05?”, you ask “What is the probability that this effect is positive?” and “Is the effect large enough to matter for business decisions?”
This final homework fits a Bayesian regression model for store sales as a function of promotions, competition, and store characteristics. It also introduces Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as a tool for deciding which variables to include and how to interpret the coefficients causally.
Learning objectives:

title: 25  Homework 7: Bayesian Linear Regression
text:
Draw and interpret a DAG for a business forecasting model
Specify weakly informative priors for regression coefficients
Read posterior coefficient distributions (HDI, probability of direction)
Apply ROPE analysis to distinguish statistical from practical significance
Use posterior samples to simulate conditional scenarios

title: 25  Homework 7: Bayesian Linear Regression
text:
25.2 Dataset and Setup
The question for this assignment is a causal one: how much does demand respond to price? That is an elasticity, and it is the number a category manager would actually act on.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
import statsmodels.api as sm
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
logging.getLogger('pymc').setLevel(logging.ERROR)

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_m5.py` from the repository root first."
    )

RANDOM_STATE = 42

weekly = (pd.read_csv(data_path("m5_weekly.csv"), parse_dates=["week_start"])
            .sort_values(["store_id", "cat_id", "week_start"]))
weekly["series"] = weekly.store_id + "_" + weekly.cat_id

df = weekly.dropna(subset=["units", "avg_price"]).copy()
df["ly"] = np.log(df.units.clip(lower=1))          # log units
df["lp"] = np.log(df.avg_price)                     # log price
df["t"]  = (df.week_start - df.week_start.min()).dt.days / 365.25
df["snap"]  = (df.snap_days >= 5).astype(float)     # high-SNAP week
df["event"] = (df.event_days > 0).astype(float)     # any event that week
codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df.series)
df["idx"] = codes
J = len(uniq)

# Center log price within series. NOT standardized -- see the note below.
df["lpc"] = df.lp - df.groupby("series").lp.transform("mean")

print(f"{len(df):,} rows | {J} series | "
      f"price range {df.avg_price.min():.2f}-{df.avg_price.max():.2f}")

Why logs on both sides. With ly and lp both logged, the price coefficient is an elasticity: the percentage change in units for a one percent change in price. That is directly interpretable, and it is what makes the scenario analysis in Q6 possible.






Do not standardize log price



It is a common reflex, and here it is a trap. Dividing lp by its standard deviation rescales the coefficient into “per standard deviation of log price” — which is no longer an elasticity, and every percentage claim you build on it in Q6 will be wrong by the factor you divided by. Leave lp in log units. Every predictor in this assignment is already on a scale a manager reads directly: log price in percent, snap and event as 0/1, t in years.
Centering within series (lpc) is different and is fine — it shifts the variable without rescaling it, leaves the elasticity untouched, and greatly improves sampling, because price levels differ across series and otherwise correlate with the intercepts.

text:
25.4 Questions

25.4.1 Q1 — Draw a DAG (Suggested prompts: 1)
Before fitting anything, think about the causal structure. This question determines what the rest of the assignment means, so do it first and do it honestly.
Draw a DAG for weekly demand including at least: units, avg_price, series (which store-category this is), time (trend), snap_days, and event_days.
No code needed — a Markdown table or ASCII diagram is fine. Justify every arrow in one sentence.
series  → avg_price   (categories differ systematically in price level)
series  → units       (categories differ systematically in volume)
time    → avg_price   (prices drift over five years)
time    → units       (demand grows over the sample)
avg_price → units     (the effect we want to estimate)
...
Then answer the question this exists to answer: is there a confounder between avg_price and units? Name it, explain the mechanism in business terms, and state what you must do about it in the regression.

Your response:




25.4.2 Q2 — OLS Benchmark, Two Ways (Suggested prompts: 2)
Fit two OLS regressions with statsmodels, and note that the difference between them is the whole point of Q1.
(a) Naive — regress ly on lp, snap, event.
(b) Controlled — regress ly on lpc, snap, event, plus a trend (t) and series fixed effects (pd.get_dummies(df.series)).
Report the coefficient table for each, and put the two price elasticities side by side.

# (a) naive OLS
# (b) OLS with trend and series fixed effects
# Compare the two price coefficients


Your response: Report both elasticities. They will differ substantially. Using your DAG from Q1, explain which one estimates the quantity you actually want, and why the other is biased in the direction it is.
Then look at the standard errors: the naive estimate is not merely different, it is at least as precise. Explain why precision is no defense here.




25.4.3 Q3 — Bayesian Linear Regression (Suggested prompts: 3)
Fit the controlled specification from Q2(b) as a Bayesian model — price, SNAP, events, trend, and a per-series intercept. Use weakly informative priors:

beta_j ~ Normal(0, 1) for each predictor (weakly informative on these scales)
alpha ~ Normal(0, 1) for the intercept
sigma ~ HalfNormal(1) for observation noise

Give the per-series intercepts a hierarchical prior, written non-centered, as in Homework 6.
Sample with pm.sample(1000, tune=1500, chains=4, target_accept=0.9) and report the posterior mean, sd and 94% HDI for each coefficient — plus \(\hat{R}\), ESS and divergences.






Ask ArviZ for the HDI explicitly



az.summary(idata) reports an 89% equal-tailed interval by default, not the HDI. For the highest-density interval this course uses, call az.summary(idata, ci_kind="hdi", ci_prob=0.94), or az.hdi(samples, prob=0.94) on raw draws.
An equal-tailed interval cuts 5.5% off each tail; an HDI is the shortest interval holding 94% of the mass. They coincide for a symmetric posterior and diverge for a skewed one.



# Build and sample Bayesian linear regression


Your response: Compare the posterior means to the controlled OLS coefficients from Q2(b). With this much data they should agree closely — say whether they do, and explain why agreement is the expected result rather than a disappointing one.
Then: what does a wide HDI tell you that a narrow one does not, and which coefficient here has the widest relative to its mean?




25.4.4 Q4 — Posterior Visualization (Suggested prompts: 2)
Plot the posterior distributions for the three coefficients that matter most for a business decision — justify the choice from your DAG.
For each, report: - Posterior mean - 94% HDI - P(beta > 0) — probability the effect is positive - Whether the HDI excludes zero (the Bayesian analog of significance)

# Plot posterior distributions and compute P(beta > 0)


Your response: For the price coefficient, report \(P(\beta_{\text{price}} < 0)\) — the probability that raising price reduces demand. Contrast that statement with what the OLS p-value in Q2 actually claims, and say which one you could put in front of a manager without having to correct it afterwards.




25.4.5 Q5 — ROPE Analysis (Suggested prompts: 2)
“Credible” and “big enough to act on” are different questions. A ROPE — region of practical equivalence — makes the second one explicit.
For each predictor, compute the fraction of posterior mass inside |beta| < 0.05. Because nothing here is standardized, that threshold reads directly: for price, an elasticity between \(-0.05\) and \(0.05\) means a 1% price change moves units by less than 0.05% — no one would act on it. For snap and event it means a weekly lift under 5%.
Present results in a table:










Predictor
Posterior Mean
94% HDI
% in ROPE
Practically significant?





A predictor is “practically significant” if less than 5% of its posterior falls in the ROPE.

# Compute % of posterior in ROPE for each predictor


Your response: Name any predictor that is credible but negligible — HDI excluding zero while most of its posterior sits inside the ROPE. That combination is common in large samples and is exactly what a p-value cannot express.
What should a manager do with such a finding, and what would have to change for it to become worth acting on?




25.4.6 Q6 — Conditional Scenario Simulation (Suggested prompts: 3)
A category manager is considering a 5% price increase across the board and wants to know what happens to volume — and how confident anyone can be about it.
Push the scenario through your posterior rather than through a point estimate.

# b = idata.posterior["b_price"].values.ravel()
# pct_change = 100 * (np.exp(b * np.log(1.05)) - 1)
# report the mean and the 94% interval of pct_change

(a) Report the mean percentage change in units and its 94% interval.
(b) Revenue rises if the percentage volume loss is smaller than the 5% price gain. Compute the probability that revenue increases, directly from the posterior samples.
(c) Repeat using the naive elasticity from Q2(a). Report how the recommendation changes.

Your response: Give the manager a two-sentence recommendation with a probability attached. Then state the caveat honestly: this is a causal claim about intervening on price, and it is only as good as the DAG in Q1. Name one arrow that, if wrong, would invalidate the answer.




25.4.7 Q7 — Course Capstone Reflection (Suggested prompts: 0 — write yourself)
